  • An action that installs into a host declares the capability hostExtend.

A conformance check holds these rules. A skill or mod names its payload and declares installs and hostExtend, and a digest matches the local copy. A local skill's tool grants and invocation are declared exactly as the skill sets them. A skill the model may load with shell, write, network or MCP tools pre-approved names a guardrail. A mod hook that rewrites or answers is high risk, fully audited and human-approved. A persistent install at user or machine scope is human-approved and names its uninstall step. Hooks and MCP servers declare processSpawn.

triggers

Keywords or intent patterns that signal this cog should be invoked by a routing layer or skill dispatcher. Declares the vocabulary a dispatching agent should match against user prompts when deciding which action-cog to call.

triggers is distinct from tags: tags exists for search and document filtering; triggers exists for dispatch, telling a runtime which cog handles a given intent. An action-cog may have tags: [audit, web] (for search) and triggers: [audit, web-audit, site, scan] (for dispatch). The two coexist and serve different jobs.

Only meaningful on action cogs and routing cogs. On info-docs, the field is silently ignored.

mx:
  contentType: action-doc
  actionType: scripted
  triggers: [audit, web-audit, site, scan, accessibility, wcag, report]
  tags: [audit, web-audit, website, accessibility, wcag, performance]

code

Source code embedded in the cog. Unlike fenced blocks in the prose (which are for display), a code block in the YAML is machine-addressable: a reader can extract and execute it.

blocks:
  - code:
      language: javascript
      purpose: "Validation logic for pricing fields"
      content: |
        function validatePrice(price) {
          return price > 0 && price < 1000000;
        }

html

HTML content that may reference emerging standards like WebMCP for embedded routines. An HTML block can carry interactive widgets, forms, or visualisations. An HTML block using WebMCP can access all other blocks in the cog: reading essence content, querying code blocks, rendering provenance. This access is governed by the cog's security block and the reader's SOP policy.

security

Declares the trust and execution policy for the cog. Readers consult the security block to determine whether they are willing to execute action blocks or render HTML blocks.

blocks:
  - security:
      attestation: required
      execution: sandboxed
      policy: "Refuse to execute unattested action blocks. HTML blocks render in sandbox only."

Readers may refuse to execute unattested cogs. This is reader agency. The security block is the cog's statement of what it expects, and the reader decides whether to comply.

The block also holds three task properties. A reader weighs them before deciding whether to run the cog at all: riskLevel (the stakes: low, medium, high, critical), reversibility (whether an error can be undone before harm: reversible, correctable, irreversible), and verifiability (whether a qualified person can inspect the output and recognise failure: inspectable, sampled, opaque). Delegation can rise when outputs are inspectable, errors are recoverable, and stakes are bounded. An irreversible action at high or critical risk belongs behind a guardrail gate. guardrail names that gate (human-approval, dry-run-first, allowed-roles, sandboxed), and policy holds any detail the enum cannot. A conformance check holds action cogs to this. At high or critical risk the pair is declared, and an irreversible action names a backed guardrail.

Two members back the guardrail and the reversibility the action declares. dryRunAction names the execute action that rehearses this one with no effect, so guardrail: dry-run-first points at something a reader can run, as allowedRoles backs allowed-roles. recovery states how an error is corrected, as a few written steps or the id of an execute action, because reversibility: correctable promises a stated recovery procedure; for a skill or mod payload it names the uninstall step.

capabilities declares what the executable content touches, from a closed vocabulary modelled on the Android permission taxonomy: processSpawn, credentialRead, networkEgress, filesystemWrite, telemetryEmit, terminalControl, destructive. An explicit empty list declares none; an absent field declares nothing. A verifier checks the declaration against the artefact's own code (Declare, Verify, Enforce), and the open block carries it to the machine that reads the published page. automationConsent says what a machine may do with the artefact on its own: act autonomously (allowed), read and recommend while a human decides (advisory-only), or not act (forbidden).

Each member of the security block has an owaspLlmRisks list in the dictionary. It names the risks from the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) that the member speaks to, by code (LLM06 for Excessive Agency, for example). The block's owaspLlmRiskNames catalogue names each code. The list records that a declaration is relevant to a risk and never claims it mitigates one. The audit suite reads it from the dictionary when it reports the risks to which a site's action declarations speak.

mx:
  security:
    riskLevel: high
    reversibility: irreversible
    verifiability: inspectable
    guardrail: dry-run-first
    dryRunAction: purge-preview
    recovery: "Re-run the publish from the last good commit; the cache refills on the next request."
    capabilities: [networkEgress, credentialRead]
    automationConsent: advisory-only
    scope:
      filesystem: [mx-outputs/**]
      network: external
Named security profiles

Most actions fall into a few familiar shapes of risk, so the dictionary declares a small set of named security profiles in securityProfiles. A cog names one instead of writing the block out:

Profile Members
read-only riskLevel: low, reversibility: reversible, verifiability: inspectable, scope.network: none, scope.allowedOperations: [read]
local-write riskLevel: medium, reversibility: reversible, verifiability: inspectable, scope.network: none, scope.allowedOperations: [read, write, create]
external-send riskLevel: high, reversibility: irreversible, verifiability: inspectable, guardrail: human-approval, scope.network: external, audit.logLevel: full
destructive riskLevel: critical, reversibility: irreversible, verifiability: inspectable, guardrail: human-approval, execution: sandboxed, scope.allowedOperations: [read, write, create, delete], audit.logLevel: full

The string is shorthand for the object form, which can also add or override members:

mx:
  security: local-write
mx:
  security:
    profile: local-write
    riskLevel: high
    verifiability: sampled
    scope:
      filesystem: [mx-outputs/pdf/**]

A reader resolves the named profile first, then applies the inline members on top. An inline member may only tighten the profile, never loosen it. Each member's tighten key in the dictionary says which direction is tighter: first or last (an earlier or later entry in validValues), lower (a smaller number), subset (the profile's list must hold every inline value) or superset (the reverse). A member with no tighten key may be added where the profile leaves it unset, and must equal the profile's value where it is set. Raising riskLevel over local-write is allowed; widening scope.network from none to external over read-only is not. A name the dictionary does not hold is an error, never an empty block. The conformance check runs its two rules on the resolved block.

sop

Standard Operating Procedures injected at read-time by MX implementations. The SOP block is virtual; it does not exist in the cog file on disk. When an MX implementation reads a cog, it merges the relevant SOP block from its uber doc into the cog at read-time. The file stays clean. The procedures are always current.

provenance

Records the origin and lineage of the cog's content: where it came from, how it was derived, what transformations were applied.

blocks:
  - provenance:
      origin: "https://example.com/product-specs"
      derivedFrom: "product-catalog-v3.cog.md"
      method: "Extracted and restructured from HTML source"
      date: 2026-02-13

version

Changelog and version history within the cog itself. Complements the version field in base frontmatter with detailed history.

blocks:
  - version:
      history:
        - version: "2.0"
          date: 2026-02-13
          changes: "Block architecture introduced. Single cog type."
        - version: "1.0"
          date: 2026-02-08
          changes: "Initial specification."

mcpServer

Experimental. Pins one Model Context Protocol server: its identity, SHA-256 digests of the lists it serves, what it may return and where it may send data, and its registry status and expiry. Unlike the blocks above, it is written as a field in the mx: block rather than an entry in blocks, the way security is. The members, the pre-connection check and an example are in 22.AN.

Reader agency

A reader of a cog is not obligated to process every block:

  1. Ignore blocks. A reader may skip any block type it does not understand or does not need. An HTML-unaware reader ignores HTML blocks. The prose block is always readable.

  2. Mixin blocks. A reader may inject its own blocks before reading the cog, either prepending (adding before the cog's blocks) or substituting (replacing a block of the same type).

  3. Refuse execution. A reader may refuse to execute action blocks from unsigned cogs, following its security block or SOP policy. The cog remains readable as documentation even when execution is refused.

Reader agency means cogs degrade gracefully. A minimal reader that only understands prose blocks can still read every cog. A full MX implementation processes all block types. Everything in between works too.

12. Carrier formats

MX follows the embrace-and-extend model. Every file type has established conventions for metadata. MX does not replace them; it recognises existing structures as native blocks and adds an MX identity layer on top.

The carrierFormats array in the YAML above defines every carrier with its metadata location, MX identity mechanism, and parsing section reference. This section provides the full parsing rules and examples.

The embrace-and-extend principle

A JavaScript file already has JSDoc tags. MX recognises @description as the prose block. The @param/@returns tags become the definition block. An HTML file already has <meta> tags. MX recognises <meta name="description"> as a prose excerpt and Schema.org JSON-LD as a definition block. MX never duplicates what the file already says.

The MX identity layer adds governance and discoverability (name, version, purpose, audience, category) using the native comment or metadata convention of each file type.

Backward compatibility: .cog.html is valid HTML. .cog.js is valid JavaScript. .cog.css is valid CSS. Adding MX metadata does not break the file for tools that do not understand MX.

12.1. Markdown (.cog.md)

The canonical cog format. YAML frontmatter for machines, markdown body for humans.

Metadata location: YAML frontmatter between --- delimiters at the top of the file.

MX identity: Standard cog fields in YAML. The mx: block contains MX-operational fields.

Parsing rule: Standard YAML parser. Extract content between the first and second --- lines.

Pre-existing structures recognized as blocks:

  • Markdown body = prose block (implicit)
  • Fenced code blocks = display code (not machine-addressable; use the code block type for that)
---
title: "Pricing Validator"
description: "Validates pricing data to catch errors before AI agents misinterpret them."
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
created: 2026-02-09
modified: 2026-03-03
version: "1.0"

mx:
  status: active
  contentType: specification
  tags: [pricing, validation]
---

## Pricing Validator

Human-readable documentation goes here...

12.2. HTML (.cog.html)

HTML files carry metadata in <meta> tags in the <head> element and Schema.org JSON-LD in <script> elements.

Metadata location: <meta> tags in <head>, data-mx-* attributes on elements.

MX identity: <meta name="mx:*"> tags for MX-operational fields. data-mx-* attributes for element-level metadata.

Parsing rule: Parse <meta> tags in <head>. Names without prefix are standard HTML metadata. Names with mx: prefix are MX-operational. Names with x-mx: prefix are vendor extensions.

Pre-existing structures recognized as blocks:

  • Schema.org JSON-LD = definition block
  • <meta name="description"> = prose excerpt
  • <main> content = essence block
  • <style> elements = embedded CSS carrier (see 12.4)
  • <script> elements = embedded JS carrier (see 12.3)
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en-GB">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="description" content="Product pricing validation tool">
  <meta name="author" content="Tom Cranstoun">
  <meta name="mx:contentType" content="tool">
  <meta name="mx:status" content="active">
  <meta name="mx:audience" content="machines">
  <link rel="mx" href="pricing.cog.md">
  <script type="application/ld+json">
  {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "SoftwareApplication",
    "name": "Pricing Validator"
  }
  </script>
</head>
<body>
  <main data-mx-block="essence">
    <!-- Content here -->
  </main>
</body>
</html>

Pointer to full cog: Any HTML page can reference a .cog.md file using <link rel="mx" href="page.cog.md">. This allows lightweight HTML pages to point to their full cog definition without embedding all metadata inline.

Embedded blocks in HTML: A .cog.html file may contain <style> and <script> elements. Each embedded language uses its own native metadata convention: CSS comments within <style>, JSDoc within <script>. A single HTML file can therefore carry multiple blocks, each with its own metadata. This is the foundation of "the doc IS the app."

12.3. JavaScript (.cog.js)

JavaScript files carry metadata in JSDoc comment blocks.

Metadata location: JSDoc /** */ comment block at the top of the file.

MX identity: @mx: tags in the JSDoc block.

Parsing rule: Parse the JSDoc block. Standard JSDoc tags (@description, @param, @returns) are recognised as native metadata. Tags prefixed with @mx: are MX-operational. Tags prefixed with @x-mx: are vendor extensions.

Pre-existing structures recognized as blocks:

  • @description = prose block
  • @param / @returns = definition block
  • Function bodies = code block (implicit)
  • @example = code block (display)
/**
 * @description Validates pricing data to catch range errors
 * @version 1.0.0
 * @author Tom Cranstoun
 * @mx:contentType validator
 * @mx:status active
 * @mx:audience machines
 * @mx:tags pricing, validation, commerce
 *
 * @param {Object} priceData - The pricing object to validate
 * @returns {ValidationResult} Validation outcome with errors
 */
function validatePrice(priceData) {
  // Implementation
}

12.4. CSS (.cog.css)

CSS files carry metadata in comment blocks at the top of the file.

Metadata location: /* */ comment block at the top of the file.

MX identity: @mx: tags in the CSS comment block.

Parsing rule: Parse the opening comment block. Lines with @ prefixes follow the same convention as JSDoc: @description is standard, @mx: is MX-operational, @x-mx: is vendor extension.

Pre-existing structures recognized as blocks:

  • File description = prose block
  • :root custom properties = definition block (design tokens)
  • Media queries and selectors = code block (implicit)
/**
 * @description Core design tokens for MX branding
 * @version 2.0.0
 * @author Tom Cranstoun
 * @mx:contentType theme
 * @mx:status active
 * @mx:audience machines
 */

:root {
  --mx-primary: #1a1a2e;
  --mx-accent: #e94560;
  --mx-font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
}

12.5. Images (.cog.png, .cog.jpg)

Image files carry their primary metadata in EXIF, IPTC, and XMP, which are mature external standards. MX does not duplicate those vocabularies (see §14). MX operational fields (mx:contentType, mx:status, mx:audience, mx:runbook) embed into the existing XMP metadata via the mx: XMP namespace, alongside the image's native EXIF and XMP records.

Metadata location: EXIF/IPTC/XMP embedded in the image file; MX operational fields under the mx: XMP namespace.

Parsing rule: Read EXIF/IPTC/XMP with a standard metadata library. The native EXIF fields (camera, GPS, timestamp) and XMP description are consumed as the provenance and prose-excerpt blocks; MX does not redefine them. The mx: XMP namespace carries MX operational metadata only.

Reading it back: the practice pairs the write with a one-fetch read. A single inspection pass returns everything the image declares (the full native metadata, the mx: operational fields, and any embedded provenance chain) as one machine-readable document, so a consumer never learns per-carrier read rules. An image that declares nothing reports the absence explicitly rather than raising an error, which makes the same read a gap-finder across an undecorated library.

Rights and licensing: use Schema.org (license, creator), Creative Commons, or the standard XMP rights fields, not an MX-specific rights vocabulary.

<!-- XMP metadata in image file. Native XMP rights fields remain; mx: adds operational. -->
<rdf:Description xmlns:mx="https://allabout.network/ns/mx/1.0"
                 xmlns:xmpRights="http://ns.adobe.com/xap/1.0/rights/"
                 xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
  <mx:contentType>photograph</mx:contentType>
  <mx:status>active</mx:status>
  <mx:audience>humans</mx:audience>
  <xmpRights:Marked>true</xmpRights:Marked>
  <xmpRights:WebStatement>https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/</xmpRights:WebStatement>
  <dc:creator>Tom Cranstoun</dc:creator>
</rdf:Description>

12.6. Shell scripts

Shell scripts (and any #-comment language) carry metadata in comment-block frontmatter.

Metadata location: # --- delimited comment block after the shebang line.

MX identity: Standard fields in # key: value format. MX-operational fields use # mx.field: value.

Parsing rule: Strip the leading hash and one space from each line between # --- delimiters. The result is valid YAML. Any tool that parses YAML can parse script metadata.

Pre-existing structures recognized as blocks:

  • Comment blocks with structural intent = prose block
  • Function signatures and case structures = code skeleton
##!/bin/bash
## ---
## title: "mx.ls - Directory listing"
## version: "1.0"
## created: 2026-02-10
## modified: 2026-02-10
## author: Tom Cranstoun
## description: "Wraps eza with sensible defaults and named modes"
## category: mx-tools
## status: active
## tags: [eza, ls, directory, filesystem]
## dependencies: [eza]
## builds-on: [script-helper]
## ---

The cut compute principle. When an AI agent needs to work with a script, the workflow has three tiers. First, read metadata only: the comment block tells the agent what the script does, its dependencies, and its status. Second, read the skeleton if needed: the comments and structure, without implementation lines. Third, read the full script only if necessary. This three-tier approach reduces token consumption for typical script interactions, because most tasks stop at the first or second tier.

Applicability beyond bash. This convention works for any language that uses # for comments: Python, Ruby, Perl, YAML configuration files, Dockerfiles. For languages using other comment styles (//, /* */, --), the same fields and structure apply. Only the prefix changes.

12.7. Media sidecars

Media sidecar files provide machine-readable metadata for binary assets that cannot carry their own YAML frontmatter.

Metadata location: A companion .mx.yaml.md or .mx.yaml file alongside the media asset.

MX identity: Standard two-zone YAML structure. Zone 1 for document identity, Zone 2 (mx: block) for MX-operational fields. Media-specific vocabulary (dimensions, codec, duration, license, creator) comes from Schema.org, EXIF, or XMP; see §14 for the deferral detail.

Naming convention: The sidecar takes the asset's filename with .mx.yaml.md appended. For example, hero-image.png has a sidecar at hero-image.png.mx.yaml.md.

Relationship to embedded metadata: The sidecar is authoritative where both exist. Where EXIF/XMP metadata is present in the binary, the sidecar may mirror selected fields (confirmed with the alignedMetadata marker) or link out to it via a Schema.org ImageObject / VideoObject / AudioObject block.

---
title: "Product Hero Image"
description: "Main product photograph for landing page"
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
created: 2026-01-15
modified: 2026-03-01

mx:
  status: active
  contentType: photograph
  sidecar:
    targetFile: "hero-image.png"
    alignedMetadata: [title, author, created]

# Media-specific vocabulary from Schema.org (see §14)
schema:
  "@context": "https://schema.org"
  "@type": "ImageObject"
  contentUrl: "hero-image.png"
  width: 1920
  height: 1080
  encodingFormat: "image/png"
  creator: { "@type": "Person", name: "Tom Cranstoun" }
  license: "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/"
---

12.8. Code repositories

Repository-level metadata provides project-wide context for AI agents working with code.

Metadata location: A .mx.yaml.md file at the repository root, or a dedicated mx.config.yaml.

MX identity: Standard two-zone YAML structure with code-specific profiles.

Inheritance: Repository metadata flows down to directories and files. Child .mx.yaml.md files inherit from the repository root and may override specific fields.

---
title: "MX Audit"
description: "Web audit tooling for MX compliance analysis"
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
created: 2025-11-01
modified: 2026-03-03

mx:
  status: active
  contentType: tool
  project:
    name: mx-audit
    language: javascript
    framework: node
    packageManager: npm
    testFramework: jest
  conventions:
    style: eslint
    commits: conventional
    branching: trunk-based
---

12.9. Database sidecars

Database metadata sidecars let AI agents understand schemas and datasets without direct database access. MX does not define a database vocabulary (see §15); database-specific fields come from DCAT v3, CSVW, or Dublin Core. MX provides identity (title, author, created) and operational metadata (contentType, status, audience); the external standards provide the schema.

Metadata location: A .mx.yaml.md file alongside the database, SQL schema, or CSV, carrying MX identity fields plus a DCAT/CSVW/Dublin Core block.

SQL comment format: For inline metadata within SQL files, use -- --- delimiters with -- key: value lines. The parsing rule is identical to shell script metadata: strip the leading double-dash prefix and parse as YAML. Keep the SQL comment metadata to MX operational fields; full schema documentation belongs in a sidecar or CSVW-annotated file.

-- ---
-- title: "Users Table"
-- description: "Core user accounts with authentication data"
-- mx.contentType: dataset
-- mx.audience: tech
-- mx.status: active
-- ---

CREATE TABLE users (
  id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email      VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

Sidecar format using CSVW for the schema detail:

---
title: "E-Commerce Database Schema"
description: "Core schema for product catalog and orders"
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
created: 2026-01-10
modified: 2026-03-03

mx:
  status: active
  contentType: dataset
  audience: [tech, machines]
  sidecar:
    targetFile: "ecommerce-schema.sql"

# Schema vocabulary from CSVW / DCAT - not MX (see §15)
csvw:
  "@context": "http://www.w3.org/ns/csvw"
  tables:
    - url: "users"
      tableSchema:
        columns:
          - name: id
            datatype: integer
            required: true
          - name: email
            datatype: string
            required: true
        primaryKey: [id]
---

13. Code metadata

Code metadata enables AI agents to understand code context, constraints, and intent without parsing implementation details. The fields defined in this section belong to the code-* profiles in the YAML above.

13.1. Repository metadata

Repository-level metadata declares project-wide context. This metadata is in a .mx.yaml.md file at the repository root, or in a dedicated mx.yaml.

File location precedence:

  1. .mx.yaml.md (MX standard)
  2. mx.yaml or mx.yml
  3. .mx/config.yaml
  4. package.json under an mx key (Node.js projects)
  5. pyproject.toml under [tool.mx] (Python projects)

The repository metadata covers project identity (project.* fields), audience context, domain and constraints (context.* fields), technology stack (stack.* fields), and development conventions (conventions.* fields).

## mx.yaml at repository root
mx:
  version: "1.0"
  project:
    name: "Order Service"
    description: "API backend for order processing"
    repository: https://github.com/example/order-service
  context:
    domain: "e-commerce"
    purpose: "API backend for order processing"
    constraints:
      - "Must handle 10,000 requests per second"
      - "GDPR compliant"
  stack:
    language: typescript
    runtime: node
    version: "20.x"
    framework: express
  conventions:
    style: prettier
    testing: jest
    documentation: jsdoc

13.2. File metadata

File-level metadata declares context for individual source files. This metadata appears at the top of the file in the native comment format.

The @mx marker signals the beginning of MX metadata within a comment block. Everything between @mx and the end of the comment is parsed as YAML.

JavaScript / TypeScript:

/**
 * @mx
 * audience: machine
 * purpose: "Validates user input against schema"
 * stability: stable
 * dependencies:
 *   - zod
 * ai:
 *   editable: true
 *   contextRequired: ["src/types/user.ts"]
 */

Python:

"""
@mx
audience: machine
purpose: "Validates user input against schema"
stability: stable
ai:
  editable: true
  contextRequired: ["src/types/user.py"]
"""

Go:

/*
@mx
audience: machine
purpose: "Validates user input against schema"
stability: stable
ai:
  editable: true
*/

Rust:

//! @mx
//! audience: machine
//! purpose: "Validates user input against schema"
//! stability: stable

13.3. Function and class metadata

Function metadata provides granular context for individual code units. The @mx marker works within function-level JSDoc, docstrings, or comment blocks.

Function metadata example (TypeScript):

/**
 * Calculates the total price including tax and discounts.
 *
 * @mx
 * pure: true
 * complexity: O(n)
 * throws: [InvalidDiscountError, NegativePriceError]
 * ai:
 *   confidence: 0.9
 *   testCoverage: true
 *   edgeCases:
 *     - "Empty cart returns 0"
 *     - "Negative discounts are rejected"
 *
 * @param items - Array of cart items
 * @param discountCode - Optional discount code
 * @returns Total price in smallest currency unit
 */
function calculateTotal(items: CartItem[], discountCode?: string): number {
  // ...
}

Class metadata example (TypeScript):

/**
 * Manages user authentication state and token refresh.
 *
 * @mx
 * pattern: singleton
 * threadSafe: false
 * state:
 *   - currentUser: "Authenticated user or null"
 *   - tokens: "Access and refresh tokens"
 * invariants:
 *   - "If currentUser is set, tokens must be valid"
 * ai:
 *   sensitive: true
 *   reason: "Handles authentication tokens"
 *   contextRequired: ["src/types/auth.ts"]
 */
class AuthManager {
  // ...
}

13.4. Inline annotations

Inline annotations provide context for specific code blocks or lines without requiring full metadata blocks.

Block annotations mark regions of code with semantic context:

// @mx:begin security-critical
// All code in this block handles authentication tokens.
// AI assistants should not modify without human review.
const token = await refreshToken(currentToken);
validateTokenSignature(token);
storeToken(token);
// @mx:end security-critical

Block annotation tags: security-critical, performance-critical, compatibility, workaround, generated, legacy.

Line annotations mark individual lines:

const API_KEY = process.env.API_KEY; // @mx:sensitive no-log no-expose
await sleep(100);                    // @mx:intentional rate-limiting
if (value === null) {                // @mx:ai do-not-remove edge case #1234
  return defaultValue;
}

Line annotation tags: @mx:sensitive, @mx:intentional, @mx:todo, @mx:fixme, @mx:hack, @mx:ai.

AI-specific annotations: @mx:ai do-not-remove, @mx:ai do-not-modify, @mx:ai preserve-logic, @mx:ai explain-before-changing, @mx:ai generated, @mx:ai reviewed.

13.5. Dependency metadata

Dependency metadata declares why dependencies exist and how they should be managed. This extends native package manifests (package.json, pyproject.toml) with an mx key.

{
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^4.18.0",
    "zod": "^3.22.0"
  },
  "mx": {
    "dependencies": {
      "express": {
        "purpose": "HTTP server framework",
        "critical": true,
        "upgradePolicy": "conservative",
        "alternativesConsidered": ["fastify", "koa"]
      },
      "zod": {
        "purpose": "Runtime type validation",
        "critical": true,
        "ai": {
          "replacementPermitted": false,
          "reason": "Schema definitions throughout codebase"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

13.6. Environment metadata

Environment metadata declares runtime requirements and configuration, stored in .mx/environment.yaml or equivalent.

mx:
  environments:
    development:
      description: "Local development environment"
      requirements:
        node: ">=20.0.0"
      services:
        - postgres:15
        - redis:7
      envVars:
        required: [DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL]
        sensitive: [DATABASE_URL]
    production:
      description: "Production deployment"
      envVars:
        sensitive: [API_KEY, JWT_SECRET, DATABASE_URL]
      ai:
        access: prohibited
        reason: "Production secrets must not be exposed to AI assistants"

13.7. Test metadata

Test metadata declares test context, coverage targets, and AI generation permissions.

/**
 * @mx
 * testType: unit
 * coverageTarget: 90%
 * subject: src/utils/validation.ts
 * fixtures:
 *   - valid_users.json
 *   - invalid_users.json
 * ai:
 *   generationPermitted: true
 *   mustCover:
 *     - "Empty input"
 *     - "Invalid email format"
 *     - "Missing required fields"
 */
describe('validateUser', () => {
  // ...
});

13.8. API metadata

API metadata declares endpoint context for web services. This extends OpenAPI specifications with MX fields using the x-mx: extension prefix.

## OpenAPI with MX extensions
paths:
  /users/{id}:
    get:
      summary: Get user by ID
      x-mx:
        audience: machine
        rateLimit: 100/minute
        cache:
          enabled: true
          ttl: 300
        ai:
          safeToCall: true
          idempotent: true
          sensitiveResponseFields: [email, phone]

Route annotations in code use the same fields:

/**
 * @mx
 * method: GET
 * path: /users/:id
 * auth: required
 * rateLimit: 100/minute
 * ai:
 *   safeToCall: true
 *   testMode: "Add ?test=true for mock data"
 */
router.get('/users/:id', getUser);

13.9. Code metadata inheritance

Code metadata inherits down the hierarchy of repository, directory, file, and function or class.

mx.yaml (repository)
  > src/ (directory)
    > src/payments/ (directory)
      > src/payments/stripe.ts (file)
        > processPayment() (function)

Child levels inherit from parents unless explicitly overridden. A directory without its own configuration inherits directly from its nearest configured ancestor.

Repository root detection. The repository root is identified by presence of mx.yaml with a version property, or by the version control directory (.git). Build systems must not traverse above the repository root when resolving inheritance.

13.10. Mod metadata

A mod is code that an application loads into its own event loop, where it can observe what happens, rewrite an action before the host takes it, or answer in its place. Claude Code mods are the worked example: a plugin whose hooks module sees every prompt, tool call and turn in the session. Placed between what an agent decides and what the machine does, a mod declares what it hooks, what it may touch, and what it promises. The code-mod profile defines four fields for this.

  • modHooks lists each hooked event as event{matcher}:move, where the move is observe, rewrite or answer. Required.
  • modCapabilities lists the API surfaces the mod's code uses, in the host's own names. Required.
  • modGuarantee states in one sentence what the mod promises and what it does not. A machine reads it as a declared limit.
  • testedWith names the host and version the mod was last tested against, as host@version.

The hook string. Each modHooks entry matches this ABNF grammar (RFC 5234), with unreserved and pct-encoded taken from RFC 3986 section 2:

mod-hook = event [ "{" matcher *( "," matcher ) "}" ] ":" move
event    = name *( "." name )
name     = ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "_" / "-" )
matcher  = key "=" value
key      = ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "_" )
value    = 1*( unreserved / pct-encoded )
move     = "observe" / "rewrite" / "answer"

The grammar admits no whitespace, and names, keys and values are case-sensitive. In canonical form the matchers are sorted by key with no key repeated, and every octet of a value outside the unreserved set is percent-encoded from its UTF-8 bytes in uppercase hexadecimal. A checker brings the declared hooks and the host-derived hooks to canonical form and compares them byte for byte; an entry outside the grammar fails. A matcher value containing a delimiter is written tool.call{cwd=%2Fsrv%2Fapp,tool=Bash}:answer.

In the plugin manifest the fields go in a root mx object, the JSON carrier that package manifests also use:

{
  "name": "blast-radius",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Holds risky Bash commands and shows what they would change before they run.",
  "mx": {
    "modHooks": ["tool.call{tool=Bash}:answer", "ui.render{component=Pane}:observe"],
    "modCapabilities": ["process", "ui", "session"],
    "modGuarantee": "A safety net that reads the command text; not a permission system.",
    "testedWith": "claude-code@2.1.287"
  }
}

In the mod module the same fields go in the leading JSDoc block:

/**
 * @mx
 * modHooks: ["tool.call{tool=Bash}:answer", "ui.render{component=Pane}:observe"]
 * modCapabilities: [process, ui, session]
 * modGuarantee: "A safety net that reads the command text; not a permission system."
 * testedWith: claude-code@2.1.287
 */
export function register(on) { /* ... */ }

In YAML form, as a frontmatter block or a sidecar:

type: code-mod
modHooks:
  - tool.call{tool=Bash}:answer
  - ui.render{component=Pane}:observe
modCapabilities: [process, ui, session]
modGuarantee: "A safety net that reads the command text; not a permission system."
testedWith: claude-code@2.1.287

Declared against derived. The declaration is held by a check, not by trust. Some hosts derive a mod's hooks and API calls from source; claude plugin validate does this for Claude Code. Where they do, a hook or capability found in the code but missing from the declaration fails the check, and a declared one the source no longer uses is reported as stale. A mod that answers or rewrites contributes a step to the provenance record of any decision it shaped; a mod that only observes does not.

Configured against observed. A declaration says what a mod intends; it does not say what was in force when an agent acted. The provenance record of an agent step can carry an execution context: the task, the model, the host and its version, the loaded mods and hooks, the instruction files, the tools, the organisation policy, the permission that reached the action, and the effect. Each link records its basis: configured when taken from settings, a manifest or a policy, and observed when read from the running session. The verdict is derived from those bases and is never written by hand: configuration-only until the permission is observed, effect-unverified until someone checks the outcome, and effect-verified after they do. Claude Code 2.1.287 shows why the distinction is needed: it fixed an organisation per-tool permission ceiling that had been dropped for one MCP tool name, so the configured ceiling and the enforced one differed.

13.11. AI guidance fields

The ai.* fields tell an agent how to treat a piece of code before it changes it. They sit in the code profiles: a file carries ai.contextRequired, ai.contextProvides, ai.generationNotes and ai.reason; a function or class carries ai.confidence, ai.testCoverage, ai.edgeCases, ai.refactorNotes, ai.doNotModify, ai.sensitive and ai.modificationImpact; a dependency carries ai.replacementPermitted and ai.upgradePermitted; a test carries ai.generationPermitted, ai.mustCover and ai.doNotMock; an API endpoint carries ai.safeToCall, ai.testMode, ai.sensitiveRequestFields, ai.sensitiveResponseFields and ai.sideEffects.

Field Type What it tells the agent
ai.contextRequired array The files to read before editing this one
ai.contextProvides array The concepts this file defines that others depend on
ai.generationNotes string How to generate similar code
ai.reason string Why a restriction on this resource exists
ai.confidence number Confidence in the implementation's correctness, 0 to 1
ai.testCoverage boolean Whether the function has test coverage
ai.edgeCases array Known edge cases and their expected behaviour
ai.refactorNotes string How to refactor it safely
ai.doNotModify boolean Leave this function as it is
ai.sensitive boolean It handles sensitive data
ai.modificationImpact string What might break if it changes
ai.replacementPermitted boolean Whether replacing this dependency may be suggested
ai.upgradePermitted boolean Whether upgrading this dependency may be suggested
ai.generationPermitted boolean Whether tests may be generated for this module
ai.mustCover array Scenarios the tests must cover
ai.doNotMock array Dependencies the tests must not mock
ai.safeToCall boolean Whether an agent may call this endpoint
ai.testMode string How to reach the endpoint's test mode
ai.sensitiveRequestFields array Request fields that carry sensitive data
ai.sensitiveResponseFields array Response fields that carry sensitive data
ai.sideEffects array What calling the endpoint changes 
/**
 * Charge a stored card.
 * @mx:ai.doNotModify true
 * @mx:ai.reason Reconciled against the payment provider's ledger; a change needs finance review.
 * @mx:ai.sideEffects ["charges the customer", "writes a ledger entry"]
 * @mx:ai.safeToCall false
 */

14. Media metadata - deferred to external standards

MX does not define a media-metadata vocabulary. Images, video, audio, and documents have mature standards that cover the ground: Schema.org for web-facing structured data, and EXIF, IPTC, XMP, and ID3 for embedded metadata in the media files themselves.

Per the MX principle "reuse existing standards, do not duplicate" (see §27), an MX document that describes a media asset uses those vocabularies directly.

What MX provides

  • Cross-reference only. Use MX identity fields (title, author, created, contentType: image) on the enclosing document; name the media asset; and point at the Schema.org, EXIF, or XMP record that holds the media-specific metadata.
  • Sidecar convention (optional). A .mx.yaml.md file adjacent to a binary asset may carry the MX identity fields plus a Schema.org ImageObject, VideoObject, or AudioObject block. Where both it and embedded metadata exist, the sidecar is authoritative. MX does not redefine the Schema.org fields; it just names their home.

Example - a page that references an image via Schema.org

---
title: "Case Study: The MX Audit Dashboard"
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
created: 2026-03-18
description: "Walkthrough of the audit report format with screenshots."
mx:
  contentType: article
  audience: [humans, machines]
---

<!-- in the body -->
![Dashboard overview](dashboard.png)

The image sidecar (dashboard.png.mx.yaml.md):

---
title: "mx-audit dashboard - overview"
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
created: 2026-03-18

mx:
  contentType: image
  about: "dashboard.png"

schema:
  "@context": "https://schema.org"
  "@type": "ImageObject"
  contentUrl: "dashboard.png"
  width: 1920
  height: 1080
  encodingFormat: "image/png"
  creator:
    "@type": "Person"
    name: "Tom Cranstoun"
  license: "https://spdx.org/licenses/CC-BY-4.0.html"
---

Width, height, format, creator, and license are declared under schema: using Schema.org's vocabulary. MX owns the identity fields and the pointer at the asset.

For images with embedded EXIF/XMP metadata, the alignedMetadata field (a pass-through from Dublin Core/Schema.org) can declare which embedded fields the sidecar confirms, preventing drift between the two representations. The vocabulary used is whatever EXIF/XMP defines; MX does not enumerate it.

15. Database metadata - deferred to external standards

MX does not define a database-metadata vocabulary. Datasets, their schemas, column semantics, and query manifests have mature standards: DCAT v3 for dataset catalogues, CSVW for tabular schemas, Dublin Core for generic resource identity. Per §27, MX defers to them.

What MX provides

  • Cross-reference only. An MX document that describes a dataset, table, or schema declares its identity with MX fields (title, author, created, description) and points at a DCAT dcat:Dataset or CSVW tableSchema block.
  • Sidecar convention (optional). A .mx.yaml.md file adjacent to a SQL schema, CSV, or database dump may carry MX identity plus a DCAT or CSVW metadata block.
  • No database-* profiles in the MX canon. The old database, database-table, database-column, database-relationship, database-view, database-query, database-procedure, database-schema, database-dictionary profiles were removed on 2026-04-15.

Example - a CSV sidecar using CSVW

Source file: monthly-revenue.csv. Sidecar: monthly-revenue.csv.mx.yaml.md.

---
title: "Monthly revenue - FY2026 Q1"
author: "Finance team"
created: 2026-04-01
description: "Revenue by product line, reported monthly. Units in GBP minor."

mx:
  contentType: dataset
  ownership: finance
  audience: [business, machines]
  stability: evolving

csvw:
  "@context": "http://www.w3.org/ns/csvw"
  url: "monthly-revenue.csv"
  tableSchema:
    columns:
      - name: "month"
        titles: "Month"
        datatype: "date"
        required: true
      - name: "product_line"
        titles: "Product line"
        datatype: "string"
        required: true
      - name: "revenue_minor"
        titles: "Revenue (GBP minor)"
        datatype: "integer"
        required: true
    primaryKey: ["month", "product_line"]
---

Column types, primary keys, and required-ness are declared under csvw: using CSVW's vocabulary. MX owns the identity layer (title, author, created, ownership, audience, stability) and the pointer at the dataset file.

For published data catalogues, the same pattern applies with dcat: instead of csvw:: declare the dataset's DCAT record inline. MX does not redefine dataset-catalogue vocabulary; see the DCAT specification for distributions, licenses, temporal coverage, and spatial scope.

16. AI interpretation guidance

This section consolidates guidance for AI agents interpreting MX metadata across all carriers. The principles apply regardless of whether the metadata is in YAML frontmatter, HTML meta tags, code comments, or database sidecars.

16.1. General principles

  1. Read metadata first. Before parsing implementation, read the structured metadata. Twelve lines of YAML provide more reliable context than scanning hundreds of lines of code or markup.

  2. Respect declared rights. When rights.aiTraining or rights.aiGeneration fields are present, honor them without exception. These are explicit declarations, not suggestions.

  3. Honor sensitivity markers. Fields marked pii: true, classification: sensitive, or ai.access: prohibited must not be logged, cached, or included in responses without explicit authorisation.

  4. Follow the inheritance chain. Metadata inherits downward: repository to directory to file to function, database to schema to table to column. Always resolve the full chain before acting.

  5. Profile-scope your interpretation. The same field name may mean different things in two profiles. purpose in a code-file profile describes what the file does. purpose in a database-table profile describes what data the table holds. Use the profile context.

16.2. Code-specific guidance

  • Check stability before modifying. A field or function marked stability: frozen must not be changed. stability: stable means changes require careful review. stability: experimental allows modification.
  • Read ai.contextRequired before editing. If a file declares context dependencies, read those files first to understand the broader impact.
  • Respect @mx:ai annotations. Inline annotations like @mx:ai do-not-remove and @mx:ai preserve-logic are direct instructions to AI agents.
  • Check ai.editable at file and function level. A file may allow editing but specific functions within it may not.

16.3. Media-specific guidance

  • Never reproduce restricted media. If rights.aiGeneration: prohibited, do not generate content based on the asset.
  • Check rights.attribution before referencing. If attribution is required, include it in any response that references the asset.
  • Use sidecar.alignedMetadata to verify consistency. If the sidecar declares alignment with embedded metadata, trust its values.

16.4. Database-specific guidance

  • Classification overrides access. If a column is classified as pii or sensitive, do not include its values in responses regardless of other permissions.
  • Check ai.safeToCall before executing procedures. Stored procedures with safeToCall: false require human approval.
  • Use the data dictionary. When translating between business terms and technical column names, consult the dictionary profile entries.
  • Respect retention policies. Do not suggest actions that would violate declared retention policies or legal requirements.

17. Related documents

  • Structure: mx-canon/mx-the-gathering/specifications/cog-unified-spec.cog.md defines how cogs are built (this dictionary defines what goes inside them)
  • Guide: mx-canon/ssot/writing-guides/mx-yaml-md-guide.md is the practical how-to for folder metadata (references this dictionary for field definitions)

One definition per field. No ambiguity. No overlap. The metadata is for machines. The prose is for humans. Design for both.

22.N Genuineness - the trust-verification family

The standard's trust lens is anchored by a named family of three fields. Each aligns with an existing external trust standard rather than inventing new vocabulary. An adopter claims any subset, and claiming all three gives the strongest trust signal.

Field Type Purpose Aligns with
proofOfAuthorship object Verifiable link between the named author and the artefact. Cryptographic signature, trust-chain identifier (e.g. DID), or published-by-known-entity assertion. Answers "I made this, and I can prove it." W3C Verifiable Credentials; Signed Exchanges
integritySignature object Hash or cryptographic signature over the artefact's content that lets a reader detect tampering since publication. Typically a content hash with algorithm identifier. Answers "what you read is what was written." RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures; Subresource Integrity
provenancePedigree object Traceable chain from this artefact back to its source, including any transformations along the way. Derivation tree with authorities at each step. Answers "where did this come from, and through whom?" W3C PROV-O; C2PA Content Credentials

"Genuineness" is the family name in prose; it is not itself a field. The three fields are siblings in the mx: block, any subset may be claimed, and tools that care about trust consult them in turn: proof of who, signature of what, pedigree of how. See §22 of the triage rubric for the rule that admitted this family.

A document that claims all three, with the integrity digest taken over the prose body so that metadata edits never invalidate it:

mx:
  canonicalUri: https://mx.allabout.network/blog/governance-when-ai-acts.html
  proofOfAuthorship:
    method: did
    identifier: did:web:allabout.network
    signature: z3FXQ...
  integritySignature:
    algorithm: sha-256
    covers: body
    value: 3b7e1f0c9a2d4e6f8b1c3d5e7f9a0b2c4d6e8f0a1b3c5d7e9f1a3b5c7d9e1f3a
  provenancePedigree:
    derivedFrom: https://mx.allabout.network/blog/source-post
    steps:
      - agent: human
        action: authored
        by: Tom Cranstoun
      - agent: ai-assisted
        action: edited
        by: Maxine

A reader that meets the file away from its source recomputes the digest over the body and compares it with integritySignature.value, resolves proofOfAuthorship.identifier to confirm who signed, and walks provenancePedigree.steps to see how the content reached its present form. None of the three needs the originating site to be reachable, which is the point: the trust checks travel with the file.

22.O provenanceOrigin - declaring machine authorship

provenanceOrigin records how a piece of content was created: the human-machine authorship balance, declared in the file itself so a reader, an agent, or a validator learns it without inference. It is a single string drawn from a fixed value set.

Value Meaning
human-directed Content authored by a human, possibly with AI tooling assistance.
ai-assisted Content substantially generated by AI, with human review and direction.
ai-generated Content created by a machine with no substantive human authorship or editorial control.
ai-manipulated Human-origin content materially altered or transformed by a machine (for example a deepfake, a synthetic edit, or a machine-rewritten passage).
automated-fact-check Content generated and verified by automated processes.

Note: This section describes regulatory frameworks in general terms only. Nothing here is legal advice. Requirements vary by jurisdiction, organisation type, and use case. Consult qualified legal specialists for guidance specific to your situation.

The two machine-authorship values, ai-generated and ai-manipulated, map directly onto the way transparency regimes describe machine-made content. The EU AI Act Article 50 names exactly this pair, "AI-generated or AI-manipulated", as the content a deployer must label and a provider must mark in a machine-readable way that can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated. Declaring provenanceOrigin: ai-generated on an artefact, and carrying that declaration in the artefact's own carrier, is how an MX-described file states which case it is.

A boundary worth holding precisely: provenanceOrigin is a provenance declaration, not a content-authenticity watermark. A marking standard such as C2PA Content Credentials or a watermark such as SynthID embeds a detectable signal that an artefact is synthetic; provenanceOrigin records who, or what, authored it. The two are complementary, and an implementer may carry both. MX does not claim to be the watermark; it is the machine-readable layer that states the authorship and travels with the file alongside whatever marking the artefact also carries. Distinct from the genuineness family above, which answers proof of who, integrity of what, and pedigree of how, provenanceOrigin answers the prior question of how the content came to exist at all.

Outside vocabularies answer the same question in their own terms, and MX recognises them rather than replacing them. The music industry's delivery standard, DDEX, defines three generative-AI designations that labels and distributors declare when they deliver tracks, and that YouTube Music uses for its player-page labels. A publisher who declares a DDEX designation can state the matching provenanceOrigin beside it:

DDEX designation Closest provenanceOrigin Where the two differ
Fully Gen AI ai-generated None material: the whole work came from a generative model.
Partly Gen AI ai-assisted DDEX counts any generated component, such as a generated string section under human vocals; ai-assisted describes content substantially generated with human direction. A small generated part may sit closer to human-directed.
No Gen AI human-directed Both allow non-generative tooling; DDEX names pitch correction and automated mastering as No Gen AI.
(no designation) (no value) An absent value means not declared, never human-directed.

The correspondence is approximate, because each scheme draws its threshold in its own place. For music, the DDEX definition governs the designation; provenanceOrigin states the MX claim beside it and travels with the file, where the DDEX value travels in the delivery feed. IPTC DigitalSourceType plays the same role for images and is carried in the image's own metadata: its trainedAlgorithmicMedia value corresponds to ai-generated.

22.R provenanceUri - the canonical address of the provenance chain

provenanceOrigin states how the content came to exist; provenanceUri says where the full account of that existence lives. It is the canonical URL of the file's AI-governance provenance cog, the hosted record that stands beside the file and holds the parties, the regulatory frameworks it cites, and every recorded action in the chain. A machine reads provenanceUri, fetches the named record, and walks the evidence without needing the chain embedded in the file itself.

mx:
  provenanceOrigin: ai-assisted
  provenanceUri: https://mx.allabout.network/blog/governance-when-ai-acts.mxprov.json

The hosted record is a provenance cog carried in its own extension (see the carrier-formats guide for the .mxprov.json convention). It is a JSON-carrier cog whose body is the provenance chain, addressable by URL and served side-by-side with the artefact it describes. provenanceUri is the pointer; the cog is the record.

provenanceUri complements an embedded chain rather than replacing it. An artefact may both embed a snapshot of its provenance (so the chain travels offline, in the file's own carrier) and declare provenanceUri (so a reader can reach the current, canonical record). When both are present the embedded copy is what a machine reads with no network, and the URL names the authoritative version for comparison. This mirrors canonicalUri: the file carries what it can, and names where the canonical form lives.

The record describes itself. A provenance record is a document in its own right, and it meets readers with no context: an agent that followed provenanceUri, a regulator who extracted it from a PDF, a crawler that found the .mxprov.json beside the page. It therefore carries its own MX metadata. A JSON carrier holds that metadata in one root mx object, the same place a package manifest (§13.5) or an API response carries it. A JSON payload has no second zone, so the identity fields, the OKF fields and the governance fields sit together there. Both sidecars of the pair (the AI and the deterministic record) carry one, third in the file after $schema and schemaVersion. The writer rebuilds it each time it runs: created is the day the chain started, modified the day of the last write, version the run revision.

{
  "$schema": "https://mx.allabout.network/schemas/provenance-ai/v2",
  "schemaVersion": "2.0",
  "mx": {
    "@context": "https://mx.allabout.network/canon/context.json",
    "title": "AI provenance record for q3-report.md",
    "description": "Evidence chain of the non-deterministic steps (model calls, agent work, human-committed actions) behind q3-report.md.",
    "author": "Tom Cranstoun",
    "created": "2026-09-16",
    "modified": "2026-09-16",
    "version": "1",
    "type": "provenance-record",
    "tags": ["provenance", "ai-evidence-chain", "reginald"],
    "status": "active",
    "purpose": "Let a reader (human, agent, or regulator) walk every non-deterministic step behind q3-report.md and find the accountable party for each. An evidence vehicle, not a compliance grant.",
    "audience": ["machines", "humans"],
    "inLanguage": "en",
    "isGenerated": true,
    "generatedBy": "mx-reginald/lib/provenance.js",
    "canonicalUri": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/example-org/example-repo/main/reports/q3-report.provenance.ai.json",
    "refersTo": ["reports/q3-report.md"],
    "refersToExternal": ["https://example.org/reports/q3"]
  },
  "auditId": "q3-2026-09-16",
  "parties": [],
  "frameworks": [],
  "steps": []
}

A reader keys on type: provenance-record. refersTo names, repo-root-relative, the artefact for which the record is evidence, and refersToExternal names a URL target when the audit had one. canonicalUri is derived from the repository's own remote and is omitted, never guessed, when the record is written outside one. isGenerated and generatedBy say that the object was written by the provenance primitive, not by hand. The deterministic record holds the same object with its own title, tags, and purpose. The house rules for the pair are in provenance-sidecars.cog.md.

22.AI servedPdfUri - where the rendered PDF is published

A markdown source that renders to a published PDF names the public address of that PDF in servedPdfUri. Anyone holding the source can reach the published rendering from it. The PDF pipeline uses the same address for the badge's walk link, which then opens the inspector on the served copy. The value is an absolute http(s) URL; a relative path is ignored.

mx:
  canonicalUri: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Digital-Domain-Technologies-Ltd/MX-hub/main/mx-site/mx-explained.md
  servedPdfUri: https://mx.allabout.network/mx-explained.pdf

canonicalUri names the source of truth; servedPdfUri names one published rendering of it.

22.P The four trust signals - which fields carry each

The trust lens decomposes into four named signals, each answering a different question a machine weights separately at the decision point instead of collapsing them into a single yes or no. Three are properties of the registry record; the fourth is a property of the content. They are named, not numbered, in principles.cog.md under Trust Is Structural and Corroboration over Assertion. The table below maps each to the field or mechanism that realises it, so a reader of this index can see what to declare.

Signal Question it answers Carried by
Attestation Who published this, and when? The REGINALD registry record (signed, dated), anchored in the artefact by proofOfAuthorship and integritySignature from the genuineness family above
Currency Is this the current version? version plus canonicalUri (the canonical address resolves to the current edition); superseded versions stay queryable in the registry rather than vanishing
Freshness Is the publisher still standing behind this? A liveness signal from the registry account, surfaced in the artefact by expires and modified; an abandoned document still resolves but reads as no longer maintained
Corroboration Does an authoritative external source agree? corroboratedBy, the external authoritative sources that independently state the load-bearing claims, checked by a gate that rejects a declared source which is internal or cited nowhere in the body

The first three are what REGINALD's "machine-trustworthy" pillar decomposes into; the fourth makes content "machine-authoritative" and travels with it, not with the registry. Attestation proves who published a claim, never that anyone authoritative agrees with it; that gap is exactly what corroboration closes. Build one or two without the rest and the content is still discardable at the decision that matters.

22.A Identity and the decision-record family

The fields below extend the canon's identity and trust vocabulary across the cog family. The cogUrn field (canonicalUrn) holds the canonical URN form used everywhere a file's identity must survive its location. The decision-record fields below describe the audit-trail cogs an AI system produces when it acts. They share one schema family with the content cog vocabulary already documented above. They also use the same cryptographic primitives that the trust layer already provides: Ed25519 signatures, RFC 8785 canonicalisation, and RFC 6962 transparency-log inclusion proofs.

canonicalUrn - file identity beyond URL

Field Type Required Definition Reference
canonicalUrn string optional Canonical URN identifying this document independently of where it is served. Form cog:<scheme>:<authority>:<local-id> with web as the scheme for web-resolvable cogs (DNS-anchored authority) and a publisher-chosen stable local-id (ULID recommended). Distinct from canonicalUri (location): the URN survives URL rebuilds, domain changes, and CDN reshuffling. Registries map URN to current URI. RFC 8141; REGINALD specification; Handle System / DOI

The canon form has no urn: outer prefix. The bare cog: is the scheme namespace; web is the resolution-scheme sub-namespace. Earlier drafts that used urn:cog:<authority>:<identifier> are superseded. Worked example:

cog:web:example-retailer.com:01JC8X7K2N4P5Q6R7S8T9V0W1Y

The authority (example-retailer.com) anchors identity in DNS without binding to a current URL. The local-id (01JC8X7K2N4P5Q6R7S8T9V0W1Y) is a ULID, which gives lexicographic time-ordering and collision resistance without coordination. The cogUrn does not change when the publisher rebuilds the site, swaps CDNs, or moves to a new platform; the registry entry updates the URI and the URN keeps resolving.

responsiblePerson - structured accountability identity

A responsiblePerson block names the human accountable for a file, an AI-generated artefact, or a provenance chain. It gives structured evidence under the UK ICO AI guidance accountability principle and the United States NIST AI Risk Management Framework GOVERN function (roles, responsibilities, lines of communication). EU AI Act Article 4 places a duty on providers and deployers concerning the AI literacy of the staff who operate their AI systems (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as amended: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj). It does not require a named person, but a named owner is one way to show who answers for that duty. A reader walking from a finding to the person responsible finds the full identifier in one step, without having to cross-reference an external directory or guess from a commit author.

Field Type Required Definition Reference
responsiblePerson object optional Block of six sub-keys identifying the legally accountable individual. Distinct from stewardship (mutable ongoing maintenance): responsiblePerson records the legally accountable individual at the moment the artefact or chain was produced. EU AI Act Art. 4; UK ICO AI guidance; NIST AI RMF (GOVERN); EAA Directive 2019/882
responsiblePerson.name string required (within block) Legal individual answerable for the artefact. -
responsiblePerson.email string required Contact channel for the accountable party. An organisation or role address, never a personal one: the block travels inside public carriers, and personal data never travels in provenance. -
responsiblePerson.identifier string (URL) required Resolvable URL an auditor can dereference to verify the identity claim against an independent record such as a public biography or directory. -
responsiblePerson.role string required Plain-language description of what this person did with respect to the file (audit operator, primary author, accountable signatory). -
responsiblePerson.organisation string optional Legal entity behind the work. Distinguished from the public brand where the two differ. -
responsiblePerson.country string required ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code naming the jurisdiction whose accountability rules apply. ISO 3166-1

Worked example in YAML frontmatter:

mx:
  responsiblePerson:
    name: Tom Cranstoun
    email: info@cognovamx.com
    identifier: https://allabout.network
    role: Audit operator and accountable individual
    organisation: Digital Domain Technologies Ltd (trading as CogNovaMX)
    country: GB

The block travels at the top of provenance sidecars (the AI stream .provenance.ai.json and its deterministic counterpart .provenance.deterministic.json) and may be declared in any cog frontmatter where named accountability matters.

Carrier representations. The JSON form is canonical. Other carriers transcribe the same six fields into their native metadata format:

Carrier Representation
Markdown YAML frontmatter with responsiblePerson: as a nested map under mx:
HTML <meta name="mx:responsiblePerson.name" content="..."> through the six dotted sub-fields, placed alongside other mx:* meta tags in the document head
PDF The full block sits inside the AI provenance sidecar embedded in the XMP packet (xmp:ProvenanceAiPayload); extractable with exiftool -b -XMP-mx:ProvenanceAiPayload <file>.pdf
JavaScript / TypeScript JSDoc tags @mx:responsiblePerson.name, @mx:responsiblePerson.email, through the six dotted sub-fields
Shell scripts YAML block in #-prefixed comments at the head of the file, with the same nested-map shape as the markdown frontmatter form
CSS @mx:responsiblePerson.* tags inside a leading comment block

The values are the same across carriers; the wrappers differ. Adding a new carrier means defining how that carrier's native metadata format expresses the canonical JSON shape, not redefining the field set.

Override mechanism. An audit pipeline that needs to record a non-default operator sets the MX_AUDIT_RESPONSIBLE_PERSON_FILE environment variable to point at an alternate JSON file with the same six-field shape. A contractor running an audit for a client and a delegated reviewer signing off on someone else's behalf are two such operators. The default file, responsible-person.json, names the operator who normally runs the pipeline.

Multi-party, regime-tagged provenance fields

A real audit routinely names more than one accountable party, claims relevance to more than one regulatory regime, and stretches across multiple re-runs of the same identifier. The provenance chain has five field shapes that cover those cases alongside the single-block responsiblePerson form. responsiblePerson is the canonical single-operator shape; parties[], frameworks[], runRevision, lastWriteAt, and per-step jurisdictionalEvidence carry the structured detail a regulator walking a multi-party chain expects to find.

Field Type Required Definition Reference
parties array recommended Role-attributed identity entries accountable for parts of the chain. Each entry carries the same six-field core as responsiblePerson (name, email, identifier, organisation, country) plus a controlled role. Multiple entries per role are permitted; the same record can name multiple providers, multiple auditors, or all four EU AI Act value-chain roles at once. EU AI Act Articles 16, 23, 24, 25, 26, 53; Colorado AI Act SB 26-189; NYC Local Law 144; GDPR Articles 4, 37; ISO/IEC 42001; ISO/IEC 23894
frameworks array recommended Regulatory regimes the chain claims relevance to. Each entry carries id, title, version, jurisdiction, appliesTo, and a reserved x-<framework> extension namespace for jurisdiction-specific fields. The default registry enumerates thirty regimes; per-audit entries may extend the list or downgrade an entry to appliesTo: not-applicable with a reason. mx-canon/ssot/registries/ai-regimes.json; provenance-regime-compatibility.md
runRevision integer required Monotonic counter. First initialisation of the chain writes 1; every subsequent re-initialisation of the same auditId increments. recordStep appends do not touch this counter; only initProvenance does. A reader pairing (auditId, runRevision) identifies the exact run that produced the current bytes without walking the steps timeline. -
lastWriteAt string (ISO-8601) required Timestamp of the most recent write to the sidecar. Updated on every write, including recordStep appends. Pair with startedAt (which pins to the first write and never moves) and the steps timeline to know the time-range the chain covers; pair with runRevision to identify the specific run. -
jurisdictionalEvidence object (per step) optional Map keyed by framework identifier (drawn from the file-level frameworks[] array) and valued with a small object naming the article, section, function, or clause that step satisfies. Optional. A chain without it remains valid generic evidence under every framework named in the file-level registry. Its presence pre-routes a clause-to-evidence walk so a regulator's read becomes one lookup. EU AI Act articles map; NIST AI RMF GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE categories; Colorado AI Act §6-1-1701; NYC LL144 §20-870

Controlled role enum. The parties[].role field takes one of twelve values: auditOperator (the human running the pipeline), provider (EU AI Act Art. 16; Colorado developer), deployer (Art. 26; Colorado deployer), authorisedRepresentative (Art. 25), importer (Art. 23), distributor (Art. 24), auditor (NYC LL144 bias auditor; ISO 42001 internal audit), dataController (GDPR Art. 4(7)), dataProcessor (GDPR Art. 4(8)), dpo (GDPR Art. 37), modelDeveloper (Art. 53 foundation-model provisions; ISO/IEC 23894), and modelEvaluator (NIST AI RMF MAP/MEASURE). Multiple entries per role are permitted.

Worked example. A chain naming the audit operator, the EU provider, the EU deployer, and the authorised representative:

mx:
  parties:
    - role: auditOperator
      name: Tom Cranstoun
      email: info@cognovamx.com
      identifier: https://allabout.network
      organisation: Digital Domain Technologies Ltd (trading as CogNovaMX)
      country: GB
    - role: provider
      name: Example Insurance plc
      email: ai-governance@example-insurance.com
      identifier: did:web:example-insurance.com
      organisation: Example Insurance plc
      country: IE
    - role: deployer
      name: Example Insurance Operations
      email: deployer-ops@example-insurance.com
      identifier: did:web:example-insurance-ops.com
      organisation: Example Insurance Operations Ltd
      country: DE
    - role: authorisedRepresentative
      name: EU Representative GmbH
      email: rep@eu-rep-firm.com
      identifier: did:web:eu-rep-firm.com
      organisation: EU Representative GmbH
      country: DE
  frameworks:
    - id: EU-AI-Act
      version: '2024/1689'
      jurisdiction: EU
      appliesTo: all-steps
    - id: EU-EAA-Directive-2019-882
      version: '2019/882'
      jurisdiction: EU
      appliesTo: accessibility-steps
    - id: US-NIST-AI-RMF
      version: '1.0'
      jurisdiction: 'US (voluntary federal framework)'
      appliesTo: all-steps
  runRevision: 3
  lastWriteAt: 2026-05-28T09:18:00Z

Per-step example. A render step that satisfies EU AI Act Article 12 and NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.1:

steps:
  - stepId: pdf-render
    timestamp: 2026-05-28T09:17:42Z
    agent: mx.pdf.sh
    outcome: pass
    jurisdictionalEvidence:
      EU-AI-Act:
        article: '12'
        claim: automated-log
      US-NIST-AI-RMF:
        function: MEASURE
        category: MEASURE 2.1

Flat surfaces alongside the structured shape. Every sidecar also has a single-block responsiblePerson at the top, mirroring the auditOperator entry from parties[], and a flat frameworksCited string array drawn from frameworks[].id. The structured fields are the canonical source; the flat surfaces mirror them so a script reading either shape gets the same answers.

Schema. Top-level shape declared at https://mx.allabout.network/schemas/provenance-ai/v2 (AI stream) and https://mx.allabout.network/schemas/provenance-deterministic/v2 (its deterministic counterpart). The full position paper at provenance-regime-compatibility.md documents how an operator extends the chain for a regime not yet in the default registry.

Decision-record fields

A decision record is the audit trail an AI system produces when it acts. Every model invocation against every policy version is a discrete event. The fields below appear together in a single record, share one schema family with content cogs, and are attested through the same trust layer.

Field Type Required Definition Reference
decisionId string required Stable identifier for the decision event itself. Typically a ULID generated at the moment the model returns. REGINALD PRD §4.2
operator string required DID or other stable identifier of the organisation accountable for the decision. The operator is who a regulator walks back to when an inquiry opens. PRD §4.2
issued string (ISO-8601) required Timestamp of the decision event. Resolves the policyRef to the policy version in force at that moment. PRD §4.2, §7.3
policyRef object required Structured reference to the policy clause that authorised the action. Carries registry URI, the policy cogUrn, the policy version, and an optional clause fragment. Resolves against the policy as it stood at issued. PRD §4.2; mx-shared-gathering/draft-policy-records.md
model object required Identifier and version of the model that produced the output. Operator-controlled vocabulary; the registry indexes the structure, not the meaning. PRD §4.2
inputHash string required Digest of the input the model saw before deciding. The raw input stays with the operator; a regulator recovers it on demand by hash-match. The registry never holds the input itself. PRD §4.2
inputClass string optional Opaque category covering the input shape (e.g. claim, query, prescription) without exposing the input content. Used by aggregators that need shape statistics over many decisions. PRD §4.2
outputSummary string required Short factual statement of what the model decided. Not the input. Not the full output. The statement the operator stands behind for audit. PRD §4.2
humanInLoop object required Boolean plus stage description for whether a human reviewed the decision and where in the chain. Possible stages: none, pre-decision, post-decision-blocking, post-decision-advisory. PRD §4.2; mx-shared-gathering/draft-decision-records.md
sequence integer optional Position of this decision in a chain of related decisions across time. Used when later decisions reference, refine, or reverse earlier ones; the registry resolves chains by walking the sequence. PRD §4.2
reviewer object optional Identifier of the human reviewer when humanInLoop indicates human involvement. DID or other operator-controlled identifier. mx-shared-gathering/draft-decision-records.md
originalDraft string (cogUrn) optional Pointer to the cog containing the unmodified model output when the published decision was edited before issuance. Lets reviewers walk from the published decision to what the model first produced. mx-shared-gathering/draft-decision-records.md

The decision record is not specific to commerce. The same field set covers an AI assistant recommending a healthcare option, a benefits-decision system approving or denying a claim, and an incident-routing agent assigning a ticket. It covers a contract-drafting tool producing an amendment and a commerce agent acting on a shopper's behalf in the same way. Where Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) attests web-surface commerce purchases under a platform-governed standard, the decision record covers every other category under the same vendor-neutral primitives.

Policy-record fields

A policy record is a regulatory code published as a cog. Each clause is addressable by ID; each version is stable; each amendment supersedes the prior one through the same currency machinery that handles content cog versions.

Field Type Required Definition Reference
policyId string required Stable identifier for the policy itself across versions. mx-shared-gathering/draft-policy-records.md
policyVersion string required Version of this specific policy snapshot. Decision records reference both policyId and policyVersion to pin the decision to a specific text. draft-policy-records.md
issuingBody string required DID or stable identifier of the regulator or authority publishing the policy. draft-policy-records.md
jurisdiction string required Geographic and legal jurisdiction the policy applies in. draft-policy-records.md
effectiveFrom string (ISO-8601) required Date the policy comes into force. draft-policy-records.md
supersedes string (cogUrn) optional Pointer to the prior policy version this record replaces. Lets agents follow version chains and verify they are quoting the current text. draft-policy-records.md
clauses array required Addressable clauses, each with a stable identifier inside the policy. Decision records can reference a specific clause via the clause fragment in policyRef. draft-policy-records.md

Attestation-record fields

A signed cog's attestation is a separate record. The cog declares its data; the attestation references the cog by ID and digest and holds the signature.

Field Type Required Definition Reference
contentType: attestation enum required Declares the record as an attestation rather than a content cog. Trust wrappers are themselves data files conforming to a cog schema. PRD §1.6, §3.4
cogUrn string required The URN of the cog being attested. The attestation never embeds the cog itself. PRD §3.4
digest string required Hash of the cog's canonical bytes (RFC 8785 JCS canonicalisation, SHA-256). Verifier compares to the digest of bytes retrieved at the canonical URI. PRD §3.4
signature string required Ed25519 signature over the digest. For batch attestations, this is the Merkle root signature with a per-cog inclusion proof carried separately. PRD §3.4; RFC 8032
signer string (DID) required DID of the publisher or trust layer that produced the signature. Verifier resolves the DID document to obtain the public key. PRD §3.4; W3C DID
signed string (ISO-8601) required Timestamp of the signing event. PRD §3.4
inclusionProof object optional RFC 6962 Merkle inclusion proof when the attestation is part of a batch. Verifier walks the proof from the leaf to the signed root. PRD §3.4; RFC 6962

The mechanism is identical to Certificate Transparency: one signed root attests every leaf, provided each retains its inclusion proof. Attestation per cog (one signature each) and in batch (one signed root plus per-cog proofs) use the same field set. The registry serves whichever shape the publisher submitted.

Where the vocabulary is documented

Surface What it carries
mx-canon/ssot/fields-data.yaml canonicalUrn and the rest of the canonical field dictionary
mx-reginald/ The REGINALD v-next implementation (its PRD is archived per ADR 26); the decision-record, policy-record, and attestation-record field families are catalogued in this appendix
mx-shared-gathering/draft-decision-records.md Decision-record schema details
mx-shared-gathering/draft-policy-records.md Policy-record schema details
mx-shared-gathering/draft-cogs.md Cog format including the carrier-preservation rule for HTML
mx-canon/mx-the-gathering/specifications/cog-unified-spec.cog.md Unified cog specification (structure and lifecycle)
datalake/manuscripts/mx-books/mx-protocols/protocols/chapter-20/ Reader-facing introduction to cogs, REGINALD, decision records, and the QR-to-COG bridge
This appendix §22.A (here) Reference table for the identity and decision-record field families

The lockstep rule requires changes to any one surface to propagate to the others. This reference table closes the gap between what readers see in the prose and what they find when they look the fields up in the canon.

22.B Outbound communication and audience-targeting family

The fields below cover two clusters that recurred enough across CRM contact-message cogs, blog posts, and the publisher AI Usage Declaration to warrant canonisation. The cluster names are descriptive only; each field stands alone in the dictionary.

Audience-targeting companion to audience

Field Type Required Definition Reference
