targetReaders string optional Narrative description of the specific audience this document is written for. Companion to audience: audience carries the broad enum (humans, machines, tech, business, agents, both); targetReaders carries the sentence-form description of who the document is for. Both can coexist. -
intendedAgeRange string optional Intended human age band for the content, expressed as a range. A third companion to audience: where audience carries the human-versus-machine readership category and targetReaders the sentence-form reader, intendedAgeRange carries the age band. Mirrors Schema.org typicalAgeRange and follows the same convention (13- means 13 and up; 8-12, 18+, and allAges are also valid). Schema.org typicalAgeRange

Worked example in a blog frontmatter:

mx:
  audience: [business, humans, machines]
  targetReaders: "Boards and executives at organisations deploying agentic AI, plus the technical teams implementing the supporting evidence chains."

The companion shape is deliberate. The enum stays tight enough that a machine can filter on it. The sentence stays free enough that a human writer can name the actual reader. Voice calibration, tone choices, and the level of background knowledge to assume all depend on the sentence rather than the enum.

intendedAgeRange is a pass-through mirror. When a page declares the age band in its Schema.org JSON-LD (typicalAgeRange, or an Audience with requiredMinAge / suggestedMinAge / suggestedMaxAge), that declaration is authoritative; the frontmatter field restates it so a reader working from the YAML alone does not have to parse the JSON-LD. A page that targets younger readers carries it alongside the enum:

mx:
  audience: [humans]
  intendedAgeRange: "8-12"

Carried into HTML, the same value travels as <meta name="mx:intendedAgeRange" content="8-12"> next to the Schema.org typicalAgeRange in the page's JSON-LD.

Outbound-communication fields

Field Type Required Definition Reference
sentAt string (ISO-8601) optional Timestamp when an outbound communication (email, message, letter, call) was actually delivered to the recipient. Mutable. Distinct from created (origination of the draft) and modified (latest edit). -
channel string (enum) optional The medium used to deliver a direct-message cog. Enum: email, linkedin, phone, video-call, slack, signal, in-person, letter, other. -
attachments array of objects optional Files attached to a direct-message or carried alongside a document. Each entry is an object with path (relative or absolute) and label (human-readable description visible in the receiving system). -

Worked example in an outbound-email cog:

mx:
  status: sent
  sentAt: 2026-05-27
  contentType: direct-message
  channel: email
  attachments:
    - path: ../../../mx-outputs/audit/2026-05-27/example.com/example-report.pdf
      label: MX audit of example.com (PDF, 2026-05-27, EAA-compatible)

The three fields are siblings inside the mx: block. sentAt flips when status goes from draft to sent. channel is set at draft time and rarely changes. attachments may grow as the draft evolves but should be final at send. A CRM tooling layer can index these directly without parsing the prose body.

Publisher AI-usage declaration

Field Type Required Definition Reference
aiUsageDeclaration object optional Publisher's structured declaration of how AI was used in producing this work. Sits at top level (parallel to mx:) because it is a publisher-wide declaration referenced by individual works rather than a per-cog operational field. draft-cranstoun-mx-ai-usage-declaration

Worked example in the publisher's master AI-USAGE.md:

aiUsageDeclaration:
  id: https://mx.allabout.network/AI-USAGE.json
  conformance:
    draft: draft-cranstoun-mx-ai-usage-declaration
    draftVersion: "1.0"
    level: 1
    levelName: Declared

Top-level placement is deliberate. The declaration travels intact into the JSON serialisation at mx-site/AI-USAGE.json, the HTML rendering at mx-site/AI-USAGE.html, and the PDF at mx-site/AI-USAGE.pdf, all derived from the master markdown. A reader extracting the declaration from any of those carriers gets the same structure. Individual works that need to point at the publisher's declaration carry an aiUsageDeclaration.id pointing at the master JSON.

22.C Applicability - the conditions under which content is in force

audience names the readers for whom a document is written. applicability says under what conditions the document is in force. The two are independent: a guide can be written for developers and apply only in the EU, only on product releases three and above, and only from a date that has not yet arrived.

The distinction matters because a machine assembling an answer has to decide which of several documents governs the reader in front of it. Without a declaration it either returns all of them and lets the reader sort it out, or it picks one and hopes. Applicability is what turns that guess into a filter.

applicability is a Zone 2 object. Its sub-fields are registered individually because each carries semantics a reader must interpret rather than merely display.

Field Type Required Definition Reference
applicability object optional The conditions under which this document's content is in force. A reader that does not match a declared condition treats the document as not applicable to it. -
applicability.jurisdiction array optional The legal or regulatory regimes in which the content is in force. ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes and ISO 3166-2 subdivision codes, or a named regime no ISO code expresses (EU, EEA). ISO 3166
applicability.product string or array optional The product or products the content applies to. Publisher-defined identifiers. -
applicability.productVersion string optional The range of product releases the content applies to, written as a semantic-version range expression. Semantic Versioning
applicability.role array optional The reader roles the content applies to. Freetext names drawn from the publisher's own access model. -
applicability.platform array optional The platforms or runtime environments the content applies to. -
applicability.effectiveFrom string (ISO-8601) optional The date from which the content is in force. ISO 8601
applicability.effectiveUntil string (ISO-8601) optional The date after which the content is no longer in force. ISO 8601

Worked example in a maintenance procedure that is regionally and version-bound:

mx:
  audience: [tech, humans, machines]
  applicability:
    jurisdiction: [EU, EEA]
    product: turbine-controller
    productVersion: '>=4.2 <6.0'
    role: [certified-engineer]
    effectiveFrom: 2026-09-01
    effectiveUntil: 2027-06-30

How A Reader Evaluates It

Conditions combine with AND across axes and OR within an axis. The example above applies to a certified engineer, in the EU or the EEA, working on a turbine controller between releases 4.2 and 6.0, during the stated window. Failing any one axis puts the document out of scope for that reader.

An omitted sub-field means unconstrained on that axis, never excluded. A document with no applicability block at all applies everywhere, which keeps the field additive: existing content does not change meaning when the vocabulary arrives.

Fields It Is Not

Four adjacent fields answer different questions, and collapsing any of them loses information a reader needs.

inLanguage declares the language of the prose body and never a place. German prose can be in force in Austria. Content in force across the EU is often published in English. Language and jurisdiction vary independently.

Schema.org spatialCoverage says what place the content is about, and applicability.jurisdiction where it is in force. A guide written in the United Kingdom about Japanese planning law has spatialCoverage Japan and jurisdiction GB. Subject matter defers to Schema.org, which is the same boundary the field-triage rubric's Rule 1 draws: a field must describe the document, not the document's subject.

expires is a review-or-archive prompt. It says someone should look at this again, and the content stays applicable until they do. applicability.effectiveUntil is a hard boundary: past it the content does not apply, whether or not anyone has acted. A document can carry both, and effectiveUntil is the one a reader enforces.

version is the revision of the document. applicability.productVersion is the range of releases of the thing the document describes. A document at version 4 can describe product releases 2 and 3, and the two numbers have no relationship to each other.

22.Q Internationalisation and translation

MX describes a document's language, its money and date conventions, its relationship to a translation, and the terms it binds, deferring to the established standards rather than inventing new vocabulary.

Language. inLanguage declares the language of the document's content as a BCP 47 tag (en, es, en-GB), the tag Schema.org inLanguage and Dublin Core dc:language both use. Declare it on any document not written in the estate's default language, and on every translation.

Currency. currency declares the document's default currency for monetary references as an ISO 4217 three-letter code (EUR, USD, GBP), as Schema.org priceCurrency does. It is a document-level default, not a per-price field.

Dates. Every machine-read date in frontmatter is ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD, or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ with a timezone), so a machine never has to disambiguate a value like 01/07/2026. dateFormat is an optional declaration of the convention used for dates in the human-facing body: one of iso-8601 (the default), dmy, mdy, or ymd.

Translation. A translation is a distinct document that points at its source. On the translation, translationOfWork holds the canonicalUri of the source work (Schema.org translationOfWork). On the source, workTranslation lists the canonicalUri of each translation (the inverse, Schema.org workTranslation). translator names who or what performed the translation, a person or a model identifier (Schema.org translator). The translation event is also recorded as a document.translation step in the translation's AI provenance sidecar, naming the source content hash and the source and target languages, so a reader can trace who translated what, from which exact source, and when.

Example. An English letter and its Spanish translation:

# apology.md (source)
mx:
  inLanguage: en
  workTranslation:
    - https://mx.allabout.network/letters/apology-es.md
# apology-es.md (translation)
mx:
  inLanguage: es
  currency: EUR
  dateFormat: iso-8601
  translationOfWork: https://mx.allabout.network/letters/apology.md
  translator: Maxine (claude-opus-4-8)

The document.translation step on apology-es.provenance.ai.json:

{
  "stepId": "document.translation",
  "agent": "claude-opus-4-8",
  "intent": "Translate the letter from en to es",
  "inputs": { "sourceDocument": "apology.md", "sourceSha": "<git-hash>", "sourceLanguage": "en" },
  "outputs": { "targetLanguage": "es" },
  "humanIntervention": "review-after",
  "outcome": "pass"
}

Terms. termGlossary binds the key terms of a document to their senses, so a reader, a translator or an agent applies the declared sense instead of inferring one from the word. Each key is a term as the document writes it. The simplest value is the sense, in one sentence. A document bound for translation can give an object instead. Its sense key holds the meaning, and render, keyed by BCP 47 language tag, holds the term a translation must use. The avoid key, keyed the same way, lists renderings known to be wrong, and loanwords to avoid where the target language has its own word. A key corresponds to a concept entry in TBX (TermBase eXchange), whose terms carry an administrative status: the render term is the preferred term and each avoid term a deprecated one. Declare only the terms a wrong reading would change.

Example. A Spanish property letter, and an English report bound for a German translation:

# a Spanish property letter
mx:
  inLanguage: es
  termGlossary:
    notario: State-appointed mandatory signatory for property transactions under Spanish civil law; not a party's legal representative.
# an English audit report that will be translated into German
mx:
  inLanguage: en
  termGlossary:
    traffic:
      sense: The visits and requests, human or machine, arriving at a site.
      render:
        de: Zugriffe
      avoid:
        de: [Verkehr, Traffic]

22.S volatileValues - a stated value that moves, and where the current one lives

A document can be current as a whole while a figure inside it is not. A room rate, an exchange rate, an interest rate, a stock level, an availability count: each is a snapshot of a value that moves on its own cadence. A document that states one is stating what was true when someone looked. expires cannot carry this, because it retires the whole file. cacheability cannot, because it governs holding a copy of the document, not quoting a number inside it. currency cannot, because it is a document-level default and, as §22.Q says, not a per-price field. The volatileValues field is the per-value declaration those three leave open. It flags the figure as a snapshot, records when it was observed and until when it may be quoted, and points at the mechanism a machine calls for the current value. A machine that reads it stops treating the stated number as the answer and starts treating it as a hint with an address.

Sub-key Type Required Definition Reference
kind string yes What class of value moves: price, exchange-rate, interest-rate, availability, stock-level, capacity, other MX
subject string yes What the value describes, in plain words MX
appliesTo string no A URL fragment or selector naming where the value sits in the body RFC 3986
statedAt string yes The date-time at which the stated value was observed ISO 8601
validUntil string yes The date-time after which the stated value must not be quoted as current ISO 8601; aligns with Schema.org priceValidUntil
currency string no The value's currency code; defaults to the document currency ISO 4217; aligns with Schema.org priceCurrency
resolveVia object yes The mechanism that returns the current value: url, optional cogUrn, method (get, post, feed, page, contact), format (a media type), cadence (an ISO 8601 duration between refreshes), access (public, key, partner) Aligns with Schema.org EntryPoint
onStale string yes What an agent does after validUntil: resolve (call the mechanism, never quote the stated value), quote-dated (quote the stated value with its statedAt date), omit (leave the value out) MX 
mx:
  currency: GBP
  volatileValues:
    - kind: price
      subject: Standard room, one night
      appliesTo: "#rates"
      statedAt: "2026-09-09T10:00:00Z"
      validUntil: "2026-09-10T10:00:00Z"
      resolveVia:
        url: https://example.com/api/rates?room=standard
        method: get
        format: application/json
        cadence: PT1H
        access: public
      onStale: resolve
    - kind: availability
      subject: Rooms free on the requested night
      statedAt: "2026-09-09T10:00:00Z"
      validUntil: "2026-09-09T11:00:00Z"
      resolveVia:
        url: https://example.com/api/availability
        method: get
        format: application/json
        cadence: PT15M
        access: partner
      onStale: omit

The mechanism does the work. A validity window alone tells a machine when to stop trusting the number. It does not tell the machine where to go instead, so an agent comparing live values either quotes a stale figure as current or drops the page from the comparison because it has nothing to compare. resolveVia.url closes that gap in the file itself. resolveVia.cogUrn is the registry form of the same pointer. A publisher registers one mechanism record as a cog: the endpoint, its format, its cadence, its access terms. A registry attests it, and every document stating a value from it then points at the attested record instead of repeating the endpoint. What the registry attests is the pointer and the publisher's declaration about it, never the live value. The agent resolves the value at the mechanism, at the moment it matters.

Fields It Is Not

volatileValues does not replace Schema.org Offer. On a product page the offer still carries price, priceCurrency, priceValidUntil, and availability, because that is where a search engine or a shopping agent looks for them. volatileValues is the document-level statement that those figures are snapshots and where the live ones are resolved, and it applies to every carrier and every kind of volatile value, not only to products and not only to prices. It differs from temporalAnchors, which names dates the prose depends on; a volatile value is a figure, not a date. It also differs from expires, which retires the whole file; a document declaring volatileValues stays authoritative while its figures do not.

22.T The temporal-stance family - a document's relationship to the dates it describes

Many documents depend on dates that can move: a regulatory analysis written before an application date, a contract clause counted from a renewal, a compliance report measured against a deadline the legislator can shift. Without a shared vocabulary, one author bakes the date into prose, another computes "days until" in page script, and a reader cannot tell a fixed one from an anchor. The four fields below, defined by the Gathering's MX Temporal Stance note, let a document declare that relationship. A render-time agent can then compute from anchors, a steward can see what to rewrite when an anchor moves, and a verifier can read the temporal contract without parsing the prose.

The temporalStance field declares the relationship in one word. frozen means the prose records state at publication and its dates are history. living means the prose reflects state at fetch time, and date-derived values are recomputed against the reader's clock. anchored means the prose contains values computed from declared anchors and moves with them; an anchored document declares temporalAnchors, and a frozen one never declares an anchor that can move.

The temporalAnchors field names the dates the prose depends on, one stable kebab-case identifier per anchor, each carrying its current date, a description, and where the authoritative value is published elsewhere a source. The temporalComputedFields field names values computed from those anchors at render time (from an anchor or the literal now, with a compute of daysUntil, daysSince, monthsUntil, monthsSince, quartersUntil, quartersSince, or dateValue, and an optional format hint). A render-time agent treats an unknown anchor as a failure rather than a default, and never caches the result beyond one render. The temporalProseGuidance field tells a future steward what to review when an anchor moves: onMove, the affectedSections as URL fragments, and softCutoff when a move inside a tolerance needs no rewrite.

mx:
  temporalStance: anchored
  temporalAnchors:
    eu-ai-act-application:
      date: "2026-08-02"
      description: "EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations become applicable."
      source: "https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689"
    contract-renewal:
      date: "2027-04-30"
      description: "Master service agreement renewal date."
  temporalComputedFields:
    daysUntilApplication:
      from: eu-ai-act-application
      compute: daysUntil
      format: integer
  temporalProseGuidance:
    eu-ai-act-application:
      onMove: "Re-read the day-one section. If the anchor moves more than 30 days, rewrite the run-up timetable."
      affectedSections: ["#what-changes-on-day-one", "#run-up-timetable"]
      softCutoff: true

An anchor whose date changes is a substantive edit: the document's modified moves, and the steward reviews the prose against the guidance. A computed value is excluded from any signature scope, because it changes on every render. The family is about dates the prose depends on; a figure that moves on its own cadence, a price or a rate, is volatileValues (section 22.S), and the date after which the whole file stops being authoritative is expires.

22.U resource - the one asset a document describes

The resource field, reserved by OKF at the top level, names the single external asset a document describes: the dataset a data card is about, the endpoint an API note documents, the image a caption record accompanies. It belongs to Zone 1b at the top level, never under mx:, and it is optional on every profile: an abstract document (a playbook, a runbook, an info-doc) that describes no single asset omits it. It is distinct from refersToExternal, the plural array of cited sources under mx:. The two are never merged, and the OKF field map declares a resource value equal to any refersToExternal entry an error. The value should be a URI; consumers are permissive about its scheme.

---
title: "BigQuery GA4 ecommerce dataset"
description: "Sample of obfuscated GA4 BigQuery event export data."
type: dataset-card
tags: [analytics, bigquery]
resource: https://bigquery.googleapis.com/v2/projects/bigquery-public-data/datasets/ga4_obfuscated_sample_ecommerce
mx:
  status: active
  refersToExternal:
    - "GA4 documentation: https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/7029846"
---

22.AJ The Context Declaration pair - what a document offers, and what it needs first

A machine that meets a file has to decide what to read before it can use it, and without a declaration it guesses. Two fields end the guessing. contextProvides (string or array) states what knowledge this document contributes to a reader's context window, in the reader's terms rather than the author's. contextRequired (array of repo-root-relative paths, in reading order) states the files a reader must load before it can use this document safely. Together they give a corpus a self-documenting dependency graph, so an agent assembling context knows what each file offers and where to start.

mx:
  contextProvides:
    - "How the audit pipeline caches origin probes and when to bump a cache version"
    - "The two-class distinction between swept and self-managed caches"
  contextRequired:
    - mx-reginald/audit/mx-audit-architecture.cog.md
    - scripts/audit-pipeline.js

An empty contextRequired is a statement that nothing is prerequisite, not an omission; a document that needs prior reading and says nothing has handed the reader a guess. The ai block's code-carrier notation (ai.contextProvides, ai.contextRequired set in source) describes what a code file contributes and stays with the carrier dictionary. The document-level pair here is what a cog, a paper, or a page declares.

22.V The reuse-policy pair - contentPolicy and attribution

A machine that reads a document decides at that moment what it may do with the content: summarise it, quote it, extract it whole, or leave it alone. Search engines answer the question with the robots nosnippet and max-snippet directives; the MX HTML carrier answers it with the mx:contentPolicy tag. The contentPolicy field is the frontmatter form, so the answer travels with the file. Its value is a recognised token (summaries-allowed, full-extraction-allowed, extract-with-attribution, no-extraction, restricted) or a plain-language statement when none fits, which is the usual case on a binary asset whose terms are prose. The attribution field is its partner: required makes a credit a condition of reuse, requested asks for one but makes nothing depend on it, and not-required expects none. The credit itself is built from author and citeAs. This pair only states what may be done and whether a credit is owed.

mx:
  contentPolicy: extract-with-attribution
  attribution: required
  trainingDataPolicy: permitted-with-attribution

The pair is the inference-time half of the consumption policy. trainingDataPolicy and aiTraining govern the training half, and doNotIndex governs discovery; a document can permit indexing and summaries while forbidding training, and each of the three questions has its own field so a reader never infers one answer from another.

22.W alternateFormats and citeAs - the other renderings, and the identifier to cite

HTML has two discovery links for which markdown has had no field. <link rel="alternate" type="..."> names another rendering of the same document, and <link rel="cite-as"> (RFC 8574) names the persistent identifier to cite. The alternateFormats field is the frontmatter form of the first: an array of objects, each with the rendering's uri and its format as an IANA media type, so an agent that prefers markdown or JSON fetches that instead of scraping the HTML. It aligns with Schema.org encoding. A translation is not an alternate format; that is workTranslation, carried in HTML as rel="alternate" with hreflang.

The citeAs field is the frontmatter form of the second: a DOI, an ARK, a URN, or a stable URL. canonicalUri says where the current copy lives and may change when a site moves; citeAs says what to write in a reference list and does not. When it is absent, canonicalUri is the citation target.

mx:
  canonicalUri: https://mx.allabout.network/blog/example.html
  citeAs: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1234567
  alternateFormats:
    - uri: https://mx.allabout.network/blog/example.md
      format: text/markdown
    - uri: https://mx.allabout.network/blog/example.pdf
      format: application/pdf

22.X contentRating - audience suitability

HTML's <meta name="rating"> tells a search engine whether a page may be shown to a given reader; Schema.org expresses the same fact as contentRating. The contentRating field is the frontmatter form: a rating such as general, mature, adult, or a named scheme's value (PEGI 12). Absent means no rating is claimed, not that the content is suitable for everyone. It is distinct from readingLevel, which says how hard the prose is, and from audience, which names the readers for whom the document is written.

mx:
  contentRating: general
  readingLevel: intermediate

22.Y aiUsageDeclarationUri - where the publisher's AI usage declaration lives

The MX AI Usage Declaration note asks every page on a declaring host to carry <link rel="ai-usage" href="/AI-USAGE.json">, and a work with its own narrower declaration to point at that one instead. The aiUsageDeclarationUri field is the frontmatter form of that link. It is the pointer, not the record. aiUsageDeclaration is the object the declaring page itself carries, and this field is how any other document names the one that governs it. Its sibling provenanceUri names the per-file provenance chain; this field names the publisher-level disclosure.

mx:
  aiUsageDeclarationUri: https://mx.allabout.network/AI-USAGE.json
  provenanceUri: https://mx.allabout.network/blog/example.mxprov.json

22.Z entities - the named things a document is about

Schema.org's mentions property, carried in JSON-LD or as an itemprop, names the specific things a page discusses. The entities field is the frontmatter form: an array of stable identifiers (a Wikidata QID, an ORCID iD, an organisation's domain name) rather than bare names, because the identifier is what makes the declaration checkable. It is distinct from topic, which names subject areas, and from tags, which are discovery keywords.

mx:
  topic: [machine-experience, metadata]
  entities:
    - https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q95
    - https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097

22.AA The component family - the fields a rendered component carries

MX metadata is defined at the file, and a reader meets an object at a smaller grain: a card in a list, a badge beside a heading, a panel in an editor, a row in a registry. If the metadata stops at the file boundary, every rendering below it can lose the provenance, and most do. The component family, defined by the MX Component Standard, is the set of fields that lets the human and the machine reading a rendered object receive the same metadata. A component has the root fields (identity, provenance, relationships, signals) and, optionally, the fields below for how it presents them. The component kind is a value of the OKF type field: component:provenanceBadge, component:objectCard, component:relationshipLine, component:verificationPanel, component:narrativeLayer, component:gridMount, component:signalBar, component:objectInspector. Every field in the family is optional; the component profile declares the set.

Component Field Type Purpose
Provenance badge displayMode compact or expanded What the badge shows first; every trust signal stays one interaction away
Provenance badge icon URI or token name The icon the badge renders
Provenance badge verificationChanged ISO 8601 datetime The last change in verification state, conveyed in text before any motion
Object card preview URI A preview rendering of the object
Object card actions array of name, target, verifiability, withheldFrom The actions offered, the same list for both audiences, a withholding declared rather than silent
Relationship line relationshipField relationship field name The carrying field, which is also the direction
Relationship line inferred boolean Inferred rather than declared by the publisher
Relationship line visualWeight token name Derived from confidence when inferred, fixed when declared
Any component attestationStatus unattested, pending, attested, withdrawn Whether an attestation exists at all, so a considered unattested is distinguishable from an oversight
Verification panel verificationSummary string One-line outcome of the trail
Verification panel verificationSteps array of timestamp, agent, method, outcome The trail, in the provenance sidecar's step vocabulary
Verification panel finalConfidence number, 0 to 1 Confidence in the trail, never a combined trust score
Verification panel confidenceMethod string How the confidence was derived
Narrative layer cue string A short human-facing note beside the component
Narrative layer narrativeContext URI Fuller editorial context for a human reader
Grid mount gridUnit number with unit The base layout unit
Grid mount layoutConstraints array of object Declared layout, so position carries no meaning the metadata does not
Grid mount snapPoints array The positions a component may occupy
Signal bar barState field and value The bound field and its value, never a state that exists only in the rendering
Any component validationStatus string, such as PASS or FAIL Outcome of the most recent validation of the object or of the run it reports; a signal bar commonly binds to it
Signal bar pulse boolean Motion in addition to text, never instead of it
Signal bar styleToken token name One token per state, so a state looks the same everywhere
Object inspector inspectorSections array of name, fields The groups the inspector presents the fields in, in a stable order
Any component attestationRecord URI or object The registry's attestation record, or a pointer to it: who published this, and when. Reported beside currency, freshness and corroboration, never folded into one score

Three names differ from the words a reader might reach for first. narrativeContext is not context, which is the folder-metadata domain object; inspectorSections is not sections, an existing extended field; layoutConstraints is not constraints, to stay clear of context.constraints. The family is flat and camelCase like every other MX field, and it keeps the same spelling in every carrier: <meta name="mx:displayMode" content="compact"> in HTML, mx:displayMode in XMP.

A document that stands for an object card declares the kind and the fields it needs:

type: component:objectCard
mx:
  canonicalUri: https://example.com/papers/provenance-and-the-regulator.md
  authorship: solo
  attestationRecord: https://reginald.example.com/records/provenance-and-the-regulator
  displayMode: compact
  preview: https://example.com/previews/provenance-and-the-regulator.png
  actions:
    - name: open
      target: https://example.com/papers/provenance-and-the-regulator.html
      verifiability: deterministic
    - name: export-provenance
      target: https://example.com/papers/provenance-and-the-regulator.provenance.json
      verifiability: deterministic
      withheldFrom: [humans]

A verification panel shows the trail and its outcome, with freshness read from the registry rather than asserted by the object:

type: component:verificationPanel
mx:
  canonicalUri: https://example.com/papers/provenance-and-the-regulator.md
  verificationSummary: "Attested by the publisher, current version, publisher active, one claim corroborated."
  verificationSteps:
    - timestamp: "2026-09-17T08:51:12Z"
      agent: reginald.example.com
      method: ed25519-signature-check
      outcome: pass
    - timestamp: "2026-09-17T08:51:13Z"
      agent: check-blog-corroboration.cjs
      method: corroboration-source-resolves
      outcome: pass
  finalConfidence: 0.92
  confidenceMethod: weighted-step-outcomes
  verificationChanged: "2026-09-17T08:51:13Z"

A relationship line, a narrative layer, a grid mount, a signal bar, and an inspector each carry their own subset:

type: component:relationshipLine
mx:
  relationshipField: buildsOn
  inferred: false
  visualWeight: token:mx-line-declared
---
type: component:narrativeLayer
mx:
  cue: "Read alongside the regime registry before quoting a date."
  narrativeContext: https://example.com/blog/provenance-is-an-evidence-vehicle.html
---
type: component:gridMount
mx:
  gridUnit: 8px
  layoutConstraints:
    - component: provenanceBadge
      adjacentTo: objectCard
  snapPoints: [0, 8, 16, 24]
---
type: component:signalBar
mx:
  barState:
    field: validationStatus
    value: valid
  pulse: false
  styleToken: token:mx-state-valid
---
type: component:objectInspector
mx:
  inspectorSections:
    - name: identity
      fields: [title, canonicalUri, version, created, modified]
    - name: provenance
      fields: [authorship, generatedBy, provenanceUri]
    - name: trust
      fields: [attestation, integritySignature]

An agent reading a component reads the declared field rather than inferring it from the rendering: authorship says whether a person wrote the text, relationshipField says which object came first, and the separate trust signals say which one is missing instead of a single yes or no. A renderer that mirrors each field it shows into the DOM (data-mx-display-mode beside a badge, data-mx-component on every root) gives the agent the same value the human sees. The family is defined in the MX Component Standard concept paper and was approved by The Gathering on 2026-09-17; the fields are canonical in this dictionary.

22.AB workflowId and workflowRecord - the boundary a chain ran under

A provenance record proves what happened: which agent took which step, on which inputs, with which human standing behind it. It does not, on its own, say what the agent was allowed to do. That declaration belongs in a workflow record, the document that declares the workflow-record profile (§2): agentTasks and agentAuthority name the scope, reviewPoints names where a human decides, and unintendedActions records the residual risk the operator accepted. workflowId is the handle of that record and workflowRecord is its location. A reader asking whether an agent stayed inside its declared boundary then walks from the trail to the declaration in one step instead of inferring the scope from the steps.

Both are core fields: the trail is public, so it may not depend on a vendor extension. A document produced under a governed workflow declares them in its mx: block. A provenance record, being a JSON carrier with no second zone, carries them at the top level beside target, on both files of the pair, so either file met on its own names the boundary it ran under.

mx:
  provenanceOrigin: ai-assisted
  provenanceUri: https://mx.allabout.network/blog/governance-when-ai-acts.mxprov.json
  workflowId: draft-triage-2026-09
  workflowRecord: workflows/draft-triage.md
{
  "$schema": "https://mx.allabout.network/schemas/provenance-ai/v2",
  "schemaVersion": "2.0",
  "auditId": "q3-2026-09-16",
  "target": "reports/q3-report.md",
  "workflowId": "quarterly-report-drafting",
  "workflowRecord": "workflows/quarterly-report-drafting.md",
  "parties": [],
  "frameworks": [],
  "steps": []
}

workflowId is a slug, one per workflow. A redesign updates the same record, another workflow gets its own identifier, and the record's frontmatter holds the same value as its handle. workflowRecord follows the refersTo convention for a repo-root-relative path and that of refersToExternal for a URL. A null or absent value is an honest absence, never a guessed default. A chain with no workflow record is one whose scope was never declared, and a reader should weigh it as such. The pair complements provenanceUri, which points from a document to its chain. These two point from the chain to the boundary it was meant to stay inside.

22.AC residualRisk - what remains after the controls

A reader who has followed workflowId to the declared boundary and read the steps for what happened has one question left, and it is the one a regulator asks last: what risk does the operator judge to remain after those controls? residualRisk is that statement. It is a declaration, not a computation, and never defaulted: an absent block means no residual-risk statement was made, not that the risk is low.

The block has four keys. level reuses the security.riskLevel vocabulary (low, medium, high, critical), so one risk scale serves the action-cog, the workflow record, and the provenance chain, and a reader can compare them directly. basis is the one sentence stating why that level remains. Without it the level is a number nobody can check. acceptedBy is the role that accepted the residual risk, drawn from the provenance parties roles (deployer, provider, auditOperator and the rest), because the named person behind it is already in parties. reviewedAt is the date the statement was last reviewed. A statement with no date is read as unreviewed.

mx:
  workflowId: draft-triage-2026-09
  workflowRecord: workflows/draft-triage.md
  residualRisk:
    level: low
    basis: Every model output is reviewed by the editor before it is filed; a misfiled draft is recoverable.
    acceptedBy: deployer
    reviewedAt: 2026-09-17

A provenance record has the same block at the top, beside workflowId, on both files of the pair, written by initProvenance from the caller's declaration and rejected to null when the level is missing or outside the vocabulary. A regime's own classification belongs in that regime's extension room (x-eu-ai-act.riskClassification for the EU AI Act); residualRisk is the regime-neutral statement every reader can weigh without knowing the regime.

22.AD corroboratedBy, contestedBy and quotes - the sources a claim stands on, and the words a document carries

Two fields record what a document owes to other people's work, and they answer different questions. corroboratedBy is the carrier of the corroboration trust signal from 22.P: a flat list of external authoritative URLs that independently state the document's load-bearing claims. It is not a bibliography. refersToExternal says the document read a work; corroboratedBy says an authority states the claim, so a machine deciding whether to act can check that someone independent agrees rather than taking the publisher's word for it. An entry cited nowhere in the body is an orphan and fails the gate, and a URL on the publisher's own host is self-reference, not corroboration. Its other half is contestedBy, the recorded disagreements behind the same claims: an array of objects, each naming the disputed claim, the sources that contest it (a uri and what that source actually states), a status of resolved or unresolved, and the basis on which the document states the claim as it does. Unresolved is a legitimate value; it tells a machine to weight the claim as live rather than settled. An evidence layer that can only record agreement is not one, which is why the two fields are core together.

quotes declares which words in the document are someone else's: external blockquotes, cited passages, and quoted fragments, each entry the exact text as it appears in the body. Its job is to keep the author's writing and the quoted writing apart for every machine that judges prose. A style scanner, a character gate, or a dialect check reads the declared spans and leaves them alone, because the writing of someone else's words is not the author's to rewrite. Only declared spans are exempt; the author's own scare-quoted words stay in scope. A populator fills the field from the body's blockquotes; a fragment quoted inside a sentence is declared by hand. It is distinct from x-mx-allowEmdash, which exempts a span of the author's own prose from the dash rule.

mx:
  refersToExternal:
    - "TypeSafe AI, 15 September 2026, Introducing System One Models and Jev (https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev)"
  corroboratedBy:
    - https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev
    - https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives
  contestedBy:
    - claim: Jev answers in under 500 milliseconds end to end.
      sources:
        - uri: https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev
          states: 70 to 500 milliseconds, measured from the vendor's own laptops on the US West Coast
      status: unresolved
      basis: The figure is the vendor's and no independent measurement exists yet, so the claim is stated as the vendor's.
  quotes:
    - "gives up string generation"
    - "returns a probability distribution over your options or levels, never a value outside them"

Read together: the document cites the launch post, and two of its claims are independently stated by the vendor's own published material. One claim depends on a figure only the vendor has measured, and the document says so. Two fragments of the body are that material's words rather than the author's.

22.AH claimBasis and claims - how each claim is known

corroboratedBy records that an outside source agrees. It says nothing about the claims nobody has checked, and those are the ones a machine most needs to recognise. A statement a user or operator made, an inference a system drew, and a fact an outside authority states all reach a model as indistinguishable text. Once stored and retrieved, the user's own statement comes back looking like grounding, and the more often it is retrieved, the more settled it looks. The claim-basis family records where each claim stands, so a reader can tell what it was told from what has been confirmed.

claims is an array of objects, one per claim that carries weight in the document. Each names the statement and its basis, and each basis holds the evidence it needs:

Basis Meaning Evidence it requires
asserted A party states it and nobody independent has confirmed it. What a user or operator tells a machine is asserted. assertedBy: who stated it
inferred Concluded from other claims or behaviour; nobody stated it directly. inferredFrom: what the conclusion rests on
observed Recorded directly by a named system or person through a stated method. observedBy: who or what recorded it, and how
corroborated An external authoritative source independently states it. corroboratedBy: external URLs, each cited in the body
contested Authoritative sources disagree. A contestedBy block on the document (22.AD)

claimBasis is the document-level summary: the one basis every claim shares, or mixed. A reader that finds no basis for a claim treats it as asserted.

Three rules keep the record honest:

  • Repetition is not evidence. A claim retrieved, quoted, restated or agreed with many times is still asserted. Only an outside source, a direct observation, or a recorded disagreement moves a basis, and revisedBecause names the evidence that moved it.
  • A confidence value belongs to an inference. confidence (0 to 1) is allowed only on an inferred claim, and always travels with confidenceBasis, the reason it has that value. A bare figure cannot say why it dropped. A figure with its reason can.
  • An inference inherits the weakness of its premises. When an inferredFrom entry is itself only asserted, the inferred claim is no better supported than that assertion.

recordedAt dates each claim, so a reader can see how old a basis is.

Some claims are true only for a while: a pending court ruling, a compliance deadline, a figure that is revised, a date a legislator can move. Two dates keep such a claim honest. checkedOn is the date the claim was last verified against the source its basis names; a check that finds it still true moves checkedOn and leaves recordedAt alone. recheckBy is the date by which it must be verified again. Past recheckBy, a reader treats the claim as unverified, whatever its basis, until checkedOn moves past it, and the document is due for review on the earliest recheckBy among its claims. A claim that does not change carries no recheckBy.

mx:
  claims:
    - statement: A French court ordered Carrefour to make its online shop fully accessible within six months.
      basis: corroborated
      corroboratedBy:
        - https://www.faire-face.fr/
      recordedAt: '2026-06-10'
      checkedOn: '2026-10-16'
      recheckBy: '2026-12-04'
mx:
  claimBasis: mixed
  corroboratedBy:
    - https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548
  claims:
    - statement: AI assistants trained on human feedback tend to agree with the user's stated view.
      basis: corroborated
      corroboratedBy:
        - https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548
      recordedAt: '2026-10-06'
    - statement: The supplier delivers on time.
      basis: asserted
      assertedBy: operator
      recordedAt: '2026-10-06'
    - statement: The client prefers short answers.
      basis: inferred
      inferredFrom:
        - session log 2026-10-02, three requests to shorten a reply
      confidence: 0.6
      confidenceBasis: Three requests in one session; no statement from the client.
      recordedAt: '2026-10-02'

Read together: one claim stands on published research, one has only the operator's word behind it, and one is the system's own conclusion, with the reason for its confidence written beside it. A model given this record can still use all three, but it can no longer present the operator's word or its own guess as a checked fact. The family aligns with W3C PROV-O (wasAttributedTo for who asserted, wasDerivedFrom for the premises of an inference) rather than defining a new derivation vocabulary. The entries carry the alignment, not the field: claims[].assertedBy carries prov:wasAttributedTo, claims[].inferredFrom carries prov:wasDerivedFrom, and claims[].statement carries schema:text. Exported as linked data, each claim becomes a node of its own. Its statement, its basis, and the evidence behind it reach a machine together. A source written as a URL becomes a link; any other value stays text. A validator checks the family wherever it is declared on a blog source.

22.AE Evidence fields and the AIMS records - who is accountable, which regimes, and what an AI management system keeps

An auditor reading an organisation's AI management system asks the same questions of every record: who owns this, which requirement does it serve, is it still current, and what was done to the data behind it. Five fields answer those questions on any document, and a profile of four record kinds gives an AI management system (AIMS) a place to keep its inventory, its statement of applicability, its risk register and its impact assessments as COGs.

The evidence fields apply to any document:

Field Type Purpose
parties array of role, name, email, identifier, organisation, country The people and organisations accountable for the document, in the provenance record's shape, with email optional
jurisdictionalEvidence map of regime id to lists of articles, clauses, controls, functions Which parts of which regimes the document provides evidence for, keyed by the ids in the AI-regimes registry
statusNotice reason, date, contact Why a document is disputed or withdrawn, since when, and whom to ask
transformations array of type, method, tool, date, actor The preparation steps applied to the data the document derives from
resourceProfile computeEstimate, energyEstimate, unit, basis, method, baselineRef Compute and energy figures, whether each was measured, estimated or declared, and the baseline it is compared against

parties[].role shares its vocabulary with provenance records and adds the roles an AI management system assigns: systemOwner, riskOwner, assessor, and approver, with decisionOwner and consulted for the decision-right record in 22.AQ. Other fields point at a role rather than repeating a name: residualRisk.acceptedBy, transformations[].actor, and mitigations[].owner each resolve through parties to a person. status has two values for a document's standing: disputed, where the content is under challenge and a consumer weighs it as contested, and withdrawn, where the publisher no longer stands behind it and use should stop. contestedBy records a dispute claim by claim; statusNotice is the document-level notice a consumer reads first.

A regime's own section (the x-<framework> namespace) stays in the provenance record, as an opaque object. In frontmatter the regime is a key inside jurisdictionalEvidence, never a field of its own. Its id keeps its registry spelling, and every field name stays camelCase.

mx:
  status: disputed
  statusNotice:
    reason: A reader reported that the dosage table does not match the current product licence.
    date: 2026-09-27
    contact: content-standards@example.org
  parties:
    - role: systemOwner
      name: Head of Clinical Content
      organisation: Example Health
      country: GB
  derivedFrom: datalake/product-licences/
  transformations:
    - type: deduplication
      method: Removed records with identical product reference and date
      tool: scripts/dedupe.cjs
      date: 2026-09-20
      actor: dataProcessor
  resourceProfile:
    energyEstimate: 0.8
    unit: kWh per month
    basis: estimated
    method: Provider-published per-token figures multiplied by logged token counts
    baselineRef: https://example.org/baselines/leaflet-summariser-2026-09.md
  jurisdictionalEvidence:
    ISO-42001:
      controls: [A.7.6]

The AIMS set gives every record an AI management system keeps its own profile, and each kind is a value of the OKF type field:

Profile Record kind Required beyond identity, status, recordId and parties
aims-system-inventory aims:systemInventoryEntry purpose
aims-statement-of-applicability aims:statementOfApplicability aimsScope, controlApplicability, approvedAt
aims-risk-register aims:riskRegisterEntry systemRef, inherentRisk, riskTreatment
aims-impact-assessment aims:impactAssessment systemRef, affectedGroups, impacts, assessedAt
aims-policy aims:policy version, approvedAt
aims-decision-right (experimental, 22.AQ) aims:decisionRight decisionScope, approvedAt, exactly one decisionOwner

The set was built for ISO/IEC 42001 and is named for the management system, not the standard, so the same records carry evidence for other regimes through jurisdictionalEvidence. An aims-policy record takes its registry form as the REGINALD policy COG, which carries approvedBy, approvedAt, reviewBy and jurisdictionalEvidence under the same meanings.

Field Record Purpose
recordId all The organisation's own identifier for the record
systemRef risk, impact The inventory entry the record concerns
intendedUse inventory permitted and prohibited uses (retrieval, training, fineTuning, summarisation, display, decisionSupport, generation) and notes
dataSources inventory References to the COGs that describe the system's data
aimsScope applicability The boundary of the management system
controlApplicability applicability Per control: regime, controlId, applicable, justification, evidenceRefs
approvedAt applicability Approval date; the approver is a parties entry
inherentRisk risk Pre-treatment risk, in the residualRisk shape and scale
riskTreatment risk option (modify, avoid, share, retain) and actions
affectedGroups, impacts, mitigations, assessedAt impact Who is affected, how, with what severity, what addresses it, and when it was assessed

intendedUse describes an AI system. What a machine may do with a document's content stays with contentPolicy (at inference) and aiTraining or trainingDataPolicy (for training). controlApplicability is not applicability, which is the conditional-profiling field.

type: aims:systemInventoryEntry
mx:
  canonicalUri: https://example.org/aims/systems/leaflet-summariser.md
  status: active
  recordId: SYS-003
  purpose: Drafts plain-language summaries of patient leaflets for pharmacist review.
  parties:
    - role: systemOwner
      name: Head of Clinical Content
      organisation: Example Health
    - role: provider
      name: Example Model Co
  intendedUse:
    permitted: [summarisation, retrieval]
    prohibited: [decisionSupport]
    notes: Summaries are drafts for pharmacist review, never advice to patients.
  dataSources:
    - https://example.org/data/product-licences.md
  reviewBy: 2027-03-27
  jurisdictionalEvidence:
    ISO-42001:
      controls: [A.4.2, A.6.2.3, A.9.4]

The profile defines the structure of a record, never its method. MX supplies no way to score a risk, judge an impact, or decide whether a control applies. A well-formed record says nothing about whether the assessment it holds is sound. What the record adds is that the assessment is findable, attributable to a named role, dated, tied to the system it concerns, and, once registered, attested for provenance and integrity. JSON Schemas for the four kinds sit beside the decision and policy COG schemas in mx-reginald/packages/schemas/src/, and a registry that stores an AIMS record appends each change to it (created, updated, status changed, attested, withdrawn) to an append-only event log whose entries are leaves of an RFC 6962 Merkle tree.

22.AF The MX specification version - which rules a document is read by

A field dictionary changes over time, and a machine reading a document needs to know against which version of the rules the metadata was written. mxSpecVersion says so. It is a core field in the mx: block, recommended on every profile, and its value is a plain version string a machine can compare:

mx:
  mxSpecVersion: "0.9"
  status: active

It is distinct from version, which is the document's own version. A cog at version: "3.2" written against the 0.9 specification carries both.

The current value is declared once, in the field dictionary's header, together with the specification's status and timeline:

Key Value Meaning
version 0.9 The value every document declares while this version is current
status draft The specification is a draft
outOfDraft 2027-01-01 When the specification leaves draft
outOfDraftAssumed false Whether the out-of-draft date is still an assumption; false once it is confirmed
stableVersion 1.0 The first public, stable version
stableWithinMonths 18 1.0 is published no later than this many months after the specification leaves draft
stableNoLaterThan 2028-07-01 The resulting latest date for 1.0

The deadline is defined relative to the out-of-draft date and follows it when it moves. A test fails when the stored deadline and its rule disagree. At each release the new value joins the field's allowed values, the older value stays valid for documents written against it, and one sweep (npm run specversion:stamp -- --apply) moves every document to the new value. The commit-boundary heal stamps or corrects the field on every committed markdown file with an mx: block, so nothing can be committed without it.

22.AG The personal-cog family - what a person declares, and how far it travels

Most cogs describe something published: a menu, a product, a page. A personal cog describes the person reading them. It is a record a person keeps about themselves (an access need, an allergy, a consent choice, a skill) and holds on their own device. A reader app matches it against the cogs it meets, on the device, so no profile of the person is built anywhere else. The record kind is personal-cog, and the personal profile lists its fields.

The family takes its model from the palimpsest. A palimpsest is a manuscript written over an earlier text that was scraped away, though never completely: traces remain, and a careful reader can see both the text written now and the text written before. A personal cog is the layer a person writes over the content they receive. The publisher's attested layer stays beneath it and can still be verified, and the reader sees content shaped by both. The personal layer directs what the person is shown; it never rewrites what the publisher signed.

Field Type Required What it says
personalKind enum yes What the cog declares: accessibility, consent, dietary, health, interests, memberships, persona, preferences, reception, role or skills
personalRole array yes The roles the cog takes part in, such as consumer or trade-buyer; any places it in every role. On a role cog, the one role it selects
disclosureTier enum yes How far the cog may travel: private, derived or guarded
personalIdentity string recommended The identity the cog belongs to; base (the default) places it in every identity
revisionTraces enum recommended Whether earlier versions stay recoverable by the owner (kept, the default) or are erased on revision (scraped)
disclosesAs array optional The neutral preferences that travel in place of a derived cog
discloseFor array optional The kinds of transaction the guardrail may disclose the cog for
appliesToSites array optional The sites the cog takes part on, as host patterns; absent, it applies everywhere
excludeSites array optional The sites the cog never takes part on; an exclusion always beats an inclusion
declaredBy enum optional self (the default) or delegate, such as a carer acting with the owner's authority
claimBasis enum optional asserted (the reading when absent) or corroborated when an outside source confirms the content
corroboratedBy array optional The external URLs that confirm a corroborated cog

Disclosure tiers. disclosureTier is the field a reader app must honour before any other. A private cog never leaves the device: it shapes what the person sees and nothing more. A derived cog sends only the neutral preferences named in disclosesAs, so a venue learns that a brief should be audio-first and never learns that the reader is blind. A guarded cog may be shared whole, but only on a transaction the owner starts (a booking, a purchase, a request), only through the guardrail, and only for the transactions discloseFor names. A reader that finds no disclosureTier treats the cog as private. Discovery never discloses at any tier: a device that hears the cogs around it announces nothing of itself.

---
title: "Sight"
description: "Low vision. Content should be spoken and described."
author: Jane Doe
created: 2026-03-02
modified: 2026-03-02
type: personal-cog
mx:
  personalKind: accessibility
  personalIdentity: base
  personalRole: [any]
  disclosureTier: derived
  disclosesAs: [audio-first, described-images]
  declaredBy: self
---

Identities. personalIdentity places a cog in one of the person's identities (personal, consultant, author, or any name they choose). Only the active identity's cogs take part in a match, so a consultant's rates never follow the person into a restaurant. The value base holds the human fundamentals that apply whichever identity is active.

mx:
  personalKind: skills
  personalIdentity: consultant
  personalRole: [any]
  disclosureTier: guarded
  discloseFor: [client-meeting, proposal]

Roles. personalRole says the capacity a person acts in towards a site: a consumer, a trade buyer, a carer, a repairer, or any name they choose. It is separate from the identity. An identity groups the person's own cogs. A role describes what they are doing on the site in front of them, and they can act in several roles under one identity. Only cogs whose personalRole names the active role, or any, take part in a match. A trade account stays off a consumer shop, and a loyalty card stays off a supplier's counter. A reader that finds no personalRole reads any.

The active role is chosen per session or per site. A role the person picks for the current session wins everywhere until they close it, because their latest explicit choice is the one to honour. Failing that, a cog of personalKind: role selects the value of its personalRole on the hosts its appliesToSites names, by the same precedence as any other scoped cog. A role cog with no appliesToSites sets the default. When the most specific role cogs on a site disagree, none is active there and only cogs for any take part. A role cog is a setting, not a record about the person. It is never matched, and it does not travel whatever its disclosureTier, because its patterns would tell one host which others its visitor uses.

Persona. A cog of personalKind: persona is the person's system prompt for their own reader app's assistant. Its body sets the assistant's voice, manner and working habits, and it stands in for the app's built-in personality. It is a setting, not a record about the person, so it is never matched and does not go to a venue. An identity-layer persona beats the base one. When two persona cogs share a layer, the reader uses neither, rather than pick one by file order. A local model always receives the persona. A hosted model receives it only when the cog declares disclosureTier: guarded and the person started the turn. A persona holds instructions, not facts. Private facts go in ordinary personal cogs, and each one's disclosureTier governs it. The reader's own context rules, such as how each cog is known, always follow the persona and are never replaced by it.

The active role does travel. A reader that hands over a disclosure sends the role beside it as the person's own statement, actingAs: { role, claimBasis: asserted }, because the recipient reads what it receives in the light of the person's capacity. Only the name goes: never whether the person or a site rule chose it, nor the cog that did. The reader shows the person this in the preview before they confirm. With none active, the field is absent.

---
title: "Trade counters"
description: "On trade suppliers I buy as a tradesperson."
author: Jane Doe
created: 2026-10-15
modified: 2026-10-15
type: personal-cog
mx:
  personalKind: role
  personalRole: [trade-buyer]
  disclosureTier: private
  appliesToSites: ["*.supplies.example"]
---
mx:
  personalKind: preferences
  personalRole: [trade-buyer]
  disclosureTier: guarded
  discloseFor: [shopping]

Beside an unscoped role cog that selects consumer, the first cog makes the person a trade buyer on every host under supplies.example, and the second cog, holding their account details, takes part only there.

Venue choices and memberships. A preferences cog also holds the choices a venue booking offers: seating (row, aisle, accessible, recliner), table, and travel mode. A reader app ranks venues by them on the device. Loyalty and membership numbers go in a separate memberships cog, which names the brand or chain that issued each number. It is never used for ranking, and it travels only on a booking or purchase with that brand.

mx:
  personalKind: memberships
  personalRole: [consumer]
  disclosureTier: guarded
  discloseFor: [cinema]

The memberships kind is awaiting Gathering review as an addition to the approved personal-cogs draft.

Sites. appliesToSites lets a cog take part on one site or a group of sites, and excludeSites keeps it off others. A pattern is an exact host (shop.example.com) or a leading wildcard (*.example.com, *.de) that covers the domain and everything under it; it carries no scheme, path or port. A cog with no appliesToSites applies everywhere. When several cogs of the same personalKind apply on a site, the most specific wins and the others stand down there: an exact host beats a wildcard, a longer domain beats a shorter one, and a scoped cog beats an unscoped one. The winner replaces the others whole, so a less specific cog's content never travels under the winner's disclosureTier. An exclusion always beats an inclusion. A reader treats a cog with a malformed pattern as applying nowhere, because a dropped exclusion would widen the cog's reach, and with no site known it uses only unscoped cogs. Scope narrows where a cog takes part and never widens what it discloses. The patterns are the owner's alone and do not travel: a site learns the values that apply to it, never that it was singled out or which other sites the owner names.

---
title: "Preferences in Germany"
description: "Currency EUR, language de, deliver to the Berlin office."
author: Jane Doe
created: 2026-10-13
modified: 2026-10-13
type: personal-cog
mx:
  personalKind: preferences
  disclosureTier: guarded
  discloseFor: [shopping]
  appliesToSites: ["*.de"]
  excludeSites: ["*.ads.example"]
---

Beside an unscoped preferences cog that says GBP and English, this one wins on every .de site and stands down everywhere else.

Traces. revisionTraces decides whether the palimpsest keeps its earlier layers. With kept, a revised cog leaves its earlier versions recoverable by the owner, who can see what they declared before. With scraped, the reader app keeps no earlier version on the device or in its synced history. Traces are for the owner alone in either case: only the current version is ever matched or disclosed.

mx:
  personalKind: health
  disclosureTier: private
  revisionTraces: scraped

Declarations, never inferences. A personal cog is an assertion by a person. declaredBy records whether the owner made it (self) or someone acting with their authority did (delegate, named as a parties entry with role delegate). No field holds a value a system inferred from behaviour or location: a declared preference beats an inferred signal, and the record has nowhere to store one.

The owner's word, labelled as such. Because a personal cog is an assertion, a reader app tells any model or venue it shares the cog with that the content is the owner's own statement and has not been checked (22.AH). The declaration is still honoured in full; what changes is that a model cannot hand it back to the owner as independent fact, and its agreement with the cog, or the cog coming up again, never counts as confirmation. A cog may say more only by naming its evidence: claimBasis: corroborated with at least one external URL in corroboratedBy, such as a clinic letter confirming a diagnosis. A corroborated declaration with no source reads as asserted, and so does any other basis, since a personal cog holds no inference and the device has observed nothing.

mx:
  personalKind: health
  disclosureTier: guarded
  discloseFor: [dining]
  claimBasis: corroborated
  corroboratedBy:
    - https://clinic.example.com/letters/123

A preferences or reception cog holds its values (marketplace, language, currency, push reception categories) in its body; the fields describe the record and its disclosure, not the subject matter of every preference. The Gathering approved the family on 2026-10-04 (decision record: ADR 84).

22.AK reviewedBy and supersedes - who accepted a document, and what it replaced

Two fields answer the questions a reader asks before relying on a document: did a person check it, and is it the current word. reviewedBy names the person who reviewed the document and accepted or rejected it. The author of the work never sets it, and a placeholder value means nobody has reviewed it yet, so a checker can refuse a card that moved on without a named human. supersedes names the document or documents this one replaces, by path, identifier or versioned name, as a string or a list. It is the inverse of supersededBy, so a replacement can be walked in either direction.

mx:
  reviewedBy: Jane Smith
  statusNote: "Accepted: the scope matches the brief."
  supersedes:
    - policies/pricing-2025.md

22.AL legalInstruments, reviewCycle and lastReviewed - content that must be checked again

A document can be accurate on the day it is published and wrong a month later without a word of it changing. A ruling is appealed, a deadline is moved, a regulation is amended, a figure is revised. A machine reading the document cannot see any of that from the prose. Three fields, with the dated claims of 22.AH, tell it which documents are at risk and when they were last checked.

legalInstruments lists the laws and court rulings on which the document's claims rest, including any technical standard a law cites. It is operational governance, not subject matter: when a listed instrument moves, the claims are at risk and the document is due for a recheck. Its presence marks legal or regulatory content, which a reader takes as general information and never as advice unless the document says otherwise. A publisher that keeps a register of regulatory dates writes its stable identifiers; anything not listed there appears as its citation in text. Where applicability.jurisdiction (22.C) says where content is in force and entities (22.Z) names its subjects, this field names the rules that govern its accuracy.

reviewCycle says how often the content is reviewed for accuracy: daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly or annually, or an ISO 8601 duration such as P90D. lastReviewed is the date the content was last reviewed as a whole. It differs from modified, which moves on any edit, a typo fix included, and says nothing about whether anyone checked the content. A review that finds nothing to change still moves lastReviewed. The next review is due one cycle after lastReviewed; a document past that date reads as unreviewed.

mx:
  legalInstruments:
    - eu-accessibility-act
    - eu-ai-act-article-50
    - us-ada-title-ii-web-rule
    - EN 301 549
  reviewCycle: monthly
  lastReviewed: '2026-10-16'
  claims:
    - statement: The Auchan ruling is under appeal at the Cour d'appel de Douai.
      basis: corroborated
      corroboratedBy:
        - https://www.informations.handicap.fr/
      checkedOn: '2026-10-16'
      recheckBy: '2026-11-16'

Read together, the three questions a steward asks have answers in the file: which laws the document depends on, when its content was last checked as a whole, and which of its facts expire first. A document is due for attention on the earlier of its next review and the earliest recheckBy among its claims. expires (22.C) is different again: it retires the whole file, where these fields keep it in service and say when to look at it.

22.AM completeness - whether a list is all of them

A machine that finds nothing has to decide what nothing means. An entry missing from a list can mean the thing does not exist, or only that it was never meant to be named, and a page rarely says which. Web content is open-world by nature, so the honest default is that a missing entry is unknown. completeness lets a document narrow that default for the enumeration it carries: a list of stockists, partners, supported products, known issues or recalls.

The block has three keys. exhaustive is the claim itself: true says the list names every item within its scope, so an entry missing from it is absent. false says the list is a selection, the open-world reading made explicit. A block without exhaustive is not a statement and a reader treats it as absent. asOf is the date the statement held, because a negative is a claim about a moment. A statement with no date is read as unconfirmed, never as permanent. scope is one sentence naming what the enumeration covers, and so what it does not; an exhaustive claim with no scope covers only what the document visibly lists.

mx:
  completeness:
    exhaustive: true
    asOf: 2026-10-16
    scope: UK stockists with a physical shop

The field is a declaration, never defaulted, and an absent block keeps the open-world reading. Completeness is still a claim: a publisher that declares a list exhaustive and is wrong has made the silence look authoritative, so a decision that depends on it looks for corroboration like any other (corroboratedBy, 22.AD). The name is deliberate: Dublin Core's coverage names the spatial or temporal topic of a resource, which is a different question. completeness pairs with actions[].withheldFrom in the component family (22.AA), which declares one deliberate omission rather than leaving it silent.

22.AN mcpServer - the record an agent checks before it connects to an MCP server (experimental)

Experimental: defined so early implementations share one spelling while the proposal behind it is in Gathering review. It may change shape or be withdrawn without a deprecation entry, and no conformance level requires it.

An agent that connects to a Model Context Protocol server treats it as a trusted tool. Nothing in the connection says who runs it, if its tools are the ones that were approved, what it may return, or whether anyone has withdrawn it. A tool description is instruction text the model reads, so a server that rewrites one after approval changes what the agent does while everything the operator reviewed stays the same. mcpServer is the record that closes that gap: it pins the server's identity and the exact lists it serves, and an agent compares the live server with it before every session.

The block, defined in full under blockTypes: mcpServer, carries:

  • Identity: serverId (the ARD identifier where the server is in an ARD catalogue), transport, and publisher.
  • The pin: toolsetHash, and resourcesHash and promptsHash when the server offers those lists. Each is the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the RFC 8785 (JCS) form of the complete list, sorted by its key, so two implementations reading the same server compute the same value. tools lists each tool with a descriptionHash and its effect.
  • Scope: returns.classification (a ceiling in the classification properties: sensitivity, pii, piiType) and egress, the hosts to which the server may send data.
  • Standing: status and statusUrl, issuedAt and validUntil (30 days by default, never more than 90), and a detached JWS signature.

claimBasis uses a subset of the vocabulary in 22.AH. A publisher cog, written by the organisation that runs the server, is asserted until an observation corroborates it. A shadow cog, written by an auditor, a registry or a user, records what was served at observedAt and is observed or corroborated, never asserted. A shadow cog is a record of an observation, never an endorsement or a compliance grant.

effect holds exactly one of read, write or destructive, plus external where it applies. The values map to MCP's own annotation hints (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, openWorldHint). effectBasis says how the effect was established: documented, tested in a sandbox, or both.

Before the first tool call of a session, a conforming agent resolves the cog and refuses the connection if the cog is revoked, suspended, stale or unsigned. It then recomputes every digest the cog carries from what is served live, and refuses on any difference. It repeats the check on every list_changed notification, and it fails closed: a missing cog, an unreadable status or a digest it cannot compute is a refusal unless the operator has allowed that server and the allowance is recorded. An organisation's own overlay may remove tools or tighten the ceilings and never widen them.

mx:
  mcpServer:
    serverId: "urn:ai:allabout.network:mcp:mx-check"
    transport:
      type: stdio
      command: "mx-check-server"
    claimBasis: asserted
    toolsetHash: "d22faa4fff1256e4d3036f01e6b2ba673ccf1c964dd25a69a3d2ee1e543ac00a"
    tools:
      - name: mx_check_field
        descriptionHash: "3d8f6d61cef0d697ef8fc538e4152aa7f159ee80f67d4a59c2958f578cbe8d70"
        effect: [read]
        effectBasis: documented
    returns:
      classification:
        sensitivity: internal
        pii: false
    egress: []
    status: unknown
    issuedAt: "2026-10-18T23:45:00Z"
    validUntil: "2026-11-17T23:45:00Z"

The example is taken from the publisher cog for the hub's own mx-check server, shortened to one tool. npm run mcp:digest -- -- <server command> computes the values the block carries. One module holds the rules, so the cog and the check cannot disagree about how a hash is made.

22.AO agentPermissions - where an agent finds the terms for acting on this (experimental)

Experimental: defined so early implementations share one spelling while the proposal behind it is in Gathering review. It may change shape or be withdrawn without a deprecation entry, and no conformance level requires it.

A business can publish what an AI agent may do on its estate: an agent-permissions.json file from the Lightweight Agent Standards Working Group, or an A2WF site manifest. Both name what an agent may read, click or submit, which actions need a person's approval, and which API or MCP endpoint it should use instead of the web pages. Both are found on the website, at a well-known path or through a link tag, so a document that leaves the site (a PDF, a dataset, a forwarded report) loses them. agentPermissions is the URL of the manifest that governs a resource, carried in the resource's own metadata so the pointer travels with it.

The field is a pointer, not a vocabulary. The manifest format owns the terms, and MX does not restate them. It pairs with contentPolicy (22.V): contentPolicy says what a machine may do with the content it reads, and the manifest at agentPermissions says what an agent may do on the publisher's estate. Neither says which agent is acting; that is the job of the identity protocols.

mx:
  contentPolicy: extract-with-attribution
  agentPermissions: "https://mx.allabout.network/.well-known/agent-permissions.json"

A web page needs the field only when its terms differ from the site default, since both manifest formats already have their own discovery there.

22.AP The eval family - what was tested, how it was scored, and how often (experimental)

A model vendor publishes a benchmark table, and a reader picks from it. The table states results. It rarely states what a reader needs to weigh them: which version ran, at what settings, how the answers were scored, against a key fixed when, and how many times. An eval record carries those facts beside the scores. The record kind is eval-record, and the eval profile lists its fields. The family is proposed to The Gathering and is not ratified.

Field Type Required What it says
evalTask string yes The work put to each model and the capability it measures, in one sentence
evalSubjects array yes Each model tested, with model (the exact version), provider, route and settings
evalGrading enum yes How answers were scored: script (against a fixed key), human, model (a model as judge) or mixed
evalRuns integer yes How many times the task was put to each model
evalKey object recommended fixedAt, the date the answer key was fixed, and location, where it lives; location is absent when the key is withheld
evalResults array recommended Per model: score out of outOf, with optional wrong, costUsd, tokensIn, tokensOut, seconds and runAt
claimBasis enum optional asserted when the record reports someone else's run; corroborated when a second run confirms it
corroboratedBy array optional The published write-ups or reruns the record stands on
expires date optional When the result should be treated as stale, because a model name can serve a different model later

The required band. The four required fields are the ones whose absence makes a score unreadable. Without evalTask, a reader cannot tell whether the result applies to their own work. evalSubjects says which model produced it. evalGrading separates a script's count from another model's opinion, and evalRuns separates a rate from a single draw.
