A record that carries all four may still describe a weak test, but a reader can see the weakness.

---
title: "Long-context blast-radius eval"
description: "Three dependency questions over a 400-service wiki, at three document sizes."
author: Jane Doe
created: 2026-10-15
modified: 2026-10-15
type: eval-record
mx:
  evalTask: "Answer graph questions over a large wiki with planted traps."
  evalSubjects:
    - model: example-model-4
      provider: example-lab
      route: openrouter
      settings: default reasoning
  evalGrading: script
  evalRuns: 1
  evalKey:
    fixedAt: 2026-10-12
  evalResults:
    - model: example-model-4
      score: 32
      outOf: 33
      wrong: 0
      tokensIn: 935332
      tokensOut: 5158
---

Single runs. evalRuns: 1 is a valid value and an honest one. It tells the reader that the result is one sample, and that a rerun could land differently. The field does not forbid a single run; it stops one from passing as a measured rate.

Wrong answers. Where a task lets a model give more answers than the key holds (list every affected service, flag every bug), score counts the correct ones and wrong counts the rest. A model that names 20 of 33 services and invents 8 more has not given a partial answer. It has given a wrong one, and only the second count shows it.

Tokens and prices. Token counts are each vendor's own. The same document can count very differently on two tokenizers, so a cost per token compares nothing across vendors. The cost per completed task does. A cost based on a time-limited price needs a volatileValues entry of kind price with its validUntil, because the comparison it supports expires with it.

22.AQ The decision-right record - which one role owns a class of AI decision (experimental)

Experimental: defined so early implementations share one spelling while the proposal behind it is in Gathering review. It may change shape or be withdrawn without a deprecation entry, and no conformance level requires it.

An organisation can name system and risk owners across its AI estate and still have nobody accountable for the decisions that cross systems. Should one team's tool become a single shared build for all of them? Which AI investments are funded, and which AI bets become products? Those decisions are usually shared by two executives, and what two people share, nobody owns. When something goes wrong, the first question is who was supposed to own it, and the answer is reconstructed from memory and email.

The aims-decision-right profile records the allocation before that question is asked. Each record covers one class of decision and names the single role accountable for it. The record kind is aims:decisionRight.

Field Purpose
decisionScope The class of decision, stated so a person or an agent can tell whether a given decision falls inside it
parties Exactly one entry with role decisionOwner; others with role consulted give their view without sharing ownership; an approver agreed the allocation
escalation trigger, the condition under which the decision goes up a level, and to, a role on the record or the decision-right record of the forum above
approvedAt When the allocation was agreed
systemRef Optional: the inventory entry, when the right covers one system
reviewBy When the allocation is checked again
decisionRightRef On a risk entry, statement of applicability or impact assessment: the decision right whose owner should have signed it

The rule that matters is the count. The schema refuses a record with no decisionOwner and one with two, so a shared decision cannot be filed as jointly owned. A disagreement about who owns a decision has to be settled before the record validates.

type: aims:decisionRight
mx:
  canonicalUri: https://example.org/aims/decisions/dr-003.md
  status: active
  recordId: DR-003
  decisionScope: Whether an AI tool requested by one team is built once as a shared service or left to that team.
  parties:
    - role: decisionOwner
      name: Chief Information Officer
    - role: consulted
      name: Chief Technology Officer
    - role: approver
      name: AI Governance Council
  escalation:
    trigger: The tool would process personal data, or the owner and the consulted role still disagree.
    to: https://example.org/aims/decisions/dr-001.md
  approvedAt: 2026-10-19
  reviewBy: 2027-04-19
  jurisdictionalEvidence:
    ISO-42001:
      controls: [A.3.2]

A decision-right record says who should decide. The sign-off on a particular decision is written into its own record. That is residualRisk.acceptedBy on a risk entry, an approver on a statement of applicability, or humanInLoop.reviewer on a REGINALD decision COG. A risk entry, a statement of applicability or an impact assessment cites the right it falls under with decisionRightRef. A registry that holds both compares the person who signed with the recorded decisionOwner, by identifier when both parties carry one and by name otherwise. It reports a match, a mismatch, or an unresolved case with its reason (the right is not held or not active, the record carries no sign-off yet, or nobody, or more than one party, holds the signing role). A REGINALD decision COG is not compared, because its humanInLoop.reviewer is an opaque reference rather than a named party. escalation.trigger gives an agent acting inside a decision a stated point at which to stop and hand back to a person, rather than an organisation chart it has to interpret.

The profile records an allocation, never whether it is a good one. MX supplies no method for deciding who should own a decision. The JSON Schema is aims-decision-right.schema.json beside the other AIMS schemas in mx-reginald/packages/schemas/src/.

22.AR The agent-cog family - who is acting, for whom, and under what mandate (experimental)

Experimental: defined so early implementations share one spelling while the proposal behind it is in Gathering review. It may change shape or be withdrawn without a deprecation entry, and no conformance level requires it.

Authentication answers one question: who logged in. An agent acting on someone's behalf raises several more. Which agent is this, and which release? Whose authority does it carry? What may it read, change, submit or publish, and how much may it spend? What stops for a person? Where are its actions recorded, and how is its authority withdrawn? An agent that has no answer to these questions can only borrow a person's login and present itself as that person. An agent cog answers them in a record it carries and presents when it acts. The record kind is agent-cog and the profile is agent.

Field Type Required What it says
agentId string yes The agent's stable identifier, a URI its developer controls
actingFor object yes The principal whose authority the mandate carries: name and an optional id
mandate array yes The kinds of action the agent holds authority for
agentVersion string recommended The release the cog describes
humanApprovalFor array recommended The kinds of action that stop for a named person's approval
actionLog string recommended Where the agent's actions are recorded
revocationUri string recommended Where the mandate's current status is published
operatesAt array optional The publishing points the mandate covers, as host patterns or URIs
spendLimit object optional The most a pay mandate may commit: amount, currency, period

One vocabulary for action. mandate, humanApprovalFor, and the publishing-point field agentActions share a closed list: read, draft, write, submit, publish, unpublish, delete, message, pay. Because the agent and the venue use the same words, a reader can compare them without interpretation. An action that is not listed falls outside the mandate.

Who is accountable. The principal is the party the agent acts for, and it is never the developer. The developer is a parties entry with role provider. The organisation running the agent is another, with role deployer. What the agent may touch while it acts is declared in its security block: riskLevel, capabilities, automationConsent, and scope.dataBoundary. The agent cog does not repeat those fields. expires sets the date the mandate lapses, and revocationUri covers withdrawal before then.

---
title: "Editorial assistant"
description: "Drafts and corrects articles in the newsroom CMS for Example News."
author: Jane Doe
created: 2026-10-19
modified: 2026-10-19
type: agent-cog
mx:
  agentId: https://agents.example.com/editorial-assistant
  agentVersion: 2.1.0
  actingFor:
    name: Example News Ltd
    id: https://news.example.com/
  parties:
    - role: provider
      name: Example Agents Ltd
  mandate: [read, draft, write]
  operatesAt: [cms.news.example.com]
  humanApprovalFor: [publish]
  actionLog: https://agents.example.com/editorial-assistant/log
  revocationUri: https://agents.example.com/editorial-assistant/status
  expires: 2027-10-19
---

Money has a ceiling. When a mandate includes pay, the cog is expected to carry spendLimit. A pay mandate without a spendLimit declares no ceiling, and a publishing point that takes payment refuses it rather than assume one.

mx:
  mandate: [read, submit, pay]
  spendLimit:
    amount: 500
    currency: GBP
    period: month
  humanApprovalFor: [pay]

Withdrawal is checked, not assumed. Before any action at security.riskLevel high or critical, or any irreversible one, a conforming publishing point checks revocationUri. It refuses when that address reports the mandate withdrawn, and also when it cannot be reached.

A declaration, never a grant. An agent cog states what its principal gave it. It does not oblige any publishing point to admit the agent. Until something corroborates it, the cog is asserted (claimBasis, see 22.AH), and a point that admits agents by identifier weighs the cog by its basis. The agent's effective authority at a publishing point is the overlap between its mandate and the point's agentActions (22.AS).

22.AS The publishing-point family - the terms a CMS sets for the agents that act there (experimental)

Experimental: defined with the agent-cog family and under the same Gathering review.

A content management system controls a publishing point, and its owner reaches the audience through it. Agents now draft, correct, schedule and publish inside such systems, and they also read from feeds, APIs and marketplaces. A publishing-point cog states the terms the point sets for those agents: whether it admits agents, which agents, what an admitted agent may do, what stops for a person, and which interface agents use in place of the human one. The record kind is publishing-point-cog and the profile is publishing-point. The cog is the publishing-point contract written for the point's machine audience.

Field Type Required What it says
publishingPointKind string yes cms, website, feed, api, newsletter, social-channel, marketplace, or document-store
agentAccess string yes open, declared (any agent presenting an agent cog), listed, or closed
agentActions array yes The most an admitted agent may do here, in the mandate vocabulary
humanApprovalFor array recommended The kinds of action that stop for a named person, for every agent admitted
agentInterface string recommended The API, MCP server, feed or submission folder agents use
actionLog string recommended Where the point records agent actions taken through it
admittedAgents array optional The agentId values admitted when agentAccess is listed 
---
title: "Newsroom CMS: agent terms"
description: "Which agents may work in the Example News CMS, and what they may do there."
author: Jane Doe
created: 2026-10-19
modified: 2026-10-19
type: publishing-point-cog
mx:
  publishingPointKind: cms
  agentAccess: listed
  admittedAgents:
    - https://agents.example.com/editorial-assistant
  agentActions: [read, draft, write]
  humanApprovalFor: [publish, unpublish, delete]
  agentInterface: https://cms.news.example.com/api/agents
  actionLog: https://cms.news.example.com/agent-log
---

Where the two cogs overlap. An agent may act at a publishing point only if both its own mandate and the point's agentActions name the action. An action stops for a person if either cog lists it in humanApprovalFor. With the two examples above, the editorial assistant may read, draft and write in the newsroom CMS. The agent has no mandate to publish, so it cannot do so there at all. If its principal later adds publish to the mandate, the point still does not list publish in agentActions, so the agent still cannot publish there. The point would have to add publish to agentActions too, and even then every publish would wait for an editor, because both cogs list it in humanApprovalFor. Each side keeps its own actionLog, and either can reconcile its record against the other.

A ceiling, never a grant. Putting publish in agentActions does not give an agent the right to publish when its mandate lacks it. closed states that the point offers agents no route. An agent that drives the human interface of a closed point, presenting itself as a person, is acting outside the point's stated terms. A point that has not yet decided its terms carries no cog, and a reader treats the absence as no statement.

The official interface. When a point names an agentInterface, an admitted agent uses it and identifies itself there. Driving the human pages as if the agent were a person is the behaviour the cog exists to make unnecessary.

22.AT The CMS family - the controller of the publishing points (experimental)

Experimental: defined with the agent-cog and publishing-point families and under the same Gathering review.

A publishing-point cog states one point's terms. A CMS cog describes the system that controls the points: which product and release it is, how it delivers content, which publishing points it controls, and which machine-readable outputs the running instance emits. The record kind is cms-cog and the profile is cms. The vendor and the organisation that runs the instance are parties entries with roles provider and systemOwner.

Field Type Required What it says
cmsProduct string yes The product, as its vendor names it
publishingPoints array yes The points the CMS controls, as paths or URIs of their publishing-point cogs, or the URLs they serve
cmsVersion string recommended The release the instance runs
cmsArchitecture string recommended coupled, headless, decoupled, static-generator, or hybrid
machineOutputs array recommended What the instance emits: json-ld, mx-frontmatter, llms-txt, sitemap, feed, robots-txt, agent-card, mcp-server, markdown-mirror 
---
title: "Newsroom CMS"
description: "The CMS behind Example News: what it runs, what it controls, and what it emits for machines."
author: Jane Doe
created: 2026-10-19
modified: 2026-10-19
type: cms-cog
mx:
  cmsProduct: Example CMS
  cmsVersion: "10.4"
  cmsArchitecture: headless
  publishingPoints:
    - https://news.example.com/.well-known/publishing-point.md
    - https://news.example.com/feed.xml
  machineOutputs: [json-ld, sitemap, feed, llms-txt]
---

The instance, not the brochure. machineOutputs lists what the running instance is configured to emit, not everything the product could. That makes it checkable. An outside-in audit compares the list with what the publishing points actually serve. An output the cog claims and the audit cannot find is the latent breach of the publishing-point contract, brought into view before an agent finds it.

Where the content lives. cmsArchitecture tells an agent where the authoritative copy is. In a headless CMS, the API holds it. In a static generator, the source files hold it, and the served pages are a rendering. An agent that wants to correct content goes to the authoritative copy through the point's agentInterface, not to the rendering.

22.AU cancellationTerms and loyaltyPointTerms - the terms a customer's agent checks before it books (experimental)

Experimental: defined so early implementations share one spelling while the proposal behind them is in Gathering review. They may change shape or be withdrawn without a deprecation entry, and no conformance level requires them.

An agent booking for its owner skips the page design and the countdown timer and asks three things: what cancelling costs, what the full price is, and what the loyalty programme is worth. Schema.org answers most of the second through its price specifications. It answers part of the third: MemberProgram, MemberProgramTier, hasTierBenefit and validForMemberTier describe a programme, its tiers and the offers each tier gets. It doesn't answer the first at all. MerchantReturnPolicy covers returning goods, and a Schema.org Reservation can only say it was cancelled. These two blocks fill those gaps and defer to Schema.org for everything it already covers.

cancellationTerms has three keys. freeUntil says how long before the booked start a cancellation stays free, as an ISO 8601 duration (P2D, PT24H), or names the fixed RFC 3339 time after which a fee applies; P0D means a fee applies from the moment of booking. fee is the charge after that point: an amount with its ISO 4217 code (25.00 GBP) or a percentage of the total price including fees and taxes (100%). A fee of 0 means cancelling is free at any time. termsUrl points to the binding terms. The block summarises them without replacing them. When it is absent, a reader learns nothing about the terms, and certainly not that cancelling is free.

loyaltyPointTerms declares the published terms of a points programme:

  • program: the Schema.org MemberProgram the points belong to, as its URL or @id.
  • earnRate: points earned for each one unit of the document's currency spent.
  • pointValue: the redemption value of one point in that currency. Where redemption varies, it is the lowest rate guaranteed to every member.
  • expiresAfter: how long a point stays valid, as an ISO 8601 duration. Omit it when points do not expire.
  • expiryBasis: whether that duration counts from the date a point was earned or from the member's last-activity.
  • blackoutDates: ISO 8601 intervals when points cannot be redeemed.
mx:
  currency: GBP
  cancellationTerms:
    freeUntil: PT24H
    fee: 15.00 GBP
    termsUrl: https://example.com/booking-terms
  loyaltyPointTerms:
    program: https://example.com/#regulars
    earnRate: 1
    pointValue: 0.05
    expiresAfter: P12M
    expiryBasis: last-activity
    blackoutDates:
      - 2026-12-24/2026-12-26

The block states the programme's terms, never one member's balance or tier. Those belong to the member and are kept in the member's own personal cog (22.AG), so an agent joins the two on the member's side: the business declares what a point is worth and the member's record says how many they hold. Both blocks are claims by the business. An agent that acts on a quoted price or fee can set it beside the declared terms and treat a difference as a finding, and a decision that depends on the terms looks for corroboration like any other (corroboratedBy, 22.AD). Terms are stated values: when a fee or a point value moves on its own cadence, the document also lists it in volatileValues, which says until when the figure may be quoted and where an agent fetches the current one.

23. Folder Metadata - .mx.yaml.md Guide

Folder-scoped metadata, inheritance model, and the two-zone structure.

Source: formerly mx-canon/ssot/writing-guides/mx-yaml-md-guide.md (retained as a stub).

Field definitions: This guide covers practical workflow. For canonical field definitions, types, allowed values, and overlap resolution, see the Field Dictionary - the single source of truth.

.mx.yaml.md Folder Metadata Guide

What Are .mx.yaml.md Files?

.mx.yaml.md files are folder metadata files that describe the purpose, ownership, and relationships of every directory in the MX repository. They follow the MX principle of Design for Both, providing human-readable documentation while maintaining machine-readable structure.

Each .mx.yaml.md file contains:

  • YAML frontmatter with structured metadata (machine-readable)
  • Markdown narrative with human-friendly explanation

Why Do We Use Them?

MX Principles in Practice

  1. Design for Both: Single file serves humans (narrative) and machines (YAML)
  2. Metadata-Driven: Explicit folder purpose, not implicit from name
  3. Context Preservation: Clear relationships between folders
  4. Size-Neutral: Descriptions avoid file counts (which change)
  5. Explicit Over Implicit: Document relationships, don't assume

Real Benefits

  • For Humans: Understand unfamiliar folders instantly
  • For AI Agents: Navigate repository with explicit context
  • For Teams: Clear ownership and lifecycle information
  • For Automation: Build tools that understand repository structure

File Format Specification

Complete Structure

---
## === CORE IDENTITY ===
title: "Human-readable folder name"
description: "One-sentence summary"
purpose: "Detailed technical purpose"
audience: ["humans", "machines", "both"]

## === PROVENANCE ===
created: "YYYY-MM-DD"
author: "Author Name"
modified: "YYYY-MM-DD"

## === LIFECYCLE ===
stability: "stable" | "evolving" | "experimental" | "deprecated" | "archived"
status: "draft" | "active" | "published" | "deprecated" | "archived"
lifecycle: "production" | "development" | "prototype" | "legacy" | "deprecated"

## === RELATIONSHIPS ===
inherits: "../.mx.yaml.md"  # Path to parent (omit for repository roots)
relatedFolders:
  - path: "../sibling-folder"
    relationship: "depends-on" | "provides-for" | "coordinates-with"
    description: "Why this relationship exists"
dependencies:
  - type: "build" | "runtime" | "conceptual"
    target: "folder-name or package-name"
    description: "What is needed and why"

## === MX-SPECIFIC ===
mx:
  version: "1.0"
  contentType: "folder-metadata"
  domain: "category-name"

  ai:
    aiAssistance: "welcome" | "restricted" | "prohibited"
    aiEditable: true | false
    generation:
      allowed: true | false
      reviewRequired: true | false
    contextProvides:
      - "What this folder provides to AI context"

  # Only in parent folders that define inheritance
  mx:inheritable:
    - "ai.assistance"
    - "context.domain"

## === SIZE-NEUTRAL ===
folderType: "category" | "content" | "config" | "build" | "scripts" | "submodule"
primaryLanguages: ["javascript", "markdown", "python"]
hasSubfolders: true | false
---

## Folder Name - Narrative

### Purpose and Role

[2-3 paragraphs explaining what this folder does, why it exists,
and how it fits into the larger project]

### How to Use This Folder

[Practical guidance for both humans and machines]

### Architecture Context

[How this folder relates to other parts of the system]

### For AI Agents

[Specific guidance for machine readers]

Required Fields

Core Identity (4 fields):

  • title: Human-friendly name
  • description: One-sentence summary (no counts!)
  • purpose: Technical purpose statement
  • audience: Primary readers

Provenance (3 fields):

  • created: Date created (YYYY-MM-DD)
  • author: Original author (canonical; replaces legacy createdBy)
  • modified: Last modification date (canonical; replaces legacy lastUpdated)

Lifecycle (3 fields):

  • stability: Code/content stability
  • status: Maintenance status
  • lifecycle: Product lifecycle stage

Relationships (2-3 fields):

  • relatedFolders: Related directories (array)
  • dependencies: Build/runtime dependencies (array)
  • inherits: Parent metadata (omit for roots)

MX Metadata (1 field):

  • mx: MX-specific configuration (object)

Size-Neutral (3 fields):

  • folderType: Category of folder
  • primaryLanguages: Programming languages used
  • hasSubfolders: Has subdirectories

Inheritance System

How Inheritance Works

.mx.yaml.md files inherit from their parent folder, reducing duplication:

/                          # Root - no inherits
├── docs/                  # inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md
│   ├── guides/            # inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md (from docs)
│   │   └── for-humans/    # inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md (from guides)
│   └── reference/         # inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md (from docs)

Repository Boundaries

Important: Inheritance STOPS at repository boundaries (submodules):

/                                # Main repo root
├── mx-outputs/                 # SUBMODULE ROOT - no inherits!
│   ├── pdf/                    # inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md (from mx-outputs)
│   └── md/                     # inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md (from mx-outputs)

Each git submodule starts a fresh inheritance chain.

What Gets Inherited?

Parent folders define which fields children inherit via mx:inheritable:

## Parent folder defines:
mx:
  mx:inheritable:
    - "ai.assistance"
    - "ai.editable"
    - "context.domain"
    - "audience"

## Child folders inherit these fields automatically
## Only override if different from parent

Computing Effective Values

The inheritance system allows you to see the final resolved state of any folder's metadata using the mx:effective command.

Inheritance Resolution Algorithm:

  1. Walk up the chain: Start at current folder, traverse to root (or repository boundary)
  2. Collect all inheritable fields: From each ancestor, gather fields listed in mx:inheritable
  3. Apply override precedence: Child values win over parent values for the same field
  4. Output effective state: Write fully-resolved .mx.effective.yaml file

Example Resolution:

/ (root)
  mx:inheritable: [audience, ai.assistance]
  audience: [humans, machines]
  ai.assistance: welcome
    ↓ inherits
docs/
  inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md
  stability: stable
    ↓ inherits
docs/guides/
  inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md
  title: Guides
  ai.assistance: restricted  # OVERRIDES root value

Effective values for docs/guides/:
  title: Guides                      # From self
  audience: [humans, machines]       # From root
  stability: stable                  # From docs/
  ai.assistance: restricted          # From self (overrides root)

Repository Boundaries:

Effective value computation stops at repository boundaries (submodules), just like inheritance. Each submodule maintains its own effective value chain.

Use cases:

  • Machine readers: AI agents can read .mx.effective.yaml directly without resolving inheritance
  • Validation: Confirm that inheritance is producing expected results
  • Debugging: Understand why a field has a particular value
  • Caching: Pre-compute values for performance-critical systems

Creating New .mx.yaml.md Files

Automatic Generation (Recommended)

Use the generator script for consistent results:

## Generate for specific directory
npm run mx:generate:dir new-folder

## Preview what would be generated
npm run mx:generate:dry-run

## Regenerate all files (careful!)
npm run mx:generate:force

Manual Creation

  1. Copy template from parent folder
  2. Update required fields:
    • Change title, description, purpose
    • Update created/author/modified (use git log if unsure)
    • Adjust stability/status/lifecycle as appropriate
  3. Add/remove relationships as needed
  4. Write narrative (4 sections)
  5. Validate: npm run mx:validate

Manual Creation Example

## Copy parent as template
cp docs/.mx.yaml.md docs/new-section/.mx.yaml.md

## Edit file
## - Update title, description, purpose
## - Keep inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md
## - Write narrative for this specific folder

## Validate
npm run mx:validate

Editing Existing Files

What You Should Edit

✅ Safe to edit:

  • Narrative sections (Purpose, How to Use, Architecture, For AI Agents)
  • description: improve clarity
  • purpose: add detail
  • relatedFolders: add/remove relationships
  • dependencies: update as project evolves

⚠️ Edit with caution:

  • stability, status, lifecycle: only when status actually changes
  • mx.ai.* fields: affects AI agent behaviour
  • mx:inheritable: changes propagate to all children

❌ Don't edit:

  • created, author: historical record
  • inherits: only change if moving files
  • modified: should be automatic (use git hooks)

Size-Neutral Language

Never write:

  • "Contains 15 files"
  • "Has 3 subdirectories"
  • "Includes 42 markdown documents"

Instead write:

  • "Contains documentation files"
  • "Has subdirectories for different topics"
  • "Includes markdown documents"

Why? File counts change constantly and create maintenance burden.

Common Patterns

Category Folders

Top-level organizational folders:

title: "Documentation"
folderType: "category"
hasSubfolders: true
mx:
  mx:inheritable:  # Define what children inherit
    - "ai.assistance"
    - "context.domain"

Content Folders

Folders with actual content:

title: "User Guides"
folderType: "content"
primaryLanguages: ["markdown"]
relatedFolders:
  - path: "../reference"
    relationship: "coordinates-with"

Build/Script Folders

Folders with automation:

title: "Build Scripts"
folderType: "build"
primaryLanguages: ["javascript", "bash"]
mx:
  ai:
    aiAssistance: "welcome"
    aiEditable: true
    generation:
      reviewRequired: false  # Scripts can be auto-generated

Submodule Roots

Independent repositories:

title: "MX: The Protocols Manuscript"
folderType: "submodule"
## NO inherits field - fresh start
mx:
  project:
    name: "MX: The Protocols"
    repository: "https://github.com/example-org/your-manuscript-repo"
  mx:inheritable:  # Define for this submodule's children
    - "ai.assistance"
    - "context.constraints"

Available Commands

Generation

## Generate all missing .mx.yaml.md files
npm run mx:generate

## Preview generation (don't write files)
npm run mx:generate:dry-run

## Generate for specific directory
npm run mx:generate:dir <path>

## Force regenerate (overwrite existing)
npm run mx:generate:force

Migration

## Migrate old .mx.yaml files to .mx.yaml.md
npm run mx:migrate

## Preview migration
npm run mx:migrate:dry-run

Validation

## Validate all .mx.yaml.md files
npm run mx:validate

## Validate runs automatically on git commit (pre-commit hook)

Computing Effective Values

Pre-compute inheritance-resolved values for all .mx.yaml.md files:

## Compute effective values for all folders
npm run mx:effective

## Preview effective values without writing files
npm run mx:effective:dry-run

## Compute for specific directory only
npm run mx:effective --dir <path>

What are "effective values"?

Effective values are the final, resolved values after applying the complete inheritance chain. When a folder inherits from its parent, the effective value is what a machine reader actually sees after combining:

  1. All ancestor values (grandparent to parent to child)
  2. Override precedence (child overrides parent)
  3. The mx:inheritable field restrictions

Why compute effective values?

  • Speed up machine readers: Pre-computed values eliminate runtime inheritance resolution
  • Debug inheritance issues: See exactly what each folder's final state is
  • Validate inheritance behaviour: Confirm that it works as expected
  • Cache for AI agents: Provide quick-access resolved metadata

Output format:

The script creates .mx.effective.yaml files alongside each .mx.yaml.md:

docs/
├── .mx.yaml.md          # Source with inherits field
├── .mx.effective.yaml   # Computed effective values
└── guides/
    ├── .mx.yaml.md
    └── .mx.effective.yaml

Example:

## docs/guides/.mx.yaml.md (source)
---
title: Guides
inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md
mx:
  ai:
    aiAssistance: welcome
---

## docs/guides/.mx.effective.yaml (computed)
---
title: Guides
## All parent fields resolved and merged:
audience: [humans, machines]  # From root
stability: stable             # From docs/
mx:
  ai:
    aiAssistance: welcome            # From this folder
    aiEditable: true           # From root via inheritance
---

When to use:

  • After modifying mx:inheritable fields
  • When onboarding a new repository
  • Before deploying AI systems that read metadata
  • When debugging unexpected inheritance behavior

Repository Onboarding

When adding a new repository as a submodule, use the onboarding script to automatically set it up with MX metadata:

## Onboard a new repository (checks ownership)
npm run mx:onboard new-repo

## Force onboard a third-party repository (bypasses ownership check)
npm run mx:onboard third-party-repo -- --force

What the onboarding script does:

  1. Generates .mx.yaml.md files: Creates metadata for all folders
  2. Installs pre-commit hooks: Adds validation to git workflow
  3. Adds npm scripts: Installs MX commands (mx:generate, mx:validate, etc.)
  4. Updates documentation: Adds an MX section to the README and an instructions file for coding assistants

Safety check:

  • By default, only allows repositories owned by ddttom or digitaldomaintechnologies
  • Use --force to bypass this check for third-party repositories
  • Always shows clear warnings when onboarding third-party repos

Example workflow:

## Add a new submodule
git submodule add git@github.com:ddttom/new-package.git new-package

## Make it MX ready
npm run mx:onboard new-package

## Review generated files
cd new-package
npm run mx:validate

Dual Documentation: README.md and .mx.yaml.md

The Relationship

When a folder contains both README.md and .mx.yaml.md files, they serve complementary purposes following MX's "Design for Both" principle:

README.md (Human-Optimized):

  • Entry point for developers and contributors
  • Narrative flow with context and motivation
  • Installation guides, usage examples, getting started
  • Links to resources and documentation

.mx.yaml.md (Machine-Optimized):

  • Structured metadata with YAML frontmatter
  • Explicit relationships and dependencies
  • Machine-readable capabilities and context
  • Provenance tracking and lifecycle information

This is intentional redundancy: the same information presented in two forms, each optimised for its primary audience.

Information Flow

README.md is the source of truth for narrative content:

README.md (human-authored)
    ↓ Extract metadata
.mx.yaml.md (machine-structured)

What Gets Extracted

From README.md To .mx.yaml.md
YAML frontmatter description description: field
YAML frontmatter purpose purpose: field
YAML frontmatter keywords tags: array
YAML frontmatter license mx.license: field
Feature lists / capabilities ai.contextProvides: array
Prose sections Markdown narrative

Enhancement Command

Extract information from README.md to enhance .mx.yaml.md:

## Enhance all folders with both files
npm run mx:enhance

## Preview what would be extracted (dry run)
npm run mx:enhance:dry-run

Automatic enhancement: It runs automatically during repository onboarding when README.md exists.

Example: Before and After

README.md (source):

---
description: "Open-source community for Machine Experience patterns"
tags: [mx, ai-agents, community, open-source]
---

## MX-Gathering

This repository provides:
- Event organization templates
- Discussion archives
- Shared LLM prompts

After enhancement, .mx.yaml.md gains:

---
description: "Open-source community for Machine Experience patterns"
tags: [mx, ai-agents, community, open-source]
mx:
  ai:
    contextProvides:
      - Event organization templates
      - Discussion archives
      - Shared LLM prompts
---

Best Practices

  1. Write README.md first: It's human-friendly and easier to author
  2. Run enhancement: Extract metadata to .mx.yaml.md automatically
  3. Review both files: Check consistency and completeness
  4. README always wins: If conflicts exist, README.md is the source of truth

Why Both Files Matter

For humans: README.md provides the natural reading experience with narrative flow

For machines: .mx.yaml.md provides structured, parseable metadata for navigation and context

Together: They embody MX's "Design for Both" principle: same information, dual optimisation

Troubleshooting

"File already exists" Error

Problem: Running generator without --force on existing files

Solution:

## Use force to overwrite
npm run mx:generate:force

## Or delete file first
rm path/to/.mx.yaml.md
npm run mx:generate

"Missing inherits field" Warning

Problem: Non-root folder missing inherits field

Solution: Add to YAML frontmatter:

inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md

"Circular inheritance" Error

Problem: Inheritance chain loops back to itself

Solution: Check inherits paths, confirm they point upward:

## Correct
inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md

## Incorrect
inherits: ./subdir/.mx.yaml.md  # Can't inherit from child!

"Repository boundary crossed" Error

Problem: Child inherits from parent in different repository

Solution: Submodule roots should NOT have inherits field:

## Submodule root - REMOVE inherits field
title: "My Submodule"
folderType: "submodule"
## inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md  ← DELETE THIS

Validation Fails on Commit

Problem: Pre-commit hook blocks commit

Solution:

## Run validation manually
npm run mx:validate

## Fix errors shown
## Then retry commit
git commit -m "message"

Field Has Unexpected Value

Problem: A field in a .mx.yaml.md file has an unexpected value after inheritance

Diagnosis:

## Compute effective values to see resolved state
npm run mx:effective --dir <path>

## Review the effective value file
cat <path>/.mx.effective.yaml

## Check parent chain
cd <path>
cat ../.mx.yaml.md  # Parent
cat ../../../.mx.yaml.md  # Grandparent

Common causes:

  1. Parent defines field in mx:inheritable: Check parent's mx:inheritable list
  2. Value being overridden by ancestor: Walk up chain to find override point
  3. Repository boundary crossed: Submodules start fresh inheritance chains
  4. Field name mismatch: Check that field paths match exactly (e.g., ai.assistance not mx.ai.assistance)

Solution: Use .mx.effective.yaml to trace inheritance chain and identify the source of the value.

Best Practices

1. Keep Narratives Current

Update narratives when folder purpose changes:

## After major refactoring
$EDITOR docs/guides/.mx.yaml.md
## Update "Purpose and Role" section

2. Document Relationships

When folders work together, document it:

relatedFolders:
  - path: "../build-scripts"
    relationship: "depends-on"
    description: "Build scripts generate content from this folder"

3. Use Inheritance

Don't duplicate parent fields:

## Good - inherit from parent
inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md
## Only override what's different
mx:
  domain: "specific-subdomain"

## Bad - duplicating everything from parent
## (wastes space, creates maintenance burden)

4. Review on PR

Check .mx.yaml.md files in pull requests:

  • New folders should have .mx.yaml.md
  • Deleted folders should remove .mx.yaml.md
  • Renamed folders should move .mx.yaml.md

5. Validate Before Commit

Always run validation:

npm run mx:validate
git add .
git commit -m "Add feature"

6. Review Effective Values After Inheritance Changes

After modifying mx:inheritable fields or inheritance chains, always review the effective values:

## Compute effective values
npm run mx:effective

## Review changes
git diff **/.mx.effective.yaml

## Validate that inheritance produces expected results
npm run mx:validate

This check confirms that changes to inheritance configuration produce the intended results across all child folders.

Examples

Example 1: Documentation Folder

---
title: "User Guides"
description: "Step-by-step tutorials and how-to guides"
purpose: "Provide practical tutorials for using MX tools and understanding concepts"
audience: ["humans", "machines"]

created: "2026-01-15"
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
modified: "2026-02-03"

stability: "stable"
status: "active"
lifecycle: "production"

inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md

relatedFolders:
  - path: "../reference"
    relationship: "coordinates-with"
    description: "Guides provide tutorials, reference provides quick lookups"

dependencies: []

mx:
  version: "1.0"
  contentType: "folder-metadata"
  domain: "guides"

  ai:
    aiAssistance: "welcome"
    aiEditable: true
    generation:
      allowed: true
      reviewRequired: true

folderType: "content"
primaryLanguages: ["markdown"]
hasSubfolders: true
---

## User Guides

### Purpose and Role

This folder contains step-by-step tutorials and how-to guides for both human developers and AI agents. Unlike reference documentation (quick lookups) or architecture docs (design rationale), guides focus on practical, task-oriented learning.

Following the MX principle of Design for Both, guides use clear structure, explicit steps, and examples that work equally well for statistical pattern-matching systems and human comprehension.

### How to Use This Folder

Create new guides by copying the template from `templates/guide-template.md`. Each guide should:
- Have clear numbered steps
- Include practical examples
- Explain the "why" not just the "what"
- Tag with appropriate audience metadata

### Architecture Context

Guides complement other documentation:
- `/docs/reference/` - Quick reference lookups
- `/docs/architecture/` - Design decisions and rationale
- Guides - Practical tutorials and workflows

### For AI Agents

When reading guides, follow numbered steps sequentially. Examples are tested and should work as-is. Cross-references are explicit - check relatedFolders for related context.

Example 2: Build Scripts Folder

---
title: "Build Automation Scripts"
description: "Node.js and Bash scripts for build automation"
purpose: "Provide reusable scripts for content generation, validation, and repository operations"
audience: ["humans", "machines"]

created: "2026-01-01"
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
modified: "2026-02-03"

stability: "stable"
status: "active"
lifecycle: "production"

inherits: ../.mx.yaml.md

relatedFolders:
  - path: "../mx-config"
    relationship: "depends-on"
    description: "Scripts use configuration from mx-config"

dependencies:
  - type: "runtime"
    target: "Node.js 20+"
    description: "Scripts require Node.js runtime"

mx:
  version: "1.0"
  contentType: "folder-metadata"
  domain: "build-automation"

  ai:
    aiAssistance: "welcome"
    aiEditable: true
    generation:
      allowed: true
      reviewRequired: false  # Scripts don't need review

folderType: "build"
primaryLanguages: ["javascript", "bash"]
hasSubfolders: true
---

## Build Automation Scripts

### Purpose and Role

Contains automation scripts for content generation, validation, and repository management. Scripts follow Node.js best practices: prefer built-ins, clear error handling, consistent patterns.

All scripts are accessible via npm commands defined in package.json. Run `npm run` to see available commands.

### How to Use This Folder

Scripts are invoked through npm:
```bash
npm run mx:generate    # Generate .mx.yaml.md files
npm run mx:validate    # Validate metadata

Architecture Context

Scripts coordinate between source content, configuration, and output destinations. They never modify source - only read and transform.

For AI Agents

Scripts are AI-editable without review requirements. Maintain consistent patterns, document purpose in JSDoc, prefer Node.js built-ins over dependencies.


---

### Further Reading

- **MX Principles:** Core MX philosophy
- **Repository Structure:** How structure embodies MX principles

## 24. Book & Manuscript Frontmatter Template

*Required and optional fields for book chapters and manuscript pages.*

*Source: formerly `mx-canon/ssot/templates/frontmatter-yaml-guide.md` (retained as a stub).*


## YAML Frontmatter Template for Book Manuscripts

### Standard Template for All Book Chapters

```yaml
---
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
date: "YYYY-MM-DD"
description: "Brief chapter summary (1-2 sentences)"
tags: [keyword1, keyword2, keyword3]
book: "MX: The Protocols"  # or "MX: The Handbook"
chapter: N
wordCount: NNNN
runbook: |
  This is a book manuscript chapter. Write as if it has always existed.
  NEVER include: publication dates, "we added", "new feature", "launching",
  "this update", or any meta-commentary about the book's development.
  Write definitive present tense. Historical context about subject matter
  (industry events, product launches) is allowed.
---

## Chapter N: Chapter Title

Note: The H1 heading stays in the markdown content, NOT in the YAML frontmatter. This avoids MD025 (multiple H1) linting errors.

Note on numbers: quote any string value written in digits. YAML parses an unquoted version: 1.0 as the number 1; the trailing zero is gone before any reader sees it. wordCount: 4750 stays a number because it IS one. The rule: fields the dictionary types as strings take quotes when the value looks numeric (version: "1.0", but chapter: 7 stays unquoted because chapter is typed as a number). MX validators flag a string-typed field holding a bare number as a number-string warning.

Field Descriptions

Required Fields

author: Always "Tom Cranstoun"

date: Last modification date in ISO format

  • Format: "YYYY-MM-DD"
  • Example: "2026-01-22"
  • Update whenever file content changes

description: Brief chapter summary

  • 1-2 sentences
  • Describes chapter purpose and scope
  • Example: "Explores patterns that need improvement for AI agents and shows how these same patterns affect users with disabilities"

keywords: Array of relevant topics

  • 3-8 keywords
  • Lowercase unless proper nouns
  • Example: [ai-agents, web-accessibility, semantic-html, schema-org]

book: Which book this chapter belongs to

  • Values: "MX: The Protocols" or "MX: The Handbook"
  • Use exact book title
  • Use "Shared" for Chapter 0 and shared content

chapter: Chapter number (integer or letter)

  • Examples: 0, 1, 2, 3, or "A", "B" for appendices
  • Use 0 for preface/Chapter 0

wordcount: Approximate word count (integer)

  • Update after major edits
  • Use wc -w filename.md to calculate
  • Example: 4750

runbook: CRITICAL: MUST BE INCLUDED

  • Multi-line string using | YAML syntax
  • Contains the timeless manuscript rule
  • Copy exactly from template above
  • This field ensures AI systems understand writing constraints

Optional Fields

longdescription: Extended chapter summary (paragraph length)

  • Use for complex chapters needing more context
  • Example: See Chapter 0 frontmatter

purpose: Intended use or goal of the chapter

  • Example: "Educational content introducing AI agents concept"

status: Draft status indicator

  • Values: draft, review, ready, published
  • Omit if not tracking status

Examples

Chapter 0 (Shared across books)

---
author: "Tom Cranstoun"
date: "2026-01-22"
description: "Understanding AI agents as machines with technical capabilities and limitations that parallel human disabilities"
tags: [ai-agents, web-accessibility, metadata, semantic-html]
book: "Shared"
chapter: 0
wordCount: 4750
runbook: |
  This is a book manuscript chapter. Write as if it has always existed.

## Appendix A: AI-Friendly HTML Patterns Cookbook

Implementation Checklist

When adding frontmatter to existing files:

  1. Place at very top: Before any other content (before any \newpage commands)
  2. Include all required fields: See list above
  3. Copy runbook exactly: From template
  4. Keep H1 in content: Do NOT duplicate title in YAML frontmatter (avoids redundancy)
  5. Calculate wordcount: Use wc -w filename.md
  6. Set correct book value: Protocols or Handbook (or "Shared")
  7. Update date field: Use ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD)
  8. Write clear description: 1-2 sentences summarizing chapter
  9. Choose relevant keywords: 3-8 keywords covering main topics

Validation

After adding frontmatter:

npx js-yaml path/to/file.md

## Run markdown linting (should pass with frontmatter)
npx markdownlint -c .markdownlint-cli2.jsonc path/to/file.md

wc -w path/to/file.md

25. Carrier Format Metadata Map

How MX metadata lands in non-markdown carriers: shell, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, binary sidecars, and XMP.

Source: formerly mx-canon/ssot/writing-guides/carrier-format-metadata.md (retained as a stub).

Carrier Format Metadata

Non-markdown files carry MX metadata too. The field dictionary Sections 12.1-12.9 define carrier formats for every file type in the repo.

Carrier formats by file type

Carrier Format Required
Shell (.sh) # --- YAML block with # prefix title, description, status, author
JavaScript (.js) JSDoc /** */ with @mx:* tags @description + @version/@author + one @mx:* tag
HTML (.html) <meta name="mx:*"> in <head> description + author + one <meta name="mx:*">
CSS (.css) Comment /* */ with @mx:* tags @description + @version/@author + one @mx:* tag
Markdown (.md) YAML frontmatter (---) Two-zone model - see frontmatter.md
JSON (.json, .mxprov.json, the provenance sidecars) A root mx object carrying the frontmatter fields; a JSON payload has no second zone, so identity, OKF and governance fields sit together in it title, description, type, canonicalUri (see §22.R for the provenance record)

The specification version in every carrier

mxSpecVersion (§22.AF) keeps one spelling in every carrier, like every MX name:

Carrier Form
Markdown, .mx.yaml.md, shell # --- header mxSpecVersion: "0.9" inside mx:
JavaScript, CSS @mx:mxSpecVersion 0.9
HTML <meta name="mx:mxSpecVersion" content="0.9">, and in the MX-SOURCE-FRONTMATTER block
JSON (provenance sidecars and other payloads) "mxSpecVersion": "0.9" in the root mx object
PDF and image XMP mx:mxSpecVersion in the MX namespace

Compliance tooling

npm run audit:carrier              # Audit all carriers, generate compliance report
node scripts/fix-carrier-metadata.js          # Remediate missing metadata (dry run)
node scripts/fix-carrier-metadata.js --apply  # Apply metadata fixes

Report output: mx-outputs/md/reports/validation/carrier-format-audit.md
