26. HTML Carrier Writing Guide

HTML carrier layers: document fundamentals, Open Graph, Twitter Card, robots and discovery, MX carrier tags.

Source: formerly mx-canon/ssot/mx-html-writing-guide.cog.md (retained as a stub).

MX HTML Writing Guide

Single source of truth for writing HTML <head> metadata for MX. Every HTML page published under the MX umbrella follows this guide. When it conflicts with any other document, this guide wins.

Authority chain: This guide > Appendix D (AI-Friendly HTML Guide) > Appendix L (Proposed AI Metadata Patterns) > individual page implementations.

Field definitions: All field names referenced here are defined in mx-canon/ssot/fields.cog.md. Do not invent fields.

Foundational Principle: Standards Hierarchy

Everything that benefits SEO, GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation), accessibility, and usability also benefits MX. These disciplines share a common goal: making web content explicit, structured, and unambiguous. MX builds on their foundations.

The hierarchy:

  1. Established web standards come first. HTML semantics, WCAG accessibility, Schema.org structured data, Open Graph, Dublin Core, robots.txt, sitemap.xml. Use these as the primary building blocks. They are widely supported, well-documented, and understood by the broadest range of agents and tools.
  2. MX adds value where standards leave gaps. MX carrier tags (mx:status, mx:contentType, mx:contentPolicy) provide governance and lifecycle metadata that no existing standard covers. This is where MX earns its place.
  3. MX never duplicates or replaces established standards. If Schema.org already expresses a fact, do not restate it in an MX tag. If WCAG already mandates a pattern, follow WCAG; do not invent an MX equivalent.

In practice: A well-built MX page is also a well-built SEO page, a well-built accessible page, and a well-built GEO page. The standards reinforce each other. MX is the final layer that adds machine governance on top of an already-solid foundation.

Core Principle: No Duplication

Every meta tag must contribute information that is not already present elsewhere in the HTML. If a tag restates what the DOM, Schema.org JSON-LD, HTTP headers, or another meta tag already says, remove it. Duplication wastes agent context windows and creates maintenance drift: the two values will eventually disagree.

The test: For each tag, ask: "If I remove this, does the agent lose information it cannot get from another source on this page?" If the answer is no, remove the tag.

The Meta Tag Stack

Tags are listed in the order they should appear in <head>. Each section states whether it is required, recommended, or optional.

Layer 1: Document Fundamentals (Required)

Every HTML page must include these. No exceptions.

<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
<title>Page Title - Site Name</title>
<meta name="description" content="One sentence. Maximum 160 characters. Substantive, not restating the title.">
<meta name="author" content="Tom Cranstoun">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://allabout.network/path/to/page.html">

Rules:

  • viewport must never include user-scalable=no. Preventing zoom is an accessibility violation (WCAG 1.4.4). Omit user-scalable entirely; the browser default is yes, and including it explicitly triggers linting warnings in Edge DevTools.
  • description must differ from title. If they say the same thing, the description is redundant.
  • canonical must be the full absolute URL, not a relative path.
  • author is the human author, not the AI assistant.
  • lang="en-GB" goes on the <html> element, not as a meta tag.

Layer 2: Open Graph (Required for Public Pages)

Open Graph tags control how the page appears when shared on social platforms. AI agents also read these for page summaries.

<meta property="og:type" content="article">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://allabout.network/path/to/page.html">
<meta property="og:title" content="Page Title">
<meta property="og:description" content="Same as meta description.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://allabout.network/images/page-card.jpg">
<meta property="og:image:alt" content="Description of what the image shows.">
<meta property="og:image:width" content="1200">
<meta property="og:image:height" content="630">
<meta property="og:site_name" content="allabout.network">
<meta property="og:locale" content="en_GB">

Rules:

  • og:image:alt is mandatory. Never publish an Open Graph image without alt text.
  • og:image must use PNG or JPG format, never WebP. Social platforms, search engines, and AI agents that read Open Graph metadata expect PNG or JPG. WebP is for <img> tags only. Keep the original PNG/JPG files alongside any WebP conversions.
  • og:description should match <meta name="description">. One source of truth for the page summary.
  • Use og:type values that match the content: article for blog posts, website for landing pages, product for product pages.
  • For articles, add article:published_time and article:author:
<meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-03-04">
<meta property="article:author" content="Tom Cranstoun">

Layer 3: Twitter Card (Required for Public Pages)

The redundancy is intentional: some platforms read only Twitter Card tags, not Open Graph. This is acceptable duplication.

<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="Page Title">
<meta name="twitter:description" content="Same as meta description.">
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://allabout.network/images/page-card.jpg">
<meta name="twitter:image:alt" content="Description of what the image shows.">
<meta name="twitter:site" content="@tomcranstoun">

Rules:

  • twitter:image:alt is mandatory.
  • twitter:image must use PNG or JPG format, never WebP. Same rule as og:image.
  • twitter:url is unnecessary; Twitter reads the canonical URL from the page. Do not include it.

Layer 4: Robots and Discovery (Recommended)

<meta name="robots" content="index, follow">
<link rel="llms-txt" href="/llms.txt">

Rules:

  • Only include robots if the value differs from the default (index, follow). If you want the default behaviour, omit the tag entirely.
  • Use <link rel="llms-txt"> (not <meta name="llms-txt">). Link elements are the standard mechanism for pointing to related resources.
  • Do NOT include <meta name="keywords">. No major search engine or AI agent uses this tag. It is noise.

Layer 5: MX Carrier Tags (Required for MX Ecosystem Pages)

MX carrier tags identify the page within MX. They follow the mx: namespace defined by The Gathering.

<meta name="mx:status" content="active">
<meta name="mx:contentType" content="blog-post">

Required MX tags:

Tag Values Purpose
mx:status draft, active, published, deprecated Page lifecycle state
mx:contentType blog-post, article, product, guide, reference, landing-page, document What this page is

Optional MX tags (include only when the value is meaningful for this specific page):

Tag Values Purpose
mx:category mx-core, capability, integration, content-specific category Domain classification
mx:tags Comma-separated kebab-case identifiers Discovery keywords
mx:partOf Collection or suite name Parent relationship
mx:audience humans, ai-agents, developers, investors Target reader
mx:contentPolicy summaries-allowed, full-extraction-allowed, extract-with-attribution, no-extraction, restricted Per-page content usage rules for AI agents; the carrier form of the contentPolicy field
mx:attribution required, requested, not-required Whether citing this page requires attribution; the carrier form of the attribution field

Tag normalisation. Tags declared in cog frontmatter are normalised at export time to a canonical reduced set. Three classes of variant are collapsed: plural/singular pairs (cogs to cog, hooks to hook, etc.), semantic near-duplicates (verification to validation, orchestration to automation, etc.), and hyphenation variants (opengraph to open-graph). The source cog is never rewritten; the normalisation runs at query time. The canonical tag list is mx-canon/ssot/registries/registry-tags.json (generated by npm run tags:export); synonym groups for search-intent expansion are in mx-canon/ssot/registries/graph-synonyms.yaml. This means a cog tagged verification is discoverable by a graph query for validation once both are mapped in the synonym groups.

Critical rule: MX tags must match the content.

Do NOT copy-paste a standard block of MX tags onto every page. Each tag value must reflect the actual page:

  • A blog post about MX principles is mx:contentType="blog-post", NOT mx:contentType="document"
  • A blog post is NOT mx:partOf="mx-os", because it is not part of the operating system
  • A blog post's tags should describe its content, NOT be mx:tags="tool"
  • If a tag does not apply to this page, omit it

Wrong (copy-pasted boilerplate):

<meta name="mx:category" content="mx-tools">
<meta name="mx:status" content="active">
<meta name="mx:contentType" content="document">
<meta name="mx:tags" content="tool">
<meta name="mx:partOf" content="mx-os">

Correct (content-specific):

<meta name="mx:status" content="published">
<meta name="mx:contentType" content="blog-post">
<meta name="mx:tags" content="machine-experience, metadata, ai-agents">

Layer 6: Schema.org JSON-LD (Required for Content Pages)

Structured data is the primary mechanism for communicating facts to AI agents. Use the most specific Schema.org type that matches the content.

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "BlogPosting",
  "headline": "Page Title",
  "description": "Same as meta description.",
  "author": {
    "@type": "Person",
    "name": "Tom Cranstoun",
    "url": "https://allabout.network"
  },
  "datePublished": "2026-03-04",
  "dateModified": "2026-03-04",
  "inLanguage": "en-GB",
  "url": "https://allabout.network/path/to/page.html",
  "publisher": {
    "@type": "Organization",
    "name": "CogNovaMX Ltd"
  }
}
</script>

Type selection:

Content Schema.org Type
Blog post BlogPosting
Technical article TechArticle
FAQ page FAQPage
Product page Product
Event listing Event
Book or appendix Book or Chapter
Organization page Organization
Person page Person

Rules:

  • dateModified and datePublished must match actual dates. These replace the need for any "freshness" meta tag.
  • author in JSON-LD is the canonical author declaration. The <meta name="author"> tag is a fallback for agents that do not parse JSON-LD.
  • Do NOT duplicate JSON-LD facts in meta tags. If the author is in JSON-LD, that is sufficient.
  • image URLs in JSON-LD must use PNG or JPG format, never WebP. Search engines and AI agents that parse JSON-LD expect widely compatible formats. Same rule as og:image and twitter:image. WebP is for <img> tags in the visible DOM only.

Layer 7: Stylesheets (Required)

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/style.css">

Rules:

  • External stylesheets only. Zero inline style="..." attributes in the <body>. Zero <style> blocks in the <body>. See Appendix D Part 13 for rationale.
  • If an element must start hidden and be revealed by JavaScript, use a CSS class (e.g. .hidden { display: none; }) rather than style="display: none;".
  • One <style> block in <head> is acceptable for critical CSS.
  • All asset paths must be root-anchored. See "Asset Path Anchoring" below.

Asset Path Anchoring (Required)

Every in-page asset reference must begin with / (root-anchored) or a full URL. Relative paths like css/style.css, images/logo.webp, or ../js/app.js are forbidden.

Why: A page may be served at a URL its author did not anticipate. The most common case is a custom 404 page: the worker serves /404.html for /blogs/, but the browser resolves the relative css/style.css against the request URL (/blogs/css/style.css) and gets a 404. The page loads as unstyled markup. Humans see broken text. AI agents see broken images and missing stylesheets. The same failure happens to any templated page reused across URL depths, any page reached via redirect, and any page extracted to a different mount point.

This is the in-page sibling of Context-Preserving References in principles.cog.md, which governs links between documents; this rule governs the assets a single document needs to render itself. See Root-Anchored Asset Paths for the full statement.

The rule applies to every fetching attribute:

<!-- Correct: root-anchored -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/style.css">
<script src="/js/app.js"></script>
<img src="/images/logo.webp"
     srcset="/images/logo.webp 1x, /images/logo@2x.webp 2x"
     alt="Site logo">

<!-- Wrong: relative -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/style.css">
<script src="js/app.js"></script>
<img src="images/logo.webp" srcset="images/logo.webp 1x">

Covers: <link href>, <script src>, <img src>, <img srcset>, <source src>, <source srcset>, <video src>, <video poster>, <audio src>, <iframe src>, <object data>, <embed src>, <input type="image" src>, and CSS url(...) references in any inline <style> block.

The only exception: a self-contained demo bundle: a directory containing one HTML file alongside its own style.css, script.js, and images, with no references back to the parent site. These are deliberately portable and the relative paths are part of the design (the bundle can be copied anywhere and still work). Document the bundle's self-contained nature in its mx: metadata.

The test: copy any HTML file to a different URL depth (/, /foo/, /foo/bar/) and load it. If anything visible breaks, the asset paths are not anchored.

Body Rules (Required)

These rules apply to markup within <body>. They affect accessibility, agent comprehension, and validator compliance.

Zero Inline Styles

No style="..." attributes in <body>. Extract all presentation to CSS classes. This is a hard rule, not a suggestion.

Common extraction patterns:

Inline style pattern CSS class replacement
Layout containers (max-width, margin: auto) .container-narrow, .container-mid, .container-form
Flex button groups (display: flex; gap; justify-content) .cta-group
Form field wrappers (margin-bottom) .form-group
Form inputs (width: 100%; padding; border; font-family) .form-group input/select/textarea
Button variants (background-color; color) .hero__cta--secondary, .btn-full
List indentation (margin-left; line-height) .list-indented, .list-spaced
Section padding (padding; border-radius) .section--padded
Card variants (border; background-color) .card--plain, .card--highlight, .card--hero
Text utilities (color; font-size; white-space) .text-muted, .text-sm, .text-lead, .nowrap

The test: Search the HTML file for style=". If the count is not zero, extract the remaining inline styles to CSS classes before publishing.

Exceptions: SVG style attributes within <svg> elements (stop-color, fill, etc.) are acceptable; these are part of SVG's native styling model.

Form Elements

Every <select>, <input>, and <textarea> must have an accessible name. Use one of these mechanisms (in order of preference):

  1. <label for="id">: a visible label element associated by for/id pairing
  2. aria-label: when a visible label is impractical (e.g. filter dropdowns)
  3. title: fallback for user agents that do not support ARIA

For filter dropdowns without visible labels, use both aria-label and title:

<select id="filter-category" aria-label="Filter by category" title="Filter by category">
  <option value="">All Categories</option>
</select>

Rules:

  • Every <select> must have an accessible name. Validators flag elements without one.
  • The first <option> should describe the purpose (e.g. "All Categories", "Select a country"); this option is also a visible label for sighted users.
  • Do not rely on placeholder text alone for <input> elements; placeholders disappear on focus.

HTML Entities in Prose

Inside the reader's words, write the literal character, not its HTML entity. This applies to article body text, the meta description, the Open Graph and Twitter equivalents, the JSON-LD description value, the <title>, heading text, alt text, button labels, link text, author bios, and all <p>, <li>, <blockquote>, and <figcaption> content.

The principle: prose conveys the message; entities get in the way of it. A straight quote (") costs one byte and one token in every reader. Its typographic cousin (" or ") costs three bytes in UTF-8 and often multiple tokens. The named entity (&ldquo; or &rdquo;) costs seven characters of source and adds cognitive overhead for anyone reading it. The numeric form (&#8220;) is the same character through a longer spelling. The same logic applies across the typographic family.

Banned inside prose:

Entity Use instead
&ldquo; &rdquo; &lsquo; &rsquo; Straight " and '
&mdash; &ndash; Comma, semicolon, colon, parentheses, or rephrase - em-dashes are banned on every MX surface
&hellip; ...
&nbsp; A regular space, or restructure the sentence
&apos; Straight '

Numeric character references (&#8220;, &#8217;, &#8230;) are equivalent to the named forms above and equally banned in prose.

Allowed where structurally required (plumbing, not prose):

  • &amp; inside URL query strings (href="page.html?a=1&amp;b=2")
  • &lt; and &gt; when source code is being displayed as text inside <pre> or <code>
  • Layout glyphs in site chrome that are not the message: &copy; in a footer, &middot; as a visual separator in an article-meta row, &#9776; for a hamburger menu button
  • Any entity inside <script>, <style>, or attribute values where the spec requires it

The principle is no entities inside the reader's content. Where the entity carries plumbing rather than meaning, leave it alone.

The test: strip <script>, <style>, <code>, and <pre> content from the page, then every remaining tag. Search what is left for any of the banned entities. Zero matches is the only passing condition. If a renderer wants to curl your quotes or convert your ... into … at display time, that is the renderer's job, not the source's.

HTML Elements and Their MX Counterparts

HTML gives a machine signal in the <head> carrier (meta tags and link relations) and in the semantic elements and attributes of the body. MX frontmatter is document-level, so the comparison asks of each HTML signal: what does a machine learn from it, and which MX field holds the same fact when the document is not HTML. Where the answer is a field, the HTML form is its carrier and the two must agree. Where the answer is "the body", the semantic stays in the prose block; MX does not restate structure a reader can parse from the content.

Head carrier: meta tags and link relations

HTML signal What a machine reads from it MX field Carrier note
<html lang> Language of the prose body inLanguage BCP 47 tag; metadata stays neutral English
<title> Document title title
<meta name="description"> One-line summary description Native name, never mx: prefixed
<meta name="author"> Human author author Native name
<link rel="canonical"> Where the authoritative copy lives canonicalUri Must agree with mx:canonicalUri when both are present
<link rel="cite-as"> (RFC 8574) The persistent identifier to cite citeAs Falls back to canonicalUri when absent
<link rel="alternate" type="..."> Another rendering of the same document alternateFormats text/markdown, application/pdf, application/json
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="..."> A translation workTranslation, translationOfWork Translation lineage, not an alternate format
<link rel="license"> Licence terms license, rights SPDX identifier where one exists
<link rel="author">, rel="me" Verified author identity proofOfAuthorship
<link rel="ai-usage"> The publisher's AI usage declaration aiUsageDeclarationUri Per the MX AI Usage Declaration note
<link rel="prev">, rel="next" Reading order within a series partOf, chapter No previous/next pointer field; the collection's own index carries the order
<meta name="robots" content="noindex"> Keep out of indexes doNotIndex
<meta name="robots" content="nosnippet, max-snippet:N"> How much may be excerpted contentPolicy Search-engine form of the reuse policy
<meta name="mx:contentPolicy"> What a machine may do with the content contentPolicy camelCase, the same name as the field
<meta name="mx:attribution"> Whether reuse must credit the source attribution
<meta name="tdm-reservation">, tdm-policy (W3C TDMRep) Text and data mining reservation aiTraining, trainingDataPolicy, aiTrainingConditions aiTraining: prohibited is tdm-reservation set to 1
<meta name="rating"> Audience suitability contentRating Schema.org contentRating in JSON-LD
<meta name="ai-disclosure"> (WICG) AI involvement in producing the page provenanceOrigin Derivation rules in the MX AI Usage Declaration note
<meta name="generator"> The tool that produced the file generatedBy, isGenerated CogNovaMX vendor dictionary
article:published_time, article:modified_time, article:expiration_time (Open Graph) Lifecycle dates publicationDate, modified, expires JSON-LD datePublished and dateModified are the canonical HTML form
article:tag, article:section Discovery keywords, section tags, domain
og:image, og:image:alt Lead image and its description image (vendor), accessibility Open Graph stays the HTML form; MX does not restate it
<script type="application/ld+json"> Structured data ld, schema Embedded Schema.org; never duplicated in mx: tags
<link rel="llms-txt"> Site-level agent guidance none A site pointer, not a property of the document

Body: semantic elements and attributes

HTML signal What a machine reads from it MX field Carrier note
<main>, <article> The document's essence none; the prose block <main> is the essence in the HTML carrier mapping
<h1> to <h6>, <section> Outline none; the body Structure is parsed from the content
<nav>, <a rel="..."> Where to go next, and how links relate relatedTo, refersTo, buildsOn, partOf Link relations at document level
<time datetime> Machine date for a human date created, modified, publicationDate, expires, temporalAnchors A named date the prose depends on is a temporalAnchors entry
<data value> Machine value for a human figure volatileValues Only when the figure moves on its own cadence
<cite>, <blockquote cite>, <q cite> A cited work, or the source of a quoted passage refersToExternal Emitted to the served page as Schema.org citation; corroboration is the separate corroboratedBy, and the quoted passage itself is declared in quotes
<abbr title>, <dfn> Expansion of a term; the defining instance x-mx-domainTerms (vendor) The definition block type carries a formal definition
<address> Contact for the document supportContact, stewardship, publisher
<ins datetime cite>, <del datetime cite> A recorded edit and its reason modified, version, provenancePedigree The change history lives in the pedigree, not in prose
<s> No longer accurate status, stability, supersededBy Document-level retirement
<small> Side comment, legal notice none A disclaimer is prose at its first substantive mention
<figure>, <figcaption>, <img alt>, <track> Media with its description accessibility, the media sidecar .mx.yaml sidecar for the asset itself
<table>, <caption>, <th scope> Tabular data none; CSVW and DCAT Deferred to the tabular standards
<dl>, <dt>, <dd> Term and definition pairs definition block type
<code>, <pre> Code code block type Line annotations are the mx:begin family on code carriers
<details>, <summary> Collapsed content none data-agent-visible keeps it readable by machines
<mark> Relevance highlight none
lang on an element A passage in another language none inLanguage is the body's language; a span keeps its own lang
translate="no" Do not translate this span none Translation lineage is translationOfWork; no per-span field
itemscope, itemprop, itemtype Structured data on the element ld, entities itemprop="mentions" is the element form of entities
role, aria-*, DPUB-ARIA doc-* roles Accessibility and document-part roles accessibility, type, appendix, chapter doc-abstract is summary; doc-bibliography is refersToExternal
data-mx-action, data-mx-effect, data-mx-security What an element does when activated, what that changes, and how dangerous it is execute.actions[].id, effect, security The html-element carrier context; see Declaring an Action on the Element
data-* Application state none Element state is not a property of the document

Three rules follow from the tables. A signal that has a field is carried in HTML by the native element or the mx: tag named in the row, and the two forms agree or the page is ambiguous. A signal with no field stays in the body on purpose: MX describes the document, and a machine that can parse HTML reads the outline, the tables, and the highlights from the content itself. An element that acts is the exception to reading from the content: what it changes is never parsed from its label, so it declares the action itself.

Declaring an Action on the Element

Reading a page wrongly costs a citation. Using a page wrongly costs a booking, a payment, or a message that cannot be recalled. A button labelled "Cancel" may cancel a form, a booking, or a subscription, and a machine that infers which one is guessing. So an element a person or agent activates (a button, a link, a form) carries its action declaration at the point of use, in three attributes:

  • data-mx-action: the action's id, the same value as execute.actions[].id in an action-cog. Case-sensitive.
  • data-mx-effect: the effect field, what doing it changes, in plain words.
  • data-mx-security: the security block, written as name: value pairs separated by semicolons, spelled as the open standard spells them (riskLevel, reversibility, guardrail). A value with no colon names a profile from securityProfiles.

HTML lowercases attribute names, so a camelCase name cannot survive there: data-mx-riskLevel reaches a reader as data-mx-risklevel. Each attribute name is one lowercase word, and the camelCase names travel in the value, where case is kept. The field keeps one spelling in every carrier.

<button data-mx-action="cancelBooking"
  data-mx-effect="Cancels the booking and refunds 40 GBP to the card used"
  data-mx-security="riskLevel: critical; reversibility: irreversible; guardrail: human-approval">
  Cancel booking
</button>

The same declaration in an action-cog:

execute:
  actions:
    - id: cancelBooking
      name: Cancel booking
      effect: Cancels the booking and refunds 40 GBP to the card used
      security:
        riskLevel: critical
        reversibility: irreversible
        guardrail: human-approval

A reader that meets an element which acts and carries no data-mx-action treats it as one it may not use unattended. A reader that meets guardrail: human-approval shows the human the effect and waits for an explicit go-ahead. The declaration is a statement that honest agents honour, not an enforcement; the site still checks every request on the server.

Deprecated Tags - Do NOT Include

These tags duplicate information available from other sources. Do not include them.

Deprecated Tag Why It Is Redundant Replacement
ai-preferred-access="html" Redundant. If you are serving HTML, it is self-evident. Remove entirely.
ai-freshness="monthly" Duplicates HTTP Cache-Control headers and Schema.org dateModified. Use dateModified in JSON-LD.
ai-structured-data="json-ld" Self-evident. The JSON-LD <script> block is present on the page. Remove entirely.
ai-content-policy (with ai- prefix) Belongs in mx: namespace. Use mx:contentPolicy if per-page policy is needed.
ai-attribution (with ai- prefix) Belongs in mx: namespace. Use mx:attribution if attribution is required.
<meta name="llms-txt"> Meta tags are for metadata. Resource links use <link>. Use <link rel="llms-txt" href="/llms.txt">.
<meta name="keywords"> No search engine or AI agent uses this tag. Remove entirely.
<meta name="X-Robots-Tag"> This is an HTTP header, not a meta tag. Configure on the server.
<meta name="theme-color"> Browser chrome color. Not relevant to AI agents or MX. Not supported by Firefox or Opera. Remove. If needed for a PWA, add it in the web app manifest instead.

If you encounter ai-* tags in existing pages:

  1. Remove ai-preferred-access, ai-freshness, ai-structured-data; they are unnecessary.
  2. Use mx:contentPolicy with the same value (the ai-content-policy form is deprecated).
  3. Use mx:attribution="required". The text="..." attribute is unnecessary; the Schema.org author field provides the attribution text.
  4. Use <link rel="llms-txt" href="/llms.txt"> (the <meta name="llms-txt"> form is incorrect).

Complete Template

Copy this template for new pages. Replace all placeholder values with content-specific values.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en-GB">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>PAGE TITLE - SITE NAME</title>
  <meta name="author" content="Tom Cranstoun">
  <meta name="description" content="ONE SENTENCE SUMMARY. MAX 160 CHARS.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://allabout.network/PATH">

  <!-- Open Graph -->
  <meta property="og:type" content="TYPE">
  <meta property="og:url" content="https://allabout.network/PATH">
  <meta property="og:title" content="PAGE TITLE">
  <meta property="og:description" content="SAME AS META DESCRIPTION">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://allabout.network/images/CARD.jpg">
  <meta property="og:image:alt" content="IMAGE DESCRIPTION">
  <meta property="og:image:width" content="1200">
  <meta property="og:image:height" content="630">
  <meta property="og:site_name" content="SITE NAME">
  <meta property="og:locale" content="en_GB">

  <!-- Twitter Card -->
  <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
  <meta name="twitter:title" content="PAGE TITLE">
  <meta name="twitter:description" content="SAME AS META DESCRIPTION">
  <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://allabout.network/images/CARD.jpg">
  <meta name="twitter:image:alt" content="IMAGE DESCRIPTION">
  <meta name="twitter:site" content="@tomcranstoun">

  <!-- Discovery -->
  <link rel="llms-txt" href="/llms.txt">

  <!-- MX Carrier (only tags that apply to THIS page) -->
  <meta name="mx:status" content="STATUS">
  <meta name="mx:contentType" content="CONTENT-TYPE">

  <!-- Schema.org -->
  <script type="application/ld+json">
  {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "SCHEMA_TYPE",
    "headline": "PAGE TITLE",
    "description": "SAME AS META DESCRIPTION",
    "author": {
      "@type": "Person",
      "name": "Tom Cranstoun",
      "url": "https://allabout.network"
    },
    "datePublished": "YYYY-MM-DD",
    "dateModified": "YYYY-MM-DD",
    "inLanguage": "en-GB",
    "url": "https://allabout.network/PATH",
    "publisher": {
      "@type": "Organization",
      "name": "CogNovaMX Ltd"
    }
  }
  </script>

  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/style.css">
</head>

Checklist Before Publishing

  1. Does viewport omit user-scalable=no? (Accessibility: browser defaults to yes)
  2. Does every tag contribute unique information? (No duplication test)
  3. Do MX carrier tags match this specific page's content? (No boilerplate)
  4. Does og:image:alt and twitter:image:alt describe the image? (Accessibility)
  5. Does description differ from title? (Substantive test)
  6. Are dates in JSON-LD accurate? (Freshness)
  7. Is the Schema.org type the most specific match? (Type selection)
  8. Are there zero ai-* prefixed tags? (Deprecated)
  9. Are there zero theme-color meta tags? (Deprecated)
  10. Are there zero inline styles in <body>? (CSS separation)
  11. Does every <select> and <input> have an accessible name? (Form accessibility)
  12. Does every asset path (href, src, srcset) begin with / or a full URL? (Asset path anchoring)

27. Canon Layout - Split by Role

The machine-readable MX field dictionary is split by role across sibling files in mx-site/canon/, published at https://mx.allabout.network/canon/. This section explains what each file owns, why the split exists, and how tooling merges them.

Why the split

Publishing a single monolithic dictionary conflated several different contracts. A reader of The Gathering's open standard had to wade through CogNovaMX-specific audit scoring, CRM pipeline fields, aspirational AI-policy vocabulary, and cog-specific structural fields to find the core document-identity primitives. The split separates concerns:

  • Standard core (document metadata): part of the open standard; what any MX-aware file needs (identity, classification, relationships, pass-through fields).
  • Cog layer: part of the open standard; the optional vocabulary a .cog.md file declares to be navigable, composable, and runnable. Documents that are not cogs do not need any of this.
  • Carriers companion: part of the open standard; adds code-carrier provenance vocabulary.
  • CogNovaMX extensions: owned by CogNovaMX; vendor fields (both openly published and private-operational).
  • Workflow vocabulary: owned by CogNovaMX; process-state fields for tooling artefacts that borrow frontmatter syntax. Neither part of the standard nor a vendor extension to the content vocabulary.

File inventory

File Owner Fields Scope
mx-site/canon/fields-data.yaml The Gathering core Open standard core - document identity, classification, relationships, lifecycle, machine-readability infrastructure, folder metadata, non-YAML markup carriers (mx:*, mx-*), Dublin Core / Schema.org pass-through fields (date, duration, format, rights, displayName, usage, url), namespacePolicy, deprecations, validationPolicy, blockTypes, carrierFormats. No cog content.
mx-site/canon/fields-data-cogs.yaml The Gathering cog layer Cog-specific structural fields (partOf, buildsOn, dependencies, refersTo, cogHeader) plus the cog profile composition. Cogs are an OPTIONAL layer over MX; documents that are not cogs do not declare any of these.
mx-site/canon/fields-data-carriers.yaml The Gathering carriers Carrier-format companion - code-only provenance (sourceRepo, derivedFromCommit). Databases defer to DCAT and CSVW. Media defers to Schema.org, EXIF, IPTC, and XMP. MX does not duplicate standards that already cover these carriers.
mx-site/canon/cognovamx-fields.yaml CogNovaMX vendor Vendor extensions - x-mx- public (hub-mount pattern, workflow contract extensions, etc.) and x-mx-p- private (CRM pipeline, audit infrastructure, scoring, directors' reports, book pipeline, REGINALD routing, the ai.* aspirational namespace).
mx-site/canon/workflow-fields.yaml CogNovaMX workflow Workflow and process-state vocabulary for tooling artefacts (submission packages, workflow records), grouped into one profile per workflow. Outside the standard and outside the content vocabulary.

External standards MX defers to

The MX framework reuses existing web standards wherever they cover the ground. The standard core includes aligned pass-through fields (see §22 date, duration, format, rights, displayName, schema, usage, classification) that point at their external equivalents rather than redefining them. Specifically:

Concern Defers to
Dataset / data catalog metadata DCAT v3
Data-product description (input and output ports, the product rather than the dataset) Data Product Ontology (DPROD) (OMG, 1.0 beta 1), a profile of DCAT that composes ODRL for rights, PROV for lineage, and DQV for quality. See the external-standards registry.
Tabular / CSV schemas, columns, keys CSVW
Generic resource identity (date, format, rights, language) Dublin Core
Content language tags (inLanguage) BCP 47 / RFC 5646 (the tag Schema.org inLanguage and Dublin Core dc:language both carry)
Currency codes (currency) ISO 4217 (the code Schema.org priceCurrency uses)
Date and time representation ISO 8601 (every machine-read MX date; see §22.Q)
Translation relationships (translationOfWork, workTranslation, translator) Schema.org
Web content vocabulary (images, video, audio, rights, organizations, people) Schema.org
Authorship and publisher (author, publisher) Schema.org. MX defines no separate provenance-authorship field: the retired provenanceAuthor and provenancePublisher duplicated meanings Schema.org already names, and documents carrying both wrote the same value into each. The Zone 1 author field and publisher carry these, and the deprecation entries in the field dictionary map the retired names onto them. OKF defines neither field, so the OKF-first precedence rule is not engaged here.
Audience age band / age range Schema.org (typicalAgeRange; Audience requiredMinAge / suggestedMinAge / suggestedMaxAge). The core field intendedAgeRange is the aligned pass-through mirror.
Embedded media metadata EXIF, IPTC, XMP, ID3
Usage policy: permissions, prohibitions, and duties over an asset (the rights language of a data contract between agents) ODRL Information Model 2.2 (W3C Recommendation). MX carries no rights-language field of its own; a policy travels as ODRL and MX records who published it and whether it is current. See the external-standards registry and the multi-agent read in MX and the Semantic Web.
Content provenance and authenticity across every medium, including text and claim-level provenance C2PA Content Credentials; general provenance graphs defer to W3C PROV-O. MX defers the content-authenticity binding to C2PA for images, audio, video, and text alike (the Gathering accepted the extension to text and claim-level provenance, ADR 50): MX carries a claim about any addressable artefact and may embed or point at a C2PA manifest as its evidence, and the provenancePedigree genuineness field aligns with both (see §22). MX is the layer above C2PA, not a competing primitive: C2PA seals the bytes, MX makes them machine-readable, and REGINALD adds the trust signals a per-file manifest cannot (attestation, currency, freshness and liveness, discovery).
API surface specification OpenAPI
Standards-document authoring IETF RFC format (RFC style guide, title/abbrev/docname/normative/informative frontmatter, --- abstract/--- middle/--- back delimiters)
Accessibility WCAG 2.1, ARIA
Calendar and scheduling data (events, to-dos, recurrence, alarms) iCalendar (RFC 5545). MX carries calendar data as VEVENT / VTODO with X-MX-* provenance extensions rather than inventing a format. See the external-standards registry and the contributor-calendar PRD.
Visual design system / design tokens for coding agents DESIGN.md (Google Labs; machine-readable tokens in YAML front matter plus prose rationale) and the W3C Design Tokens Format Module (DTCG) it exports to. MX interoperates rather than duplicates; a site brand guide authored as a DESIGN.md is agent-readable, and its tokens export to the DTCG format an MX asset can consume. See the external-standards registry.
Agent and capability discovery Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD) (v0.9 draft), over domain-anchored /.well-known/ai-catalog.json manifests and federated registry search. REGINALD participates as a conformant ARD registry rather than duplicating the mesh: ARD discovers agents and capabilities, REGINALD describes and attests content and decisions, and the MX provenance chain feeds ARD's thinner trustManifest. ARD ranks above MX in the field-name precedence rule (OKF first, ARD second, MX third). See the external-standards registry.
Operation semantics for agent-operable interface actions (intent, action type, parameters, preconditions and side effects, risk, confirmation and approval, idempotency, error codes) AXAG (Agent Experience Accessibility Guidelines, v1.0.0, a proposed community standard), declared as reserved axag- HTML attributes that compile to a semantic manifest and MCP tool definitions. The MX actions field names the actions an object card offers and stops there; what an action does when invoked is AXAG's ground, and MX defines no rival vocabulary for it. MX records who published the interface and whether its declarations are current. See the external-standards registry.
Markdown vault frontmatter as an RDF graph Vault-LD (The Knowledge Graph Guys; YAML frontmatter resolved through a shared context.jsonld, wiki links as edges, a lossless projection to RDF and back). MX interoperates rather than duplicates: the format's Appendix B lifts an OKF-style bundle into linked data without modifying a file, and the MX Zone 1b reserved surface is that OKF surface. MX declares its own "@context" - the served context generated from the field dictionary's alignsWith mappings at https://mx.allabout.network/canon/context.json - so the capability is exercised, not merely available. See the external-standards registry and the positioning read in MX and the Semantic Web.
Package manifests package.json (npm), pyproject.toml (Python), equivalents

An MX-aware document describing a dataset, image, API, or package uses those vocabularies directly. MX adds only the governance layer those standards omit (AI-agent policy, cog routing, provenance attribution).

Tooling: the merged view

All compliance and reporting scripts load every dictionary file through a shared canon loader and merge mx.fields[], mx.deprecations[], and mx.profiles into a single view. The governance sections (namespacePolicy, validationPolicy, blockTypes, carrierFormats, overlap-resolution, contentTypeToProfile, defaultsPolicy) are kept in the standard file as the canonical source of truth.

The field validators, drift checks and usage reports all read the merged view.

Run npm run fields:dict for a quick summary (counts per file, plus profile and deprecation totals).

The tier is the file, not the prefix (for now)

The namespace policy specifies that CogNovaMX public extensions carry the x-mx- prefix on the field name itself and private extensions x-mx-p-. Those prefixes are the rule for any new field. Fields that predate the split keep their bare names across all the files; the destination file is the tier marker. This avoids a forced rename of content references in live documents. A later migration can apply the prefix convention retroactively if desired.

Publishing path

The Gathering publishes fields-data.yaml, fields-data-cogs.yaml, and fields-data-carriers.yaml. cognovamx-fields.yaml stays in-repo as an example extension pack; other vendors would author their own parallel files (x-mx-<vendor>-fields.yaml) under the same pattern. The MX draft notes (at ddttom/mx-shared-gathering) reference the standard files:

  • MX Core Metadata note: fields-data.yaml (document metadata + the pass-through fields section)
  • MX Cogs note: fields-data-cogs.yaml (the .cog.md file format as an optional layer; partOf, buildsOn, requires, refersTo, cogHeader)
  • MX Extensions note: governs the vendor namespace. It sets the prefix rule and the levels; it defines no vendor field, because a vendor's fields belong to that vendor's own extension pack. Workflow contract extensions and per-document tooling configuration are the two shapes the namespace is built to carry.
  • MX Carrier Formats note: fields-data-carriers.yaml
  • MX Contract Fingerprinting and Signing note: defines contractFields and metadataFields as first-class top-level fields. Signing is optional; when used, mandatory fields are title, validatesAgainst (with resolvable validators), and schema. REGINALD (proprietary, from CogNovaMX) is one implementation of the open format; reference implementations also exist in mx-upgraded-reginald/ (cog-spec v1.0 uses kebab-case; MX canon adopts camelCase per NDR-02).

Adding a new field - which file?

First ask: does an existing standard already cover this? If Dublin Core, Schema.org, DCAT, CSVW, EXIF, XMP, OpenAPI, WCAG, or ARIA defines the concern, use their vocabulary and do not add to the MX canon. If MX needs to reference the field for governance purposes, add a minimal pass-through entry in the standard core with an alignsWith: pointer (see existing date, format, rights, etc.).

If no existing standard covers the concern:

The field is… Goes to
A universal identity, classification, relationship, or machine-readability primitive that any MX-aware document would use fields-data.yaml (standard core, document metadata)
A field a rendered component carries to its reader (the component family, section 22.AA): any field a human or an agent meets in a rendering is core, never vendor, because the vendor namespace is stripped from every published artefact fields-data.yaml (standard core, component profile)
Specific to the cog file format (registry classification, dependencies, body-block declarations, execute contract, identification) fields-data-cogs.yaml (cog layer)
A code-annotation primitive for functions, classes, APIs, tests, inline annotations, dependencies, or repositories (and no JSDoc / OpenAPI equivalent exists) fields-data-carriers.yaml
Specific to a CogNovaMX workflow, tool, or business process, but visible in published content cognovamx-fields.yaml under the x-mx- public section; add x-mx- prefix to the field name
CogNovaMX operational / confidential (CRM pipeline, audit metrics, AI policy aspirations) cognovamx-fields.yaml under the x-mx-p- private section; add x-mx-p- prefix to the field name
Process state carried by a tooling artefact that borrows frontmatter syntax (a submission act, a build act, a workflow record), not a fact about the document's content workflow-fields.yaml (workflow vocabulary), under the profile for that workflow

Database and media metadata is explicitly not in scope for MX standards. Use DCAT/CSVW/Dublin Core for datasets and tables; Schema.org/EXIF/XMP/ID3 for images, video, audio, and documents.
